abstract: It has been observed in numerical simulations that a weight decay can im(cid:173) prove generalization in a feed-forward neural network. This paper explains why. It is proven that a weight decay has two effects in a linear network. First, it suppresses any irrelevant components of the weight vector by choosing the smallest vector that solves the learning problem. Second, if the size is chosen right, a weight decay can suppress some of the effects of static noise on the targets, which improves generalization quite a lot. It is then shown how to extend these results to networks with hidden layers and non-linear units. Finally the theory is confirmed by some numerical simulations using the data from NetTalk.

paragraphs: The paper explains why encouraging a neural network to keep its weights small can improve predictions on new examples. It begins with linear networks, where the effects of weight decay can be analyzed directly. The analysis separates two benefits that help explain previously observed improvements in numerical experiments.

First, weight decay removes irrelevant components of the weight vector by selecting the smallest vector that solves the learning problem. This means the solution avoids weight components that do not help satisfy the task. Second, a suitably chosen amount of decay reduces some effects of fixed noise in the training targets, improving generalization.

The strength of decay matters to the noise-related benefit: the claim depends on choosing its size appropriately. The paper then extends the results to networks containing hidden layers and nonlinear units, and reports numerical confirmation using NetTalk data. Together, the analysis and simulations explain weight decay through both the removal of unnecessary weight components and reduced sensitivity to noisy target values.
summary.tldr: Weight decay can improve generalization by removing irrelevant weight components and reducing the influence of noisy targets.

title: A Simple Weight Decay Can Improve Generalization

paragraphs: This paper explains how Bayesian model comparison can guide decisions about feedforward neural networks. It distinguishes fitting parameters within a chosen model from comparing different models. That distinction matters because finding suitable weights for a network does not, by itself, determine whether its architecture or regularization choices are appropriate.

The framework incorporates a Bayesian version of Occam’s razor and supports comparisons between solutions using different network architectures. It also provides a basis for choosing both the strength and the form of weight decay, which discourages particular weight configurations during fitting. These choices become parts of a common inference framework rather than unrelated adjustments.

The framework additionally produces uncertainty estimates for network parameters and outputs, along with an effective parameter count reflecting how many parameters the data actually determine. This distinguishes the network’s nominal size from its data-supported complexity. The paper also discusses connections to predicting generalization, bringing model selection, regularization, uncertainty, and effective complexity into one account of neural-network modeling.
summary.tldr: Bayesian model comparison provides a unified approach to network architecture selection, weight decay, uncertainty estimation, and effective model complexity.

title: Bayesian Model Comparison and Backprop Nets

abstract: It is widely accepted that the use of more compact representations than lookup tables is crucial to scaling reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms to real-world problems. Unfortunately almost all of the theory of reinforcement learning assumes lookup table representa(cid:173) tions. In this paper we address the pressing issue of combining function approximation and RL, and present 1) a function approx(cid:173) imator based on a simple extension to state aggregation (a com(cid:173) monly used form of compact representation), namely soft state aggregation, 2) a theory of convergence for RL with arbitrary, but fixed, soft state aggregation, 3) a novel intuitive understanding of the effect of state aggregation on online RL, and 4) a new heuristic adaptive state aggregation algorithm that finds improved compact representations by exploiting the non-discrete nature of soft state aggregation. Preliminary empirical results are also presented.

Preliminary empirical results are also presented.

paragraphs: The paper tackles a gap between reinforcement learning theory and the compact representations needed for larger problems. Lookup tables store information separately for states, but practical learning often requires a smaller representation. The authors investigate how function approximation can be combined with reinforcement learning while retaining a mathematical account of convergence.

Their approximation method extends state aggregation, which groups states to reduce representation size. Soft aggregation makes the grouping non-discrete, allowing a more flexible relationship between states and aggregates. The authors develop convergence theory for arbitrary but fixed soft aggregation and offer an interpretation of how aggregation affects learning as experience arrives.

They also propose a heuristic that adapts the aggregation to find improved compact representations. It exploits the flexibility of soft membership rather than treating grouping as a purely discrete decision. Preliminary empirical results accompany the method. A crucial distinction is that the stated convergence theory applies to fixed aggregation, while the adaptive procedure is presented as a heuristic for improving the representation.
summary.tldr: Soft state aggregation provides compact reinforcement learning representations, convergence theory for fixed groupings, and a heuristic for adapting them.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Soft State Aggregation

However, we often have high-level knowledge about the learning problem. In optical character recognition (OCR), for in(cid:173) stance, we know that the classification should be invariant under a set of transformations like rotation or translation. We propose a new modular classification system based on several autoassociative multilayer percep(cid:173) trons which allows the efficient incorporation of such knowledge. The classical implementation in the domain of neural networks is the backpropagation algorithm. If this learning set is sufficiently representative of the underlying data distributions, one hopes that after learning, the system is able to generalize correctly to other inputs of the same distribution. 992 Holger Schwenk, Maurice Milgram It would be better to have more powerful techniques to incorporate knowledge into the learning process than the choice of a set of examples. The use of additional knowledge is often limited to the feature extraction module. Besides simple operations like (size) normalization, we can find more sophisticated approaches like zernike moments in the domain of optical character recognition (OCR). title: Transformation Invariant Autoassociation with Application to Handwritten Character Recognition

abstract: This paper describes a new technique for object recognition based on learning appearance models. The image is decomposed into local regions which are described by a new texture representation called "Generalized Second Mo(cid:173) ments" that are derived from the output of multiscale, multiorientation filter banks. Class-characteristic local texture features and their global composition is learned by a hierarchical mixture of experts architecture (Jordan & Jacobs). The technique is applied to a vehicle database consisting of 5 general car categories (Sedan, Van with back-doors, Van without back-doors, old Sedan, and Volkswagen Bug). This is a difficult problem with considerable in-class variation. The new technique has a 6.5% misclassification rate, compared to eigen-images which give 17.4% misclassification rate, and nearest neighbors which give 15 .7% misclassification rate.

paragraphs: This paper learns object appearance by combining descriptions of local image regions with their overall arrangement. Each region receives a texture representation called Generalized Second Moments. These descriptors are derived from filters operating at multiple scales and orientations, allowing the representation to describe local appearance from several spatial perspectives.

A hierarchical mixture of experts learns both the local texture features characteristic of a class and how those features compose a whole object. The approach therefore links regional evidence to a global classification decision. Its recognition model is built around learned relationships between local appearance and object category.

The evaluation uses a vehicle database with five categories: sedans, vans with back doors, vans without back doors, old sedans, and Volkswagen Bugs. Despite considerable variation within categories, the method reports a 6.5 percent misclassification rate, compared with 17.4 percent for eigen-images and 15.7 percent for nearest neighbors. These results support the usefulness of the combined texture representation and hierarchical model on the stated recognition task.
summary.tldr: Local texture descriptors and a hierarchical mixture of experts improve recognition across five vehicle categories in the reported comparison.

title: Learning Appearance Based Models: Mixtures of Second Moment Experts

abstract: As already known, the expected return of a policy in Markov Decision Problems is not always the most suitable optimality criterion. For many applications control strategies have to meet various constraints like avoiding very bad states (risk-avoiding) or generating high profit within a short time (risk-seeking) although this might probably cause significant costs. We propose a modified Q-learning algorithm which uses a single continuous parameter κ ∈ [-1, 1] to determine in which sense the resulting policy is optimal. For κ = 0, the policy is optimal with respect to the usual expected return criterion, while κ → 1 generates a solution which is optimal in worst case. Analogous, the closer κ is to -1 the more risk seeking the policy becomes. In contrast to other related approaches in the field of MDPs we do not have to transform the cost model or to increase the state space in order to take risk into account. Our new approach is evaluated by computing optimal investment strategies for an artificial stock market.

paragraphs: This paper modifies Q-learning to account for preferences about risk. Maximizing expected return can be inappropriate when a controller should avoid very bad outcomes or pursue high gains despite possible costs. The proposed method changes the optimality criterion through one continuous parameter, kappa, ranging from minus one to one.

At zero, the parameter recovers the usual expected-return objective. As it approaches one, the resulting solution becomes optimal for the worst case. Moving toward minus one makes the policy increasingly risk-seeking. The parameter therefore provides a single way to adjust the kind of outcome preference expressed by the learned policy.

The approach incorporates risk without transforming the cost model or enlarging the state space. The authors evaluate it by computing investment strategies in an artificial stock market. That application illustrates the intended role of the method: learning policies under different attitudes toward uncertain outcomes while retaining the original cost and state representation of the decision problem.
summary.tldr: A modified Q-learning rule uses one parameter to move between expected-return optimization, worst-case protection, and risk-seeking behavior.

title: Risk Sensitive Reinforcement Learning

abstract: As a benchmark task, the spiral problem is well known in neural net(cid:173) works. Unlike previous work that emphasizes learning, we approach the problem from a generic perspective that does not involve learning. We point out that the spiral problem is intrinsically connected to the in(cid:173) side/outside problem. A generic solution to both problems is proposed based on oscillatory correlation using a time delay network. Our simu(cid:173) lation results are qualitatively consistent with human performance, and we interpret human limitations in terms of synchrony and time delays, both biologically plausible. As a special case, our network without time delays can always distinguish these figures regardless of shape, position, size, and orientation.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the spiral benchmark as a problem of perceptual organization that can be approached without learning. The authors connect it to determining inside/outside relationships. That connection motivates a common solution based on how activity in a network coordinates over time, rather than on training the network to classify examples.

The proposed mechanism uses oscillatory correlation in a network with time delays. Its simulation results agree qualitatively with human performance. The authors interpret human limitations through synchronization and delays, treating these as biologically plausible ingredients. The agreement supports their proposed interpretation at a qualitative level rather than establishing a precise behavioral fit.

A special version of the network removes the time delays. The authors state that this version can always distinguish the figures in question regardless of shape, position, size, or orientation. The contrast between delayed and delay-free versions gives timing a central explanatory role: the same general mechanism can express perceptual limitations with delays and unrestricted discrimination of these figures in the stated special case.
summary.tldr: An oscillatory network connects spiral discrimination with inside/outside perception, using time delays to interpret qualitative human limitations.

title: Perceiving without Learning: From Spirals to Inside/Outside Relations

abstract: Suppose you are given some dataset drawn from an underlying probabil(cid:173) ity distribution P and you want to estimate a "simple" subset S of input space such that the probability that a test point drawn from P lies outside of S equals some a priori specified l/ between 0 and 1. We propose a method to approach this problem by trying to estimate a function f which is positive on S and negative on the complement. The functional form of f is given by a kernel expansion in terms of a poten(cid:173) tially small subset of the training data; it is regularized by controlling the length of the weight vector in an associated feature space. We provide a theoretical analysis of the statistical performance of our algorithm. The algorithm is a natural extension of the support vector algorithm to the case of unlabelled data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a simple region containing most of the probability mass of a data distribution. The target is set by a chosen probability that a new observation falls outside this region. Because the training data are unlabelled, the task is to estimate a boundary from the distribution represented by the examples.

The proposed method learns a function that is positive inside the region and negative outside it. The function takes the form of a kernel expansion using a potentially small subset of training observations. Regularization controls the length of its weight vector in an associated feature space, connecting the desired simplicity of the region to a mathematical constraint on the function.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's statistical performance and present it as an extension of support vector learning to unlabelled data. The prescribed outside probability defines the estimation objective, rather than an automatically exact finite-sample outcome. The contribution is a support-vector formulation of novelty detection based on learning a region of typical observations.
summary.tldr: A regularized kernel method learns a region of typical unlabelled observations with a specified target probability of falling outside.

title: Support Vector Method for Novelty Detection

abstract: This paper presents predictive gain scheduling, a technique for simplify(cid:173) ing reinforcement learning problems by decomposition. Link admission control of self-similar call traffic is used to demonstrate the technique. The control problem is decomposed into on-line prediction of near-fu(cid:173) ture call arrival rates, and precomputation of policies for Poisson call ar(cid:173) rival processes. At decision time, the predictions are used to select among the policies. Simulations show that this technique results in sig(cid:173) nificantly faster learning without any performance loss, compared to a reinforcement learning controller that does not decompose the problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to simplify reinforcement learning for deciding whether a communications link should admit incoming calls. The traffic follows a self-similar arrival process, and the proposed technique, predictive gain scheduling, divides the control problem into parts. Its purpose is to make learning easier while preserving the quality of admission decisions.

One part predicts call arrival rates in the near future while the system is operating. Another prepares control policies in advance for Poisson arrival processes. At each decision, the predicted arrival rate determines which prepared policy to use. Prediction therefore connects the changing traffic conditions to a collection of policies computed for simpler arrival models.

Simulations compare this decomposition with a reinforcement learning controller that handles the problem without separating it into those components. The authors report significantly faster learning without a loss in performance in that comparison. The result supports using prediction to select among prepared policies as a useful simplification for the admission-control problem studied.
summary.tldr: Predicting arrival rates and selecting precomputed policies speeds up learning without performance loss in the reported admission-control simulations.

title: Decomposition of Reinforcement Learning for Admission Control of Self-Similar Call Arrival Processes

abstract: We describe an algorithm for automatically learning discriminative com- ponents of objects with SVM classiﬁers. It is based on growing image parts by minimizing theoretical bounds on the error probability of an SVM. Component-based face classiﬁers are then combined in a second stage to yield a hierarchical SVM classiﬁer. Experimental results in face classiﬁcation show considerable robustness against rotations in depth and suggest performance at signiﬁcantly better level than other face detection systems. Novel aspects of our approach are: a) an algorithm to learn component-based classiﬁcation experts and their combination, b) the use of 3-D morphable models for training, and c) a maximum operation on the output of each component classiﬁer which may be relevant for bio- logical models of visual recognition.

Component-based face classiﬁers are then combined in a second stage to yield a hierarchical SVM classiﬁer. Experimental results in face classiﬁcation show considerable robustness against rotations in depth and suggest performance at signiﬁcantly better level than other face detection systems. paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm that learns object components useful for classification. It uses support vector machines to judge image parts and grows those parts by minimizing theoretical bounds on classification error probability. The choice of components is therefore guided by their discriminative value within the learning procedure.

For face classification, the learned component classifiers feed into a second stage that combines them into a hierarchical SVM. The approach also uses three-dimensional morphable models for training and applies a maximum operation to each component classifier's output. The authors identify that operation as potentially relevant to biological accounts of visual recognition.

Experiments show considerable robustness when faces rotate in depth, changing the appearance of their parts. The results also suggest performance substantially better than other face detection systems. The stated evidence supports learning and combining component experts as a promising recognition strategy, while the comparison is presented as a suggestion from the experiments and the biological connection remains a possibility.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical SVM learns useful face parts and combines their predictions, showing robustness to depth rotations in experiments.

title: Categorization by Learning and Combining Object Parts

abstract: With the increasing number of users of mobile computing devices (e.g. personal digital assistants) and the advent of third generation mobile phones, wireless communications are becoming increasingly important. Many applications rely on the device maintaining a replica of a data-structure which is stored on a server, for exam(cid:173) ple news databases, calendars and e-mail. ill this paper we explore the question of the optimal strategy for synchronising such replicas. We utilise probabilistic models to represent how the data-structures evolve and to model user behaviour. We then formulate objective functions which can be minimised with respect to the synchronisa(cid:173) tion timings. We demonstrate, using two real world data-sets, that a user can obtain more up-to-date information using our approach.

paragraphs: The paper asks when a mobile device should synchronize its local copy of information stored on a server. Examples include news, calendars, and email. Because the server’s data can change, a local replica may become outdated between synchronization events. Choosing the timing determines which version of the information is available to the user.

The authors use probabilistic models for both the evolution of the data structures and user behavior. They then formulate objective functions that can be minimized with respect to synchronization times. This makes scheduling an optimization problem informed by how information changes and how the user interacts with it.

Evaluations on two real-world datasets show that the proposed approach can provide users with more up-to-date information. The result supports modeling both the data and its use when choosing synchronization schedules. The contribution is a framework for turning those models into timing decisions, with empirical evidence that the resulting schedules improve information freshness in the two studied datasets.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic models of data changes and user behavior guide synchronization times that improve information freshness on two real-world datasets.

title: Optimising Synchronisation Times for Mobile Devices

abstract: Using a Markov chain perspective of spectral clustering we present an algorithm to automatically ﬁnd the number of stable clusters in a dataset. The Markov chain’s behaviour is characterized by the spectral properties of the matrix of transition probabilities, from which we derive eigenﬂows along with their halﬂives. An eigenﬂow describes the ﬂow of probabil- ity mass due to the Markov chain, and it is characterized by its eigen- value, or equivalently, by the halﬂife of its decay as the Markov chain is iterated. A ideal stable cluster is one with zero eigenﬂow and inﬁ- nite half-life. The key insight in this paper is that bottlenecks between weakly coupled clusters can be identiﬁed by computing the sensitivity of the eigenﬂow’s halﬂife to variations in the edge weights. We propose a novel EIGENCUTS algorithm to perform clustering that removes these identiﬁed bottlenecks in an iterative fashion.

paragraphs: This paper approaches clustering through the behavior of a Markov chain on a dataset. Probability mass moves between data points according to transition probabilities. The goal is to identify stable groups and automatically determine their number by examining how that probability flow behaves as the chain is repeatedly updated.

The authors derive eigenflows from the spectral properties of the transition matrix. Each eigenflow describes a component of probability movement, with an eigenvalue determining how quickly it decays. Its half-life expresses that decay in temporal terms. An ideal stable cluster has no eigenflow leaving it and an infinite half-life.

The key step is to examine how an eigenflow's half-life changes when edge weights change. This sensitivity identifies bottlenecks connecting otherwise weakly coupled clusters. The proposed EIGENCUTS algorithm repeatedly removes those bottlenecks to form clusters. The approach turns the stability of probability flow into a criterion for deciding where to separate the data, rather than requiring a cluster count in advance.
summary.tldr: EIGENCUTS identifies stable clusters by measuring how probability-flow half-lives respond to changes in graph connections.

title: Half-Lives of EigenFlows for Spectral Clustering

abstract: We propose probabilistic generative models, called parametric mix- ture models (PMMs), for multiclass, multi-labeled text categoriza- tion problem. Conventionally, the binary classi(cid:12)cation approach has been employed, in which whether or not text belongs to a cat- egory is judged by the binary classi(cid:12)er for every category. In con- trast, our approach can simultaneously detect multiple categories of text using PMMs. We derive e(cid:14)cient learning and prediction algo- rithms for PMMs. We also empirically show that our method could signi(cid:12)cantly outperform the conventional binary methods when ap- plied to multi-labeled text categorization using real World Wide Web pages.

paragraphs: A document can belong to several categories at once, making text categorization a problem of assigning multiple labels. This paper proposes probabilistic generative models called parametric mixture models for that setting. The models are designed to detect several categories for the same text within a shared modeling approach.

The conventional approach described in the paper uses a separate binary classifier for each category. Each classifier decides whether its particular label applies. Parametric mixture models instead support simultaneous detection of multiple categories. The authors derive efficient algorithms for both learning the models and using them to predict categories for text.

Experiments use real World Wide Web pages with multiple labels. The authors report that their method could significantly outperform the conventional binary approaches in this setting. This provides empirical support for jointly modeling the categorization problem, while keeping the claim tied to the evaluated text data. The contribution includes both the generative formulation and the algorithms needed to apply it.
summary.tldr: Parametric mixture models jointly detect multiple text categories and can significantly outperform separate binary classifiers on the evaluated web pages.

title: Parametric Mixture Models for Multi-Labeled Text

abstract: Classiﬁcation trees are one of the most popular types of classiﬁers, with ease of implementation and interpretation being among their attractive features. Despite the widespread use of classiﬁcation trees, theoretical analysis of their performance is scarce. In this paper, we show that a new family of classiﬁcation trees, called dyadic classiﬁcation trees (DCTs), are near optimal (in a minimax sense) for a very broad range of clas- siﬁcation problems. This demonstrates that other schemes (e.g., neural networks, support vector machines) cannot perform signiﬁcantly better than DCTs in many cases. We also show that this near optimal perfor- mance is attained with linear (in the number of training data) complexity growing and pruning algorithms. Moreover, the performance of DCTs on benchmark datasets compares favorably to that of standard CART, which is generally more computationally intensive and which does not possess similar near optimality properties. Our analysis stems from the- oretical results on structural risk minimization, on which the pruning rule for DCTs is based.

paragraphs: Classification trees are attractive because they are relatively easy to implement and interpret, but their widespread use has not been matched by equally extensive performance theory. This paper introduces dyadic classification trees and analyzes them using structural risk minimization. That theoretical framework also supplies the rule used to prune the trees.

The authors show that these trees are nearly optimal in a minimax sense across a broad range of classification problems. This concerns performance relative to the best achievable worst-case behavior within the relevant problem classes. Consequently, in many of these cases, other methods cannot improve substantially on their performance; it is not a claim of superiority on every dataset.

The paper also shows that this statistical performance is attainable with growing and pruning algorithms whose complexity is linear in the number of training examples. On benchmark datasets, the trees compare favorably with standard CART. The contribution joins broad theoretical guarantees with computational efficiency and favorable empirical results in one tree-learning framework.
summary.tldr: Dyadic classification trees achieve broad minimax near-optimality guarantees with growing and pruning costs linear in training-set size.

title: Dyadic Classification Trees via Structural Risk Minimization

abstract: Multiple realizations of continuous-valued time series from a stochastic process often contain systematic variations in rate and amplitude. To leverage the information contained in such noisy replicate sets, we need to align them in an appropriate way (for example, to allow the data to be properly combined by adaptive averaging). We present the Continuous Profile Model (CPM), a generative model in which each observed time series is a non-uniformly subsampled version of a single latent trace, to which local rescaling and additive noise are applied. After unsupervised training, the learned trace represents a canonical, high resolution fusion of all the replicates. As well, an alignment in time and scale of each observation to this trace can be found by inference in the model. We apply CPM to successfully align speech signals from multiple speakers and sets of Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry proteomic data.

paragraphs: Repeated measurements of a process can differ in timing, amplitude, and noise even when they reflect shared underlying structure. Combining them usefully requires aligning those differences. This paper introduces the Continuous Profile Model to learn a common representation and align multiple continuous-valued time series to it.

The model assumes that each observed series comes from one latent trace through non-uniform subsampling, local rescaling, and additive noise. These operations account for varying sampling rates along the trace, changing amplitude, and imperfect observations. Unsupervised training learns a canonical, high-resolution trace that fuses information from the replicates.

Inference then finds the temporal and scale alignment between each observation and that shared trace. The authors successfully apply the method to speech from multiple speakers and to proteomic measurements from Liquid Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry. These applications illustrate how a generative account of variation can support both alignment and fusion, with the shared latent trace serving as the reference that ties the observations together.
summary.tldr: The Continuous Profile Model learns a shared high-resolution trace while aligning noisy time series that vary locally in timing and amplitude.

title: Multiple Alignment of Continuous Time Series

abstract: We present a simple and scalable algorithm for large-margin estima- tion of structured models, including an important class of Markov net- works and combinatorial models. We formulate the estimation problem as a convex-concave saddle-point problem and apply the extragradient method, yielding an algorithm with linear convergence using simple gra- dient and projection calculations. The projection step can be solved us- ing combinatorial algorithms for min-cost quadratic ﬂow. This makes the approach an efﬁcient alternative to formulations based on reductions to a quadratic program (QP). We present experiments on two very different structured prediction tasks: 3D image segmentation and word alignment, illustrating the favorable scaling properties of our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper develops a scalable training algorithm for structured prediction with large margins. The models include an important class of Markov networks and combinatorial models, where outputs have internal relationships. The computational challenge is to estimate such models efficiently while preserving the structure that makes their predictions meaningful.

The authors formulate estimation as a convex-concave saddle-point problem and apply the extragradient method. The resulting algorithm uses gradient calculations and projections and has linear convergence. The projection operation can be solved with combinatorial algorithms for minimum-cost quadratic flow, providing a concrete computational route for this otherwise potentially demanding step.

This formulation offers an efficient alternative to approaches that reduce estimation to a quadratic program. Experiments examine two substantially different applications: three-dimensional image segmentation and word alignment. The authors report favorable scaling behavior across these tasks. The contribution links a saddle-point view of learning with tractable optimization operations, and the experiments illustrate its applicability across distinct kinds of structured outputs.
summary.tldr: An extragradient algorithm trains large-margin structured models through gradient and flow-based projection operations with linear convergence.

title: Structured Prediction via the Extragradient Method

abstract: The Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machine (TRBM) is a probabilistic model for sequences that is able to successfully model (i.e., generate nice-looking samples of) several very high dimensional sequences, such as motion capture data and the pixels of low resolution videos of balls bouncing in a box. The major disadvantage of the TRBM is that exact inference is extremely hard, since even computing a Gibbs update for a single variable of the posterior is exponentially expensive. This difficulty has necessitated the use of a heuristic inference procedure, that nonetheless was accurate enough for successful learning. In this paper we introduce the Recurrent TRBM, which is a very slight modification of the TRBM for which exact inference is very easy and exact gradient learning is almost tractable. We demonstrate that the RTRBM is better than an analogous TRBM at generating motion capture and videos of bouncing balls.

paragraphs: Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machines can generate convincing samples of high-dimensional sequences, including motion capture and simple videos. Their major difficulty is inference: even one Gibbs update for a single posterior variable can require exponential computation. Earlier learning therefore relied on a heuristic inference procedure that was nevertheless accurate enough to support successful training.

The paper introduces the Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machine through a small modification of the earlier model. In the revised model, exact inference becomes easy, and exact-gradient learning becomes almost tractable. This distinction matters: the abstract claims a clear simplification of inference while retaining a qualification about the tractability of exact learning.

The authors compare the recurrent model with an analogous temporal model on generating motion capture and videos of bouncing balls. The recurrent model performs better in these demonstrations. The contribution therefore links a modest architectural change to a substantial improvement in inference tractability, together with stronger generation results on the two studied types of sequence.
summary.tldr: A small recurrent modification makes exact TRBM inference easy and improves generation of motion capture and bouncing-ball videos.

title: The Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machine

abstract: We propose a general framework to online learning for classification problems with time-varying potential functions in the adversarial setting. This framework allows to design and prove relative mistake bounds for any generic loss function. The mistake bounds can be specialized for the hinge loss, allowing to recover and improve the bounds of known online classification algorithms. By optimizing the general bound we derive a new online classification algorithm, called NAROW, that hybridly uses adaptive- and fixed- second order information. We analyze the properties of the algorithm and illustrate its performance using synthetic dataset.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general framework for online classification in an adversarial setting. The learner makes predictions over time, and the analysis does not rely on a benign statistical sequence of examples. The framework uses potential functions that can change with time to support the design and analysis of learning algorithms.

The authors derive relative mistake bounds for generic loss functions. These bounds connect classification mistakes with the loss used in the analysis. Specializing the framework to hinge loss allows them to recover and improve bounds for known online classification algorithms. The framework therefore serves both as a common analytical treatment and as a way to obtain sharper guarantees.

Optimizing the general bound leads to a new algorithm called NAROW. It combines adaptive and fixed second-order information within its updates. The paper analyzes the algorithm's properties and illustrates its performance on synthetic data. Its central contribution is the progression from a flexible mistake-bound framework to a concrete algorithm whose design follows from that analysis.
summary.tldr: A general mistake-bound framework yields NAROW, an online classifier combining adaptive and fixed second-order information.

title: New Adaptive Algorithms for Online Classification

abstract: Modern classification tasks usually involve many class labels and can be informed by a broad range of features. Many of these tasks are tackled by constructing a set of classifiers, which are then applied at test time and then pieced together in a fixed procedure determined in advance or at training time. We present an active classification process at the test time, where each classifier in a large ensemble is viewed as a potential observation that might inform our classification process. Observations are then selected dynamically based on previous observations, using a value-theoretic computation that balances an estimate of the expected classification gain from each observation as well as its computational cost. The expected classification gain is computed using a probabilistic model that uses the outcome from previous observations. This active classification process is applied at test time for each individual test instance, resulting in an efficient instance-specific decision path. We demonstrate the benefit of the active scheme on various real-world datasets, and show that it can achieve comparable or even higher classification accuracy at a fraction of the computational costs of traditional methods.

paragraphs: A classification system may have many classifiers available, each contributing different information at a computational cost. Applying them through a fixed procedure can spend effort on observations that are less useful for a particular input. This paper treats classification at test time as a sequence of decisions about which classifier to consult next.

Each classifier output becomes a potential observation. A probabilistic model uses the outputs already collected to estimate how much another observation could improve classification. A value-based calculation balances this expected gain against the cost of obtaining it. Because earlier results affect later choices, different test examples can follow different paths through the same ensemble.

Experiments on real-world datasets show that this adaptive process can match or exceed the accuracy of traditional methods while using a fraction of their computation. The finding supports choosing computation separately for each instance: the useful question is not just which classifiers are available, but which one is worth running given what the system already knows.
summary.tldr: An adaptive test-time procedure selects classifiers by expected benefit and cost, achieving strong accuracy with less computation in experiments.

title: Active Classification based on Value of Classifier

abstract: Symmetric positive definite (spd) matrices are remarkably pervasive in a multitude of scientific disciplines, including machine learning and optimization. We consider the fundamental task of measuring distances between two spd matrices; a task that is often nontrivial whenever an application demands the distance function to respect the non-Euclidean geometry of spd matrices. Unfortunately, typical non-Euclidean distance measures such as the Riemannian metric $\riem(X,Y)=\frob{\log(X\inv{Y})}$, are computationally demanding and also complicated to use. To allay some of these difficulties, we introduce a new metric on spd matrices: this metric not only respects non-Euclidean geometry, it also offers faster computation than $\riem$ while being less complicated to use. We support our claims theoretically via a series of theorems that relate our metric to $\riem(X,Y)$, and experimentally by studying the nonconvex problem of computing matrix geometric means based on squared distances.

paragraphs: Symmetric positive definite matrices appear throughout machine learning and optimization. Comparing two such matrices can require more than treating their entries as ordinary coordinates: some applications need a distance that respects the curved geometry of the matrix space. The paper addresses the computational and practical difficulties of using such distances.

The authors introduce a new metric that respects this non-Euclidean geometry while offering faster computation and simpler use than the Riemannian metric considered in the paper. They support the proposal with theorems connecting the new distance to that established metric. These relationships provide a mathematical basis for comparing the two ways of measuring separation.

The experimental application is computing matrix geometric means using squared distances, a nonconvex optimization problem. Here, the distance measure affects both the meaning of an average and the computation needed to obtain it. The contribution is therefore a more accessible geometric comparison tool, supported by theoretical relationships and experiments on a concrete matrix-averaging task.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a geometry-aware distance between positive definite matrices that is simpler and faster to compute than the Riemannian metric it considers.

title: A new metric on the manifold of kernel matrices with application to matrix geometric means

abstract: We develop a framework for post model selection inference, via marginal screening, in linear regression. At the core of this framework is a result that characterizes the exact distribution of linear functions of the response $y$, conditional on the model being selected (``condition on selection framework). This allows us to construct valid confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for regression coefficients that account for the selection procedure. In contrast to recent work in high-dimensional statistics, our results are exact (non-asymptotic) and require no eigenvalue-like assumptions on the design matrix $X$. Furthermore, the computational cost of marginal regression, constructing confidence intervals and hypothesis testing is negligible compared to the cost of linear regression, thus making our methods particularly suitable for extremely large datasets. Although we focus on marginal screening to illustrate the applicability of the condition on selection framework, this framework is much more broadly applicable. We show how to apply the proposed framework to several other selection procedures including orthogonal matching pursuit and marginal screening+Lasso."

paragraphs: Selecting regression variables from data changes the statistical problem faced when reporting uncertainty about their coefficients. This paper develops confidence intervals and hypothesis tests that account for selection through marginal screening. Its central idea is to condition inference on the event that the particular model was selected.

The authors characterize the exact conditional distribution of linear functions of the response. That distribution provides the basis for valid inference after selection. Their results are non-asymptotic, so their exactness does not depend on taking a large-sample limit, and they require no eigenvalue-like assumptions on the design matrix. These are specific strengths of the framework, rather than a claim that inference requires no assumptions whatsoever.

The paper reports that screening and the associated interval construction and testing have negligible computational cost compared with linear regression, making the approach attractive for extremely large datasets. It also demonstrates the framework beyond marginal screening, including orthogonal matching pursuit and marginal screening followed by Lasso. The broader contribution is a reusable way to make the selection procedure part of the uncertainty calculation.
summary.tldr: Conditioning on model selection enables exact confidence intervals and hypothesis tests after marginal screening and several other regression selection procedures.

title: Exact Post Model Selection Inference for Marginal Screening

abstract: This paper introduces a novel mathematical and computational framework, namely {\it Log-Hilbert-Schmidt metric} between positive definite operators on a Hilbert space. This is a generalization of the Log-Euclidean metric on the Riemannian manifold of positive definite matrices to the infinite-dimensional setting. The general framework is applied in particular to compute distances between covariance operators on a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), for which we obtain explicit formulas via the corresponding Gram matrices. Empirically, we apply our formulation to the task of multi-category image classification, where each image is represented by an infinite-dimensional RKHS covariance operator. On several challenging datasets, our method significantly outperforms approaches based on covariance matrices computed directly on the original input features, including those using the Log-Euclidean metric, Stein and Jeffreys divergences, achieving new state of the art results.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the Log-Hilbert-Schmidt metric, a way to measure distances between positive definite operators on a Hilbert space. It extends the Log-Euclidean metric for positive definite matrices to an infinite-dimensional setting. This creates a mathematical framework for comparing objects whose representations go beyond finite covariance matrices.

The authors apply the framework to covariance operators in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Although these operators can be infinite-dimensional, the paper derives explicit distance formulas using their corresponding Gram matrices. This connection makes the operator-based representation computationally usable, linking the abstract distance construction to quantities that can be calculated from the data.

For multi-category image classification, each image is represented by an infinite-dimensional kernel-space covariance operator. Across several challenging datasets, the method significantly outperforms approaches using covariance matrices of the original features, including comparisons based on Log-Euclidean distance and Stein and Jeffreys divergences. The reported state-of-the-art results support the practical usefulness of the richer representation and its associated metric.
summary.tldr: The Log-Hilbert-Schmidt metric makes infinite-dimensional covariance comparisons computable through Gram matrices and improves reported image-classification results.

title: Log-Hilbert-Schmidt metric between positive definite operators on Hilbert spaces

abstract: In recent years, distributed representations of inputs have led to performance gains in many applications by allowing statistical information to be shared across inputs. However, the predicted outputs (labels, and more generally structures) are still treated as discrete objects even though outputs are often not discrete units of meaning. In this paper, we present a new formulation for structured prediction where we represent individual labels in a structure as dense vectors and allow semantically similar labels to share parameters. We extend this representation to larger structures by defining compositionality using tensor products to give a natural generalization of standard structured prediction approaches. We define a learning objective for jointly learning the model parameters and the label vectors and propose an alternating minimization algorithm for learning. We show that our formulation outperforms structural SVM baselines in two tasks: multiclass document classification and part-of-speech tagging.

paragraphs: Learned representations can allow related inputs to share statistical information, but output labels are often still treated as separate discrete objects. This paper brings representation learning to the output side of structured prediction. Its premise is that labels can have related meanings, and the model should be able to use those relationships.

The authors represent individual labels as dense vectors, allowing semantically similar labels to share parameters. They then compose label representations into larger structures using tensor products. This provides a generalization of standard structured prediction methods in which the representation of the output is itself part of what the system learns.

A joint objective learns both the model parameters and the label vectors, with an alternating minimization algorithm handling the optimization. Experiments on multiclass document classification and part-of-speech tagging outperform structural SVM baselines. The reported findings support the usefulness of learning relationships among outputs in these tasks, connecting shared label representations to better predictions rather than leaving output categories entirely independent.
summary.tldr: Learning dense label vectors and composing them into structured outputs enables parameter sharing and improves over structural SVM baselines on two tasks.

title: Learning Distributed Representations for Structured Output Prediction

abstract: Many important distributions are high dimensional, and often they can be modeled as Gaussian mixtures. We derive the first sample-efficient polynomial-time estimator for high-dimensional spherical Gaussian mixtures. Based on intuitive spectral reasoning, it approximates mixtures of $k$ spherical Gaussians in $d$-dimensions to within$\ell_1$ distance $\epsilon$ using $\mathcal{O}({dk^9(\log^2 d)}/{\epsilon^4})$ samples and $\mathcal{O}_{k,\epsilon}(d^3\log^5 d)$ computation time. Conversely, we show that any estimator requires $\Omega\bigl({dk}/{\epsilon^2}\bigr)$ samples, hence the algorithm's sample complexity is nearly optimal in the dimension. The implied time-complexity factor \mathcal{O}_{k,\epsilon}$ is exponential in $k$, but much smaller than previously known. We also construct a simple estimator for one-dimensional Gaussian mixtures that uses $\tilde\mathcal{O}(k /\epsilon^2)$ samples and $\tilde\mathcal{O}((k/\epsilon)^{3k+1})$ computation time.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many observations and how much computation are needed to estimate high-dimensional mixtures of spherical Gaussians. The authors derive an estimator using spectral reasoning, with an explicit guarantee on the L1 distance between the estimated and target distributions. Their central achievement concerns efficient use of samples as dimension grows.

For k components in d dimensions and error tolerance epsilon, the sample bound is O(d k^9 log²(d) / epsilon^4). A lower bound shows that any estimator needs at least Omega(d k / epsilon²) samples. Comparing these bounds establishes near-optimal dependence on dimension, without asserting equally tight dependence on component count or accuracy.

The computation bound is O_{k,epsilon}(d³ log^5(d)), whose hidden factor is exponential in k, though smaller than previously known. Thus, the polynomial dependence on dimension comes with a substantial component-count dependence. The paper also gives a one-dimensional estimator using roughly k / epsilon² samples up to logarithmic factors, with a separate computation bound. Together, the results distinguish sample efficiency from computational cost.
summary.tldr: A spherical Gaussian mixture estimator achieves nearly optimal sample dependence on dimension, while its runtime retains an exponential dependence on component count.

title: Near-Optimal-Sample Estimators for Spherical Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: Persistent activity refers to the phenomenon that cortical neurons keep firing even after the stimulus triggering the initial neuronal responses is moved. Persistent activity is widely believed to be the substrate for a neural system retaining a memory trace of the stimulus information. In a conventional view, persistent activity is regarded as an attractor of the network dynamics, but it faces a challenge of how to be closed properly. Here, in contrast to the view of attractor, we consider that the stimulus information is encoded in a marginally unstable state of the network which decays very slowly and exhibits persistent firing for a prolonged duration. We propose a simple yet effective mechanism to achieve this goal, which utilizes the property of short-term plasticity (STP) of neuronal synapses. STP has two forms, short-term depression (STD) and short-term facilitation (STF), which have opposite effects on retaining neuronal responses. We find that by properly combining STF and STD, a neural system can hold persistent activity of graded lifetime, and that persistent activity fades away naturally without relying on an external drive. The implications of these results on neural information representation are discussed.

title: A Synaptical Story of Persistent Activity with Graded Lifetime in a Neural System

abstract: Spectral graph partitioning methods have received significant attention from both practitioners and theorists in computer science. Some notable studies have been carried out regarding the behavior of these methods for infinitely large sample size (von Luxburg et al., 2008; Rohe et al., 2011), which provide sufficient confidence to practitioners about the effectiveness of these methods. On the other hand, recent developments in computer vision have led to a plethora of applications, where the model deals with multi-way affinity relations and can be posed as uniform hyper-graphs. In this paper, we view these models as random m-uniform hypergraphs and establish the consistency of spectral algorithm in this general setting. We develop a planted partition model or stochastic blockmodel for such problems using higher order tensors, present a spectral technique suited for the purpose and study its large sample behavior. The analysis reveals that the algorithm is consistent for m-uniform hypergraphs for larger values of m, and also the rate of convergence improves for increasing m. Our result provides the first theoretical evidence that establishes the importance of m-way affinities.

The paper studies this setting through random uniform hypergraphs, where every hyperedge involves the same number m of objects. Its aim is to give theoretical support for spectral partitioning when the input contains these multi-way affinities.

The authors develop a planted partition model, also described as a stochastic blockmodel, using higher-order tensors. This supplies a probabilistic setting with an underlying partition against which an algorithm can be analyzed. They then present a suitable spectral method and investigate its behavior as sample size becomes large.

The analysis establishes consistency for larger values of m and finds that convergence improves as m increases within the studied setting. Thus, the result gives theoretical evidence that higher-order affinities can help partition recovery. The significance is tied to the random model and its large-sample analysis: the paper supplies a reason that relationships involving more objects can improve spectral partitioning under this formulation.
summary.tldr: A planted-partition analysis establishes spectral consistency for uniform hypergraphs and faster convergence with increasing affinity order in the studied setting.

title: Consistency of Spectral Partitioning of Uniform Hypergraphs under Planted Partition Model

abstract: The success of machine learning in a broad range of applications has led to an ever-growing demand for machine learning systems that can be used off the shelf by non-experts. To be effective in practice, such systems need to automatically choose a good algorithm and feature preprocessing steps for a new dataset at hand, and also set their respective hyperparameters. Recent work has started to tackle this automated machine learning (AutoML) problem with the help of efficient Bayesian optimization methods. In this work we introduce a robust new AutoML system based on scikit-learn (using 15 classifiers, 14 feature preprocessing methods, and 4 data preprocessing methods, giving rise to a structured hypothesis space with 110 hyperparameters). This system, which we dub auto-sklearn, improves on existing AutoML methods by automatically taking into account past performance on similar datasets, and by constructing ensembles from the models evaluated during the optimization. Our system won the first phase of the ongoing ChaLearn AutoML challenge, and our comprehensive analysis on over 100 diverse datasets shows that it substantially outperforms the previous state of the art in AutoML. We also demonstrate the performance gains due to each of our contributions and derive insights into the effectiveness of the individual components of auto-sklearn.

paragraphs: An automated machine-learning system must choose preprocessing steps, a learning algorithm, and their hyperparameters for a new dataset. The paper introduces auto-sklearn, a scikit-learn-based system whose search space contains 15 classifiers, 14 feature-preprocessing methods, 4 data-preprocessing methods, and 110 hyperparameters.

The system extends Bayesian-optimization-based AutoML in two ways. It uses past performance on similar datasets to inform the search, and it constructs ensembles from models that the optimization has already evaluated. Thus, previously gathered experience guides exploration while evaluated candidates can contribute jointly to the final predictor.

Evaluation on over 100 diverse datasets reports substantial improvements over the previous AutoML state of the art, with analyses separating the gains from individual contributions. The abstract provides broad comparative evidence, although it does not give per-dataset scores or resource budgets.
summary.tldr: Auto-sklearn combines Bayesian optimization, experience from prior datasets, and ensembles.

title: Efficient and Robust Automated Machine Learning

abstract: We take a new look at parameter estimation for Gaussian Mixture Model (GMMs). Specifically, we advance Riemannian manifold optimization (on the manifold of positive definite matrices) as a potential replacement for Expectation Maximization (EM), which has been the de facto standard for decades. An out-of-the-box invocation of Riemannian optimization, however, fails spectacularly: it obtains the same solution as EM, but vastly slower. Building on intuition from geometric convexity, we propose a simple reformulation that has remarkable consequences: it makes Riemannian optimization not only match EM (a nontrivial result on its own, given the poor record nonlinear programming has had against EM), but also outperform it in many settings. To bring our ideas to fruition, we develop a well-tuned Riemannian LBFGS method that proves superior to known competing methods (e.g., Riemannian conjugate gradient). We hope that our results encourage a wider consideration of manifold optimization in machine learning and statistics.

paragraphs: Gaussian mixture models are commonly fitted using expectation maximization. This paper investigates optimization on the manifold of positive definite matrices as a possible alternative. Such an approach works with the geometry of the matrix parameters, but the authors find that simply applying an existing Riemannian optimizer is not enough to make it competitive.

Their initial direct approach reaches the same solution as expectation maximization but takes much longer. Guided by geometric convexity, they introduce a simple reformulation that changes this outcome. With the revised formulation, manifold optimization can match expectation maximization and outperform it in many settings. The formulation is therefore central to the reported improvement.

The authors also develop a carefully tuned Riemannian LBFGS method, which outperforms competing methods including Riemannian conjugate gradient. The results support manifold optimization as a practical candidate for Gaussian mixture estimation when paired with suitable problem design and implementation. They do not establish universal superiority over expectation maximization; the stated advantage applies across many of the settings considered.
summary.tldr: A reformulation and tuned Riemannian LBFGS optimizer make manifold-based Gaussian mixture fitting competitive with EM and faster in many settings.

title: Matrix Manifold Optimization for Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: Modern discriminative predictors have been shown to match natural intelligences in specific perceptual tasks in image classification, object and part detection, boundary extraction, etc. However, a major advantage that natural intelligences still have is that they work well for all perceptual problems together, solving them efficiently and coherently in an integrated manner. In order to capture some of these advantages in machine perception, we ask two questions: whether deep neural networks can learn universal image representations, useful not only for a single task but for all of them, and how the solutions to the different tasks can be integrated in this framework. We answer by proposing a new architecture, which we call multinet, in which not only deep image features are shared between tasks, but where tasks can interact in a recurrent manner by encoding the results of their analysis in a common shared representation of the data. In this manner, we show that the performance of individual tasks in standard benchmarks can be improved first by sharing features between them and then, more significantly, by integrating their solutions in the common representation.

paragraphs: Image classification, object detection, and boundary extraction are often treated as separate perceptual tasks. This paper asks how a neural network can solve such problems together efficiently and coherently. It explores both representations useful across tasks and a mechanism through which the tasks' solutions can inform one another.

The proposed architecture, called multinet, shares deep image features but also lets tasks interact recurrently. Each task encodes the results of its analysis into a common representation of the image. This shared representation therefore contains information from task outputs as well as the image features used to produce them.

On standard benchmarks, the authors show that sharing features improves individual-task performance and that integrating task solutions yields a larger improvement. The evidence supports interaction among perceptual tasks as a useful addition to common feature extraction. While universal image representations motivate the work, the reported finding is the improvement obtained by sharing and recurrently integrating information across the tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: Multinet improves perceptual tasks by sharing image features and recurrently integrating task outputs into a common representation.

title: Integrated perception with recurrent multi-task neural networks

abstract: Supervised learning with large scale labelled datasets and deep layered models has caused a paradigm shift in diverse areas in learning and recognition. However, this approach still suffers from generalization issues under the presence of a domain shift between the training and the test data distribution. Since unsupervised domain adaptation algorithms directly address this domain shift problem between a labelled source dataset and an unlabelled target dataset, recent papers have shown promising results by fine-tuning the networks with domain adaptation loss functions which try to align the mismatch between the training and testing data distributions. Nevertheless, these recent deep learning based domain adaptation approaches still suffer from issues such as high sensitivity to the gradient reversal hyperparameters and overfitting during the fine-tuning stage. In this paper, we propose a unified deep learning framework where the representation, cross domain transformation, and target label inference are all jointly optimized in an end-to-end fashion for unsupervised domain adaptation. Our experiments show that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in both object recognition and digit classification experiments by a large margin. We will make our learned models as well as the source code available immediately upon acceptance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation, where labels are available for a source dataset but absent from a target dataset. A model trained on the source can generalize poorly when the target has a different data distribution. The challenge is to learn representations and predictions that remain useful across that change.

The authors propose an end-to-end framework that jointly optimizes three components: the representation, the transformation between domains, and inference of target labels. This brings target prediction into the same learning process as representation and domain transformation. The approach is motivated by difficulties reported for prior fine-tuning methods, including sensitivity to gradient-reversal hyperparameters and overfitting.

In object-recognition and digit-classification experiments, the proposed method significantly outperformed the state-of-the-art algorithms considered, with a large reported margin. These findings support jointly learning the interconnected parts of adaptation in the evaluated settings. The abstract presents strong empirical results for the framework, while its observations about prior methods provide motivation rather than a guarantee that every source of sensitivity or overfitting has been eliminated.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning representations, cross-domain transformations, and target labels improves unsupervised adaptation in object and digit classification experiments.

title: Learning Transferrable Representations for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: Consider learning a policy from example expert behavior, without interaction with the expert or access to a reinforcement signal. One approach is to recover the expert's cost function with inverse reinforcement learning, then extract a policy from that cost function with reinforcement learning. This approach is indirect and can be slow. We propose a new general framework for directly extracting a policy from data as if it were obtained by reinforcement learning following inverse reinforcement learning. We show that a certain instantiation of our framework draws an analogy between imitation learning and generative adversarial networks, from which we derive a model-free imitation learning algorithm that obtains significant performance gains over existing model-free methods in imitating complex behaviors in large, high-dimensional environments.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a policy from examples of expert behavior when the learner cannot interact with the expert and has no reinforcement signal. A conventional route first infers the expert’s cost function through inverse reinforcement learning, then runs reinforcement learning to obtain a policy. That two-stage process can be slow and indirect.

The authors propose a general framework that extracts a policy directly from demonstration data, with the intended effect of applying reinforcement learning after inverse reinforcement learning. This connection matters because it links direct imitation to the optimization perspective of the two-stage approach, while avoiding the need to treat recovering a cost function as a separate intermediate objective.

A particular instance of the framework connects imitation learning with generative adversarial networks. From that connection, the authors derive a model-free imitation algorithm. They report significant performance gains over existing model-free methods when imitating complex behavior in large, high-dimensional environments. The findings support the effectiveness of this adversarial formulation for the evaluated imitation problems.
summary.tldr: An adversarial imitation framework learns policies directly from expert demonstrations and improves performance on complex, high-dimensional imitation tasks.

title: Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning

abstract: The Hard Thresholding Pursuit (HTP) is a class of truncated gradient descent methods for finding sparse solutions of $\ell_0$-constrained loss minimization problems. The HTP-style methods have been shown to have strong approximation guarantee and impressive numerical performance in high dimensional statistical learning applications. However, the current theoretical treatment of these methods has traditionally been restricted to the analysis of parameter estimation consistency. It remains an open problem to analyze the support recovery performance (a.k.a., sparsistency) of this type of methods for recovering the global minimizer of the original NP-hard problem. In this paper, we bridge this gap by showing, for the first time, that exact recovery of the global sparse minimizer is possible for HTP-style methods under restricted strong condition number bounding conditions. We further show that HTP-style methods are able to recover the support of certain relaxed sparse solutions without assuming bounded restricted strong condition number. Numerical results on simulated data confirms our theoretical predictions.

paragraphs: Hard Thresholding Pursuit is a family of truncated gradient methods for optimization problems that restrict how many parameters may be nonzero. Earlier theory established strong approximation behavior and parameter-estimation consistency. This paper asks a sharper question: can these methods identify the actual sparse global solution, including which parameters are nonzero?

The authors show that exact recovery is possible under bounds on a restricted strong condition number. This condition controls the optimization problem's behavior over the relevant sparse directions. The result gives sufficient conditions for recovering a global sparse minimizer of a problem that is generally NP-hard; it does not make unrestricted sparse optimization easy.

A second result addresses a different target. HTP-style methods can recover the support of certain relaxed sparse solutions without the bounded-condition-number assumption. Separating these statements matters: identifying the nonzero positions of a relaxed solution is different from exactly recovering the original global minimizer. Simulated-data experiments confirm the theoretical predictions, connecting the recovery analysis to observed numerical behavior.
summary.tldr: HTP-style methods can exactly recover global sparse minimizers under restricted conditioning assumptions and recover certain relaxed supports without that assumption.

title: Exact Recovery of Hard Thresholding Pursuit

abstract: In this paper, we provide a rigorous theoretical study of clustering with noisy queries. Given a set of $n$ elements, our goal is to recover the true clustering by asking minimum number of pairwise queries to an oracle. Oracle can answer queries of the form ``do elements $u$ and $v$ belong to the same cluster?''-the queries can be asked interactively (adaptive queries), or non-adaptively up-front, but its answer can be erroneous with probability $p$. In this paper, we provide the first information theoretic lower bound on the number of queries for clustering with noisy oracle in both situations. We design novel algorithms that closely match this query complexity lower bound, even when the number of clusters is unknown. Moreover, we design computationally efficient algorithms both for the adaptive and non-adaptive settings. The problem captures/generalizes multiple application scenarios. It is directly motivated by the growing body of work that use crowdsourcing for {\em entity resolution}, a fundamental and challenging data mining task aimed to identify all records in a database referring to the same entity. Here crowd represents the noisy oracle, and the number of queries directly relates to the cost of crowdsourcing. Another application comes from the problem of sign edge prediction in social network, where social interactions can be both positive and negative, and one must identify the sign of all pair-wise interactions by querying a few pairs. Furthermore, clustering with noisy oracle is intimately connected to correlation clustering, leading to improvement therein. Finally, it introduces a new direction of study in the popular stochastic block model where one has an incomplete stochastic block model matrix to recover the clusters.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering a clustering by asking whether pairs of elements belong together. Each answer can be wrong with probability p, so collecting more judgments has to compensate for unreliable information. The aim is to identify the true groups while asking as few questions as possible, either interactively or with all questions chosen in advance.

The authors establish information-theoretic lower bounds on the required number of queries in both settings. They then design algorithms whose query requirements closely approach those bounds, including when the number of clusters is unknown. They also provide computationally efficient algorithms for adaptive and non-adaptive querying.

The framework is motivated by crowdsourced entity resolution, where people judge whether database records describe the same entity and each judgment has a cost. It also connects to predicting positive and negative social relationships, correlation clustering, and recovering groups from incomplete stochastic block model information. The results clarify how much noisy pairwise evidence clustering requires and provide constructive methods for using that evidence.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the noisy pairwise queries needed for clustering and develops algorithms that closely approach those bounds.

title: Clustering with Noisy Queries

abstract: Residual Networks (ResNets) have demonstrated significant improvement over traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on image classification, increasing in performance as networks grow both deeper and wider. However, memory consumption becomes a bottleneck as one needs to store all the intermediate activations for calculating gradients using backpropagation. In this work, we present the Reversible Residual Network (RevNet), a variant of ResNets where each layer's activations can be reconstructed exactly from the next layer's. Therefore, the activations for most layers need not be stored in memory during backprop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RevNets on CIFAR and ImageNet, establishing nearly identical performance to equally-sized ResNets, with activation storage requirements independent of depth.

paragraphs: Training deep residual networks requires intermediate activations to calculate gradients during backpropagation. Keeping these activations in memory becomes a bottleneck as networks grow deeper and wider. This paper changes the network architecture so that most of those intermediate values can be recovered when needed.

The proposed Reversible Residual Network, or RevNet, allows a layer’s activations to be reconstructed exactly from those of the next layer. This reversibility removes the need to retain activations for most layers throughout backpropagation. The central idea is to make recoverability a property of the model’s computation, directly addressing the storage demands of gradient calculation.

Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet show nearly identical performance to ResNets of equal size. At the same time, the reported activation-storage requirement is independent of network depth. That claim specifically concerns activation storage, the bottleneck targeted by the architecture. The findings show that substantial changes to how training retains intermediate information can preserve the predictive performance of the compared residual networks.
summary.tldr: RevNets reconstruct intermediate activations during backpropagation, making activation storage independent of depth while nearly matching equally sized ResNets.

title: The Reversible Residual Network: Backpropagation Without Storing Activations

abstract: Existing strategies for finite-armed stochastic bandits mostly depend on a parameter of scale that must be known in advance. Sometimes this is in the form of a bound on the payoffs, or the knowledge of a variance or subgaussian parameter. The notable exceptions are the analysis of Gaussian bandits with unknown mean and variance by Cowan and Katehakis [2015a] and of uniform distributions with unknown support [Cowan and Katehakis, 2015b]. The results derived in these specialised cases are generalised here to the non-parametric setup, where the learner knows only a bound on the kurtosis of the noise, which is a scale free measure of the extremity of outliers.
