Sometimes this is in the form of a bound on the payoffs, or the knowledge of a variance or subgaussian parameter. The notable exceptions are the analysis of Gaussian bandits with unknown mean and variance by Cowan and Katehakis [2015a] and of uniform distributions with unknown support [Cowan and Katehakis, 2015b]. The results derived in these specialised cases are generalised here to the non-parametric setup, where the learner knows only a bound on the kurtosis of the noise, which is a scale free measure of the extremity of outliers.

paragraphs: A finite-armed stochastic bandit learner repeatedly chooses among options with uncertain payoffs. Many existing strategies require advance knowledge of the numerical scale of those payoffs. This knowledge might take the form of a maximum possible payoff, a known variance, or another parameter describing how rewards fluctuate. Such requirements determine what the learner must know before it can begin.

This paper develops a scale-free approach under a different information requirement: the learner knows a bound on the noise's kurtosis. Kurtosis describes the extremity of outliers relative to the distribution's scale. A bound on it therefore constrains the noise without specifying how large the payoffs or their variance must be.

The contribution extends earlier results for Gaussian rewards with unknown mean and variance and uniform rewards with unknown support to a non-parametric setting. The learner is no longer restricted to those particular distribution families. The stated generalization still depends on a known kurtosis bound, so scale-free learning here removes advance scale information while retaining a specific assumption about outlier behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper extends scale-free stochastic bandit learning to non-parametric reward distributions when a bound on noise kurtosis is known.

title: A Scale Free Algorithm for Stochastic Bandits with Bounded Kurtosis

abstract: Archived data from the US network of weather radars hold detailed information about bird migration over the last 25 years, including very high-resolution partial measurements of velocity. Historically, most of this spatial resolution is discarded and velocities are summarized at a very small number of locations due to modeling and algorithmic limitations. This paper presents a Gaussian process (GP) model to reconstruct high-resolution full velocity fields across the entire US. The GP faithfully models all aspects of the problem in a single joint framework, including spatially random velocities, partial velocity measurements, station-specific geometries, measurement noise, and an ambiguity known as aliasing. We develop fast inference algorithms based on the FFT; to do so, we employ a creative use of Laplace's method to sidestep the fact that the kernel of the joint process is non-stationary.

The GP faithfully models all aspects of the problem in a single joint framework, including spatially random velocities, partial velocity measurements, station-specific geometries, measurement noise, and an ambiguity known as aliasing. We develop fast inference algorithms based on the FFT; to do so, we employ a creative use of Laplace's method to sidestep the fact that the kernel of the joint process is non-stationary.

paragraphs: Weather radar archives contain detailed measurements relevant to bird migration, but their velocity observations are partial. Historically, modeling and computational constraints led researchers to summarize velocities at only a few locations, discarding much of the available spatial detail. This paper develops a model intended to reconstruct full velocity fields at high resolution across the United States.

The proposed Gaussian process treats the sources of complexity jointly. It accounts for spatially random velocities, partial observations, the geometry of individual radar stations, measurement noise, and aliasing ambiguity. Bringing these elements into one framework connects the desired full velocity field to the particular measurements that the radar network actually supplies.

Efficient computation is another central contribution. The authors develop inference algorithms based on the fast Fourier transform, using Laplace's method to work around the non-stationary kernel of the joint process. The resulting approach addresses both representation and computation: it models the observation process while providing a route to inference at the spatial scale that earlier summaries could not retain.
summary.tldr: A joint Gaussian process model and FFT-based inference reconstruct full velocity fields from partial, noisy weather-radar observations.

title: Inferring Latent Velocities from Weather Radar Data using Gaussian Processes

abstract: Sparse Principal Component Analysis (SPCA) and Sparse Linear Regression (SLR) have a wide range of applications and have attracted a tremendous amount of attention in the last two decades as canonical examples of statistical problems in high dimension. A variety of algorithms have been proposed for both SPCA and SLR, but an explicit connection between the two had not been made. We show how to efficiently transform a black-box solver for SLR into an algorithm for SPCA: assuming the SLR solver satisfies prediction error guarantees achieved by existing efficient algorithms such as those based on the Lasso, the SPCA algorithm derived from it achieves near state of the art guarantees for testing and for support recovery for the single spiked covariance model as obtained by the current best polynomial-time algorithms. Our reduction not only highlights the inherent similarity between the two problems, but also, from a practical standpoint, allows one to obtain a collection of algorithms for SPCA directly from known algorithms for SLR. We provide experimental results on simulated data comparing our proposed framework to other algorithms for SPCA.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis and sparse linear regression both seek useful structure involving relatively few variables in high-dimensional data. This paper establishes an explicit algorithmic connection between them. It gives an efficient transformation that turns a black-box sparse-regression solver into an algorithm for sparse PCA.

The guarantee is conditional on the regression solver satisfying suitable prediction-error bounds, including bounds achieved by existing efficient methods based on the Lasso. Under the single-spiked covariance model, the resulting sparse-PCA algorithm achieves near-state-of-the-art guarantees for testing and support recovery. Support recovery concerns identifying which variables participate in the sparse component.

The comparison is to the guarantees of the best polynomial-time algorithms considered in the paper. Beyond the theoretical connection, the reduction offers a practical route to obtaining multiple sparse-PCA algorithms from existing sparse-regression methods. The authors also compare their framework with other sparse-PCA algorithms on simulated data. The main result is a reusable reduction with explicit conditions connecting the quality of a regression solver to sparse-PCA guarantees.
summary.tldr: An efficient reduction converts sparse-regression solvers with suitable prediction guarantees into sparse-PCA algorithms with strong conditional guarantees.

title: Sparse PCA from Sparse Linear Regression

abstract: We present a new method and system, called DeepZ, for certifying neural network robustness based on abstract interpretation. Compared to state-of-the-art automated verifiers for neural networks, DeepZ: (i) handles ReLU, Tanh and Sigmoid activation functions, (ii) supports feedforward and convolutional architectures, (iii) is significantly more scalable and precise, and (iv) and is sound with respect to floating point arithmetic. These benefits are due to carefully designed approximations tailored to the setting of neural networks. As an example, DeepZ achieves a verification accuracy of 97% on a large network with 88,500 hidden units under $L_{\infty}$ attack with $\epsilon = 0.1$ with an average runtime of 133 seconds.

It uses abstract interpretation, which reasons about network behavior through approximations designed to support sound conclusions. The paper's central technical contribution is tailoring those approximations to neural networks so that certification can be both precise and computationally manageable.

The system supports feedforward and convolutional architectures, along with ReLU, Tanh, and Sigmoid activations. The authors report substantially better scalability and precision than state-of-the-art automated neural network verifiers. They also state that the method is sound with respect to floating-point arithmetic, connecting its guarantees to the numerical calculations actually used by the system.

One reported example involves a network with 88,500 hidden units. Under an L-infinity attack with epsilon equal to 0.1, DeepZ achieves 97% verification accuracy with an average runtime of 133 seconds. This example makes the scalability claim concrete for a specified network and perturbation setting. The reported verification accuracy concerns the certification result and should be read in that context.
summary.tldr: DeepZ uses neural-network-specific abstract interpretation to provide scalable robustness certification that accounts for floating-point arithmetic.

title: Fast and Effective Robustness Certification

abstract: We study revenue optimization pricing algorithms for repeated posted-price auctions where a seller interacts with a single strategic buyer that holds a fixed private valuation. When the participants non-equally discount their cumulative utilities, we show that the optimal constant pricing (which offers the Myerson price) is no longer optimal. In the case of more patient seller, we propose a novel multidimensional optimization functional --- a generalization of the one used to determine Myerson's price. This functional allows to find the optimal algorithm and to boost revenue of the optimal static pricing by an efficient low-dimensional approximation. Numerical experiments are provided to support our results.

This functional allows to find the optimal algorithm and to boost revenue of the optimal static pricing by an efficient low-dimensional approximation. Numerical experiments are provided to support our results.

paragraphs: This paper studies a seller who repeatedly offers prices to one strategic buyer whose private valuation stays fixed. The seller and buyer may value future utility differently: a more patient participant discounts future gains less heavily. The question is how this difference changes the seller’s revenue-maximizing pricing strategy over repeated interactions.

The authors show that when the participants discount their cumulative utilities unequally, the best constant-price policy, which offers the Myerson price, is no longer optimal. Thus, a price that is optimal among static choices need not remain optimal when the seller can use a richer repeated-pricing algorithm. The timing of incentives becomes part of the optimization problem.

For the case where the seller is more patient, the paper introduces a multidimensional optimization functional generalizing the one used to determine the Myerson price. It can identify an optimal algorithm, and an efficient low-dimensional approximation can improve revenue over optimal static pricing. Numerical experiments support these results. The proposed construction is specifically stated for a more patient seller interacting with the fixed-valuation strategic buyer.
summary.tldr: Unequal patience changes optimal repeated pricing, and the paper develops an optimization approach for improving revenue when the seller is more patient.

title: Optimal Pricing in Repeated Posted-Price Auctions with Different Patience of the Seller and the Buyer

abstract: To recognize objects of the unseen classes, most existing Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) methods first learn a compatible projection function between the common semantic space and the visual space based on the data of source seen classes, then directly apply it to the target unseen classes. However, in real scenarios, the data distribution between the source and target domain might not match well, thus causing the well-known domain shift problem. Based on the observation that visual features of test instances can be separated into different clusters, we propose a new visual structure constraint on class centers for transductive ZSL, to improve the generality of the projection function (\ie alleviate the above domain shift problem). Specifically, three different strategies (symmetric Chamfer-distance,Bipartite matching distance, and Wasserstein distance) are adopted to align the projected unseen semantic centers and visual cluster centers of test instances. We also propose a new training strategy to handle the real cases where many unrelated images exist in the test dataset, which is not considered in previous methods. Experiments on many widely used datasets demonstrate that the proposed visual structure constraint can bring substantial performance gain consistently and achieve state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning recognizes classes without labeled training examples for those classes by relating semantic descriptions to visual features. A projection learned from seen classes may transfer poorly when unseen-class data follows a different distribution. This paper uses the visual structure of unlabeled test examples to help correct that mismatch in a transductive setting.

The approach builds on the observation that test-image features can form clusters. It constrains projected semantic centers for unseen classes to align with the visual cluster centers. The authors investigate three alignment strategies: symmetric Chamfer distance, bipartite matching distance, and Wasserstein distance. These provide different ways to connect semantic predictions with the organization of target-domain images.

The paper also proposes a training strategy for test datasets containing many unrelated images. Experiments across widely used datasets report consistent substantial gains from the visual structure constraint and state-of-the-art results. The findings support using available target-image structure to improve the projection's transfer, with access to unlabeled test data being part of the method's transductive setup.
summary.tldr: Aligning unseen-class semantic centers with clusters of unlabeled test images improves transductive zero-shot recognition.

title: Transductive Zero-Shot Learning with Visual Structure Constraint

abstract: Decision tree algorithms have been among the most popular algorithms for interpretable (transparent) machine learning since the early 1980's. The problem that has plagued decision tree algorithms since their inception is their lack of optimality, or lack of guarantees of closeness to optimality: decision tree algorithms are often greedy or myopic, and sometimes produce unquestionably suboptimal models. Hardness of decision tree optimization is both a theoretical and practical obstacle, and even careful mathematical programming approaches have not been able to solve these problems efficiently. This work introduces the first practical algorithm for optimal decision trees for binary variables. The algorithm is a co-design of analytical bounds that reduce the search space and modern systems techniques, including data structures and a custom bit-vector library. We highlight possible steps to improving the scalability and speed of future generations of this algorithm based on insights from our theory and experiments.

paragraphs: Decision trees are appealing because their decisions can be inspected, but finding an optimal tree is difficult. Common algorithms make greedy choices that can produce suboptimal models without guarantees of closeness to the best solution. The paper addresses this gap with what it presents as the first practical algorithm for optimal decision trees with binary variables.

The approach combines mathematical reasoning with implementation design. Analytical bounds reduce the search space, limiting how much of the difficult optimization problem must be explored. Specialized data structures and a custom bit-vector library support the computation. The contribution depends on designing these pieces together, so that theoretical reductions translate into an effective search procedure.

The scope of the stated result is important: the algorithm targets trees over binary variables. Within that setting, it offers optimality rather than relying solely on locally attractive decisions. The authors also use insights from their theory and experiments to identify possible improvements in speed and scalability for future versions.
summary.tldr: Combining analytical search bounds with specialized systems techniques makes optimal decision-tree construction practical for binary variables.

title: Optimal Sparse Decision Trees

abstract: The increasing popularity of online two-sided markets such as ride-sharing, accommodation and freelance labor platforms, goes hand in hand with new socioeconomic challenges. One major issue remains the existence of bias and discrimination against certain social groups. We study this problem using a two-sided large market model with employers and workers mediated by a platform. Employers who seek to hire workers face uncertainty about a candidate worker's skill level. Therefore, they base their hiring decision on learning from past reviews about an individual worker as well as on their (possibly misspecified) prior beliefs about the ability level of the social group the worker belongs to. Drawing upon the social learning literature with bounded rationality and limited information, uncertainty combined with social bias leads to unequal hiring opportunities between workers of different social groups. Although the effect of social bias decreases as the number of reviews increases (consistent with empirical findings), minority workers still receive lower expected payoffs. Finally, we consider a simple directed matching policy (DM), which combines learning and matching to make better matching decisions for minority workers. Under this policy, there exists a steady-state equilibrium, in which DM reduces the discrimination gap.

paragraphs: This paper models discrimination in a two-sided online market connecting employers and workers. Employers do not know workers' skill levels, so they combine individual reviews with prior beliefs about the worker's social group. Those beliefs may be wrong, making hiring decisions depend on both available evidence and social bias.

Using a social-learning framework with bounded rationality and limited information, the authors show how uncertainty and bias produce unequal hiring opportunities. The influence of social bias diminishes as reviews accumulate, consistent with the empirical findings described in the abstract. Nevertheless, minority workers still receive lower expected payoffs within the model, so reduced influence does not eliminate the disparity.

The authors then examine a directed matching policy that combines learning with matching to improve decisions for minority workers. They establish the existence of a steady-state equilibrium in which this policy reduces the discrimination gap. This gives a model-based result showing how platform matching decisions can address disparities that persist despite learning from reviews.
summary.tldr: A market model shows how biased beliefs can sustain unequal outcomes despite reviews, and how directed matching can reduce the gap.

title: Discrimination in Online Markets: Effects of Social Bias on Learning from Reviews and Policy Design

abstract: We propose a novel regularization-based continual learning method, dubbed as Adaptive Group Sparsity based Continual Learning (AGS-CL), using two group sparsity-based penalties. Our method selectively employs the two penalties when learning each neural network node based on its the importance, which is adaptively updated after learning each task. By utilizing the proximal gradient descent method, the exact sparsity and freezing of the model is guaranteed during the learning process, and thus, the learner explicitly controls the model capacity. Furthermore, as a critical detail, we re-initialize the weights associated with unimportant nodes after learning each task in order to facilitate efficient learning and prevent the negative transfer. Throughout the extensive experimental results, we show that our AGS-CL uses orders of magnitude less memory space for storing the regularization parameters, and it significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines on representative benchmarks for both supervised and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: AGS-CL addresses learning a sequence of tasks by managing which neural network nodes remain available for learning and which are protected. It assigns importance to nodes and updates those importance values after each task. Two penalties based on group sparsity are then applied selectively according to that importance, making the treatment of a node depend on its role in previous learning.

The optimization method is a central part of the design. Using proximal gradient descent guarantees exact sparsity and freezing during learning, giving the method explicit control over model capacity. After each task, it also reinitializes weights associated with unimportant nodes. The authors use this step to support efficient learning and prevent negative transfer from earlier tasks.

Experiments cover representative benchmarks in both supervised learning and reinforcement learning. The authors report significant improvements over several state-of-the-art baselines. They also report orders of magnitude less memory for storing regularization parameters, a specific storage advantage rather than a claim about every component of training memory.
summary.tldr: AGS-CL uses adaptive node importance, sparsity, and freezing to manage continual learning while greatly reducing regularization-parameter storage.

title: Continual Learning with Node-Importance based Adaptive Group Sparse Regularization

abstract: Convex relaxations have emerged as a promising approach for verifying properties of neural networks, but widely used using Linear Programming (LP) relaxations only provide meaningful certificates when networks are specifically trained to facilitate verification. This precludes many important applications which involve \emph{verification-agnostic} networks that are not trained specifically to promote verifiability. On the other hand, semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations have shown success on verification-agnostic networks, such as adversarially trained image classifiers without additional regularization, but do not currently scale beyond small networks due to poor time and space asymptotics. In this work, we propose a first-order dual SDP algorithm that provides (1) any-time bounds (2) requires memory only linear in the total number of network activations and (3) has per-iteration complexity that scales linearly with the complexity of a forward/backward pass through the network. By exploiting iterative eigenvector methods, we express all solver operations in terms of forward and backward passes through the network, enabling efficient use of hardware optimized for deep learning. This allows us to dramatically improve the magnitude of $\ell_\infty$ perturbations for which we can verify robustness verification-agnostic networks ($1\% \to 88\%$ on MNIST, $6\%\to 40\%$ on CIFAR-10). We also demonstrate tight verification for a quadratic stability specification for the decoder of a variational autoencoder.

paragraphs: Certifying a neural network means establishing a bound on its behavior for a specified property. The paper targets networks that were not trained specifically to make verification easier. Linear-programming relaxations can provide weak certificates for such networks, while semidefinite-programming relaxations have shown promise but face substantial computational and memory costs.

The authors introduce a first-order algorithm for the dual semidefinite problem. It provides bounds at any point during execution, uses memory linear in the total number of network activations, and has iteration costs scaling linearly with a forward/backward pass. Iterative eigenvector methods let the solver express its operations through network passes, making deep-learning hardware useful for verification itself.

The reported experiments substantially improve robustness certification for verification-agnostic image classifiers on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The authors also demonstrate tight verification of a quadratic stability property for a variational autoencoder's decoder. These results show how reformulating the solver can make a stronger class of relaxations practical for networks and specifications that are difficult to certify.
summary.tldr: A memory-efficient semidefinite solver strengthens certification of networks that were not explicitly trained for verifiability.

title: Enabling certification of verification-agnostic networks via memory-efficient semidefinite programming

abstract: We present a new approach for efficient exploration which leverages a low-dimensional encoding of the environment learned with a combination of model-based and model-free objectives. Our approach uses intrinsic rewards that are based on the distance of nearest neighbors in the low dimensional representational space to gauge novelty. We then leverage these intrinsic rewards for sample-efficient exploration with planning routines in representational space for hard exploration tasks with sparse rewards. One key element of our approach is the use of information theoretic principles to shape our representations in a way so that our novelty reward goes beyond pixel similarity. We test our approach on a number of maze tasks, as well as a control problem and show that our exploration approach is more sample-efficient compared to strong baselines.

paragraphs: When task rewards are sparse, an agent needs a useful way to decide what to explore before those rewards provide much guidance. This paper builds that guidance from a learned, low-dimensional representation of the environment. The representation is trained with a combination of model-based and model-free objectives.

Novelty is measured through nearest-neighbor distances in that representation space, and those distances supply intrinsic rewards for exploration. The method then uses planning routines in the same space to pursue those rewards. Information-theoretic principles shape the representation so that the novelty signal goes beyond pixel similarity. This links the meaning of novelty to the learned encoding rather than relying solely on visual differences.

The authors evaluate the approach on several maze tasks and a control problem, reporting better sample efficiency than strong baselines. The findings support the combination of representation learning, intrinsic reward, and planning for the hard exploration settings studied. A central contribution is making the space used to measure novelty also serve as the space in which exploratory behavior is planned.
summary.tldr: The method measures novelty and plans exploration in a learned representation space, improving reported sample efficiency on maze and control tasks.

title: Novelty Search in Representational Space for Sample Efficient Exploration

abstract: This paper studies two-layers Neural Networks (NN), where the first layer contains random weights, and the second layer is trained using Ridge regularization. This model has been the focus of numerous recent works, showing that despite its simplicity, it captures some of the empirically observed behaviors of NN in the overparametrized regime, such as the double-descent curve where the generalization error decreases as the number of weights increases to $+\infty$. This paper establishes asymptotic distribution results for this 2-layers NN model in the regime where the ratios $\frac p n$ and $\frac d n$ have finite limits, where $n$ is the sample size, $p$ the ambient dimension and $d$ is the width of the first layer. We show that a weighted average of the derivatives of the trained NN at the observed data is asymptotically normal, in a setting with Lipschitz activation functions in a linear regression response with Gaussian features under possibly non-linear perturbations. We then leverage this asymptotic normality result to construct confidence intervals (CIs) for single components of the unknown regression vector. The novelty of our results are threefold: (1) Despite the nonlinearity induced by the activation function, we characterize the asymptotic distribution of a weighted average of the gradients of the network after training; (2) It provides the first frequentist uncertainty quantification guarantees, in the form of valid ($1\text{-}\alpha$)-CIs, based on NN estimates; (3) It shows that the double-descent phenomenon occurs in terms of the length of the CIs, with the length increasing and then decreasing as $\frac d n\nearrow +\infty$ for certain fixed values of $\frac p n$. We also provide a toolbox to predict the length of CIs numerically, which lets us compare activation functions and other parameters in terms of CI length.

paragraphs: This paper studies uncertainty estimates from a two-layer neural network whose first-layer weights are random and whose second layer is trained with ridge regularization. The analysis considers growing sample size, input dimension, and hidden-layer width, with dimension-to-sample and width-to-sample ratios approaching finite limits.

The authors use this result to construct confidence intervals for individual components of the unknown regression vector. Thus, derivatives of a nonlinear trained network provide a route to frequentist uncertainty quantification under the stated model.

This connects network size to the precision of inference, beyond prediction error alone. A numerical toolbox predicts interval lengths and supports comparisons of activation functions and other parameters.
summary.tldr: For a specified random-feature neural network model, asymptotic derivative distributions yield confidence intervals whose lengths can exhibit double descent.

title: Asymptotic normality and confidence intervals for derivatives of 2-layers neural network in the random features model

abstract: To learn good joint policies for multi-agent collaboration with incomplete information remains a fundamental challenge. While for two-player zero-sum games, coordinate-ascent approaches (optimizing one agent's policy at a time, e.g., self-play) work with guarantees, in multi-agent cooperative setting they often converge to sub-optimal Nash equilibrium. On the other hand, directly modeling joint policy changes in incomplete information game is nontrivial due to complicated interplay of policies (e.g., upstream updates affect downstream state reachability). In this paper, we show global changes of game values can be decomposed to policy changes localized at each information set, with a novel term named \emph{policy-change density}. Based on this, we propose \emph{Joint Policy Search} (JPS) that iteratively improves joint policies of collaborative agents in incomplete information games, without re-evaluating the entire game. On multiple collaborative tabular games, JPS is proven to never worsen performance and can improve solutions provided by unilateral approaches (e.g, CFR), outperforming algorithms designed for collaborative policy learning (e.g. BAD). Furthermore, for real-world game whose states are too many to enumerate, \ours{} has an online form that naturally links with gradient updates. We test it to Contract Bridge, a 4-player imperfect-information game where a team of $2$ collaborates to compete against the other. In its bidding phase, players bid in turn to find a good contract through a limited information channel. Based on a strong baseline agent that bids competitive bridge purely through domain-agnostic self-play, JPS improves collaboration of team players and outperforms WBridge5, a championship-winning software, by $+0.63$ IMPs (International Matching Points) per board over $1000$ games, substantially better than previous SoTA ($+0.41$ IMPs/b against WBridge5). Note that $+0.1$ IMPs/b is regarded as a nontrivial improvement in Computer Bridge.
originalAbstract: To learn good joint policies for multi-agent collaboration with incomplete information remains a fundamental challenge. While for two-player zero-sum games, coordinate-ascent approaches (optimizing one agent's policy at a time, e.g., self-play) work with guarantees, in multi-agent cooperative setting they often converge to sub-optimal Nash equilibrium. On the other hand, directly modeling joint policy changes in incomplete information game is nontrivial due to complicated interplay of policies (e.g., upstream updates affect downstream state reachability). In this paper, we show global changes of game values can be decomposed to policy changes localized at each information set, with a novel term named \emph{policy-change density}. Based on this, we propose \emph{Joint Policy Search} (JPS) that iteratively improves joint policies of collaborative agents in incomplete information games, without re-evaluating the entire game. On multiple collaborative tabular games, JPS is proven to never worsen performance and can improve solutions provided by unilateral approaches (e.g, CFR), outperforming algorithms designed for collaborative policy learning (e.g. BAD). Furthermore, for real-world game whose states are too many to enumerate, \ours{} has an online form that naturally links with gradient updates. We test it to Contract Bridge, a 4-player imperfect-information game where a team of $2$ collaborates to compete against the other. In its bidding phase, players bid in turn to find a good contract through a limited information channel. Based on a strong baseline agent that bids competitive bridge purely through domain-agnostic self-play, JPS improves collaboration of team players and outperforms WBridge5, a championship-winning software, by $+0.63$ IMPs (International Matching Points) per board over $1000$ games, substantially better than previous SoTA ($+0.41$ IMPs/b against WBridge5). Note that $+0.1$ IMPs/b is regarded as a nontrivial improvement in Computer Bridge.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents can become stuck when they improve their policies one at a time. An individually unhelpful change may become useful if a teammate also changes. With incomplete information, coordinating such updates is especially difficult because an earlier policy change can alter which later situations are reached.

The paper introduces policy-change density to decompose changes in overall game value into policy changes at individual information sets. Joint Policy Search uses this decomposition to improve collaborative policies without reevaluating the entire game. In the tabular settings discussed, it is proved not to worsen performance and can improve solutions produced by unilateral methods. An online form connects the approach to gradient updates when game states cannot be fully enumerated.

For Contract Bridge bidding, JPS improves a strong self-play baseline by strengthening cooperation between teammates. Against WBridge5, it achieves an advantage of 0.63 IMPs per board over 1,000 games, compared with the previous reported state-of-the-art advantage of 0.41. These results provide empirical evidence for coordinated policy improvement in a large imperfect-information game, alongside the tabular guarantees.
summary.tldr: Joint Policy Search coordinates collaborative policy updates through a local decomposition of game-value changes and improves competitive bridge bidding.

title: Joint Policy Search for Multi-agent Collaboration with Imperfect Information

abstract: Many recent AI architectures are inspired by zero-sum games, however, the behavior of their dynamics is still not well understood. Inspired by this, we study standard gradient descent ascent (GDA) dynamics in a specific class of non-convex non-concave zero-sum games, that we call hidden zero-sum games. In this class, players control the inputs of smooth but possibly non-linear functions whose outputs are being applied as inputs to a convex-concave game. Unlike general zero-sum games, these games have a well-defined notion of solution; outcomes that implement the von-Neumann equilibrium of the ``hidden" convex-concave game. We provide conditions under which vanilla GDA provably converges not merely to local Nash, but the actual von-Neumann solution. If the hidden game lacks strict convexity properties, GDA may fail to converge to any equilibrium, however, by applying standard regularization techniques we can prove convergence to a von-Neumann solution of a slightly perturbed zero-sum game. Our convergence results are non-local despite working in the setting of non-convex non-concave games. Critically, under proper assumptions we combine the Center-Stable Manifold Theorem along with novel type of initialization dependent Lyapunov functions to prove that almost all initial conditions converge to the solution. Finally, we discuss diverse applications of our framework ranging from generative adversarial networks to evolutionary biology.

summary.tldr: Hidden convex-concave structure yields conditional convergence guarantees for gradient descent ascent in certain non-convex, non-concave games.

title: Solving Min-Max Optimization with Hidden Structure via Gradient Descent Ascent

abstract: We present a sound and complete algorithm, called iterative causal discovery (ICD), for recovering causal graphs in the presence of latent confounders and selection bias. ICD relies on the causal Markov and faithfulness assumptions and recovers the equivalence class of the underlying causal graph. It starts with a complete graph, and consists of a single iterative stage that gradually refines this graph by identifying conditional independence (CI) between connected nodes. Independence and causal relations entailed after any iteration are correct, rendering ICD anytime. Essentially, we tie the size of the CI conditioning set to its distance on the graph from the tested nodes, and increase this value in the successive iteration. Thus, each iteration refines a graph that was recovered by previous iterations having smaller conditioning sets---a higher statistical power---which contributes to stability. We demonstrate empirically that ICD requires significantly fewer CI tests and learns more accurate causal graphs compared to FCI, FCI+, and RFCI algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper introduces iterative causal discovery, ICD, for learning causal graph structure when hidden confounders and selection bias may be present. Under the causal Markov and faithfulness assumptions, the algorithm recovers the equivalence class of the underlying causal graph. Its target therefore represents causal structures compatible with the available independence information.

ICD begins with every pair of nodes connected and repeatedly refines the graph through conditional-independence tests. It links the size of each conditioning set to its graph distance from the tested nodes, increasing this value across iterations. Earlier rounds use smaller conditioning sets, whose greater statistical power helps provide a stable graph for later refinement.

The algorithm is sound and complete under its stated assumptions, and the independence and causal relations established after each iteration are correct within that framework. This makes ICD an anytime method: intermediate iterations already supply valid deductions. Empirical comparisons show significantly fewer independence tests and more accurate recovered graphs than FCI, FCI+, and RFCI.
summary.tldr: ICD progressively refines causal graphs under stated assumptions, with valid intermediate deductions and fewer independence tests in reported comparisons.

title: Iterative Causal Discovery in the Possible Presence of Latent Confounders and Selection Bias

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are limited in their expressive power, struggle with long-range interactions and lack a principled way to model higher-order structures. These problems can be attributed to the strong coupling between the computational graph and the input graph structure. The recently proposed Message Passing Simplicial Networks naturally decouple these elements by performing message passing on the clique complex of the graph. Nevertheless, these models can be severely constrained by the rigid combinatorial structure of Simplicial Complexes (SCs). In this work, we extend recent theoretical results on SCs to regular Cell Complexes, topological objects that flexibly subsume SCs and graphs. We show that this generalisation provides a powerful set of graph "lifting" transformations, each leading to a unique hierarchical message passing procedure. The resulting methods, which we collectively call CW Networks (CWNs), are strictly more powerful than the WL test and not less powerful than the 3-WL test. In particular, we demonstrate the effectiveness of one such scheme, based on rings, when applied to molecular graph problems. The proposed architecture benefits from provably larger expressivity than commonly used GNNs, principled modelling of higher-order signals and from compressing the distances between nodes. We demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art results on a variety of molecular datasets.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often tie their message-passing structure directly to the input graph. This can restrict expressivity, long-range interaction, and the treatment of higher-order structures. This paper develops CW Networks by moving message passing onto regular cell complexes, mathematical structures that flexibly include graphs and simplicial complexes.

Different ways of lifting a graph into a cell complex produce different hierarchical message-passing procedures. The authors establish that the resulting methods are strictly more expressive than the Weisfeiler-Lehman test and at least as powerful as the 3-WL test. The architecture also provides principled handling of higher-order signals and compresses distances between nodes, addressing several limitations of ordinary graph-based computation.

The theoretical and empirical contributions complement each other: cell complexes provide a broader representational framework, while the molecular experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of one concrete way to use that flexibility.
summary.tldr: CW Networks perform hierarchical message passing on cell complexes, gaining stronger expressivity and achieving leading results on molecular datasets.

title: Weisfeiler and Lehman Go Cellular: CW Networks

abstract: Consider the following instance of the Offline Meta Reinforcement Learning (OMRL) problem: given the complete training logs of $N$ conventional RL agents, trained on $N$ different tasks, design a meta-agent that can quickly maximize reward in a new, unseen task from the same task distribution. In particular, while each conventional RL agent explored and exploited its own different task, the meta-agent must identify regularities in the data that lead to effective exploration/exploitation in the unseen task. Here, we take a Bayesian RL (BRL) view, and seek to learn a Bayes-optimal policy from the offline data. Building on the recent VariBAD BRL approach, we develop an off-policy BRL method that learns to plan an exploration strategy based on an adaptive neural belief estimate. However, learning to infer such a belief from offline data brings a new identifiability issue we term MDP ambiguity. We characterize the problem, and suggest resolutions via data collection and modification procedures.Finally, we evaluate our framework on a diverse set of domains, including difficult sparse reward tasks, and demonstrate learning of effective exploration behavior that is qualitatively different from the exploration used by any RL agent in the data. Our code is available online at \url{https://github.com/Rondorf/BOReL}.

paragraphs: The paper asks how training logs from agents solving different tasks can teach a new agent to learn quickly on an unseen task from the same distribution. The challenge includes learning how to explore: the new agent must extract regularities across past experience that help it decide what information to seek and when to pursue reward.

Taking a Bayesian reinforcement-learning perspective, the authors build an off-policy extension of VariBAD. It plans exploration using an adaptive neural estimate of beliefs about the task. Learning those beliefs from offline data introduces an identifiability problem they call MDP ambiguity. The paper characterizes this issue and proposes data collection and modification procedures to address it.

Evaluations span multiple domains, including difficult tasks with sparse rewards. The learned agent displays effective exploration that is qualitatively different from the exploration of any individual agent supplying the logs. This supports the possibility of learning new exploration behavior from offline experience, while highlighting that the data must support useful task identification. Learning a Bayes-optimal policy is the stated objective, rather than an unconditional achieved guarantee.
summary.tldr: An offline Bayesian meta-RL method learns exploration across tasks while addressing ambiguity in inferring task beliefs from logged data.

title: Offline Meta Reinforcement Learning -- Identifiability Challenges and Effective Data Collection Strategies

abstract: We consider a standard distributed optimisation setting where $N$ machines, each holding a $d$-dimensional function $f_i$, aim to jointly minimise the sum of the functions $\sum_{i = 1}^N f_i (x)$. This problem arises naturally in large-scale distributed optimisation, where a standard solution is to apply variants of (stochastic) gradient descent. We focus on the communication complexity of this problem: our main result provides the first fully unconditional bounds on total number of bits which need to be sent and received by the $N$ machines to solve this problem under point-to-point communication, within a given error-tolerance. Specifically, we show that $\Omega( Nd \log d / N\varepsilon)$ total bits need to be communicated between the machines to find an additive $\epsilon$-approximation to the minimum of $\sum_{i = 1}^N f_i (x)$. The result holds for both deterministic and randomised algorithms, and, importantly, requires no assumptions on the algorithm structure. The lower bound is tight under certain restrictions on parameter values, and is matched within constant factors for quadratic objectives by a new variant of quantised gradient descent, which we describe and analyse. Our results bring over tools from communication complexity to distributed optimisation, which has potential for further applications.

paragraphs: In distributed optimization, separate machines hold different functions and cooperate to minimize their sum. Computation is only part of the cost: the machines must also exchange information. This paper studies the total number of communicated bits needed to reach a specified additive error when communication occurs directly between pairs of machines.

The main result is an unconditional communication lower bound that applies to deterministic and randomized algorithms without restricting their structure. It relates necessary communication to the number of machines, function dimension, and error tolerance. This breadth matters because the bound is not limited to a particular gradient-descent implementation or a prescribed pattern of algorithmic steps.

Under certain restrictions on parameter values, the lower bound is tight. For quadratic objectives, the authors also develop and analyze a quantized gradient-descent variant that matches the bound within constant factors. The work thus connects an impossibility result with an achievable communication cost in the stated setting. It brings tools from communication complexity into distributed optimization to identify which communication savings are fundamentally attainable.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes algorithm-independent communication lower bounds for distributed optimization and matches them in specified settings with quantized gradient descent.

title: Towards Tight Communication Lower Bounds for Distributed Optimisation

abstract: Voting systems have a wide range of applications including recommender systems, web search, product design and elections. Limited by the lack of general-purpose analytical tools, it is difficult to hand-engineer desirable voting rules for each use case. For this reason, it is appealing to automatically discover voting rules geared towards each scenario. In this paper, we show that set-input neural network architectures such as Set Transformers, fully-connected graph networks and DeepSets are both theoretically and empirically well-suited for learning voting rules. In particular, we show that these network models can not only mimic a number of existing voting rules to compelling accuracy --- both position-based (such as Plurality and Borda) and comparison-based (such as Kemeny, Copeland and Maximin) --- but also discover near-optimal voting rules that maximize different social welfare functions. Furthermore, the learned voting rules generalize well to different voter utility distributions and election sizes unseen during training.

paragraphs: Voting rules aggregate preferences in elections and in applications such as recommendation, search, and product design. Designing a suitable rule by hand is difficult when analytical tools do not cover every desired use case. This paper explores learning voting rules automatically using neural architectures designed to accept sets as inputs.

The authors study Set Transformers, fully connected graph networks, and DeepSets, providing theoretical and empirical support for their suitability. The networks can imitate established rules with compelling accuracy, including rules based on ranking positions and rules based on comparisons between alternatives. The examples cover Plurality and Borda as well as Kemeny, Copeland, and Maximin.

The models also learn near-optimal rules for different social welfare objectives, moving beyond imitation of existing procedures. The authors report that learned rules generalize well to voter utility distributions and election sizes absent from training. These findings support a flexible approach to preference aggregation: choose the welfare objective for a scenario and learn a rule suited to it, with empirical evidence of transfer across the tested election settings.
summary.tldr: Set-input neural networks can imitate established voting rules and learn near-optimal rules for different social welfare objectives.

title: Learning to Elect

abstract: Policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) without human intervention are often needlessly complex, making them difficult to analyse and interpret. In a run with $n$ time steps, a policy will make $n$ decisions on actions to take; we conjecture that only a small subset of these decisions delivers value over selecting a simple default action. Given a trained policy, we propose a novel black-box method based on statistical fault localisation that ranks the states of the environment according to the importance of decisions made in those states. We argue that among other things, the ranked list of states can help explain and understand the policy. As the ranking method is statistical, a direct evaluation of its quality is hard. As a proxy for quality, we use the ranking to create new, simpler policies from the original ones by pruning decisions identified as unimportant (that is, replacing them by default actions) and measuring the impact on performance. Our experimental results on a diverse set of standard benchmarks demonstrate that pruned policies can perform on a level comparable to the original policies. We show that naive approaches for ranking policies, e.g. ranking based on the frequency of visiting a state, do not result in high-performing pruned policies. To the best of our knowledge, there are no similar techniques for ranking RL policies' decisions.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy chooses an action at every step, but the authors conjecture that only a small subset of those choices adds value over a simple default action. They investigate whether identifying these consequential decisions can make a trained policy easier to understand and simplify.

summary.tldr: A statistical ranking identifies policy decisions that can be replaced with default actions while preserving comparable performance in benchmark experiments.

title: Ranking Policy Decisions

abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) offer flexible distribution parametrization. However, due to the intractable partition function, they are typically trained via contrastive divergence for maximum likelihood estimation. In this paper, we propose pseudo-spherical contrastive divergence (PS-CD) to generalize maximum likelihood learning of EBMs. PS-CD is derived from the maximization of a family of strictly proper homogeneous scoring rules, which avoids the computation of the intractable partition function and provides a generalized family of learning objectives that include contrastive divergence as a special case. Moreover, PS-CD allows us to flexibly choose various learning objectives to train EBMs without additional computational cost or variational minimax optimization. Theoretical analysis on the proposed method and extensive experiments on both synthetic data and commonly used image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and modeling flexibility of PS-CD, as well as its robustness to data contamination, thus showing its superiority over maximum likelihood and $f$-EBMs.

paragraphs: Energy-based models represent flexible probability distributions, but converting their energy scores into normalized probabilities requires a partition function that is often intractable. Contrastive divergence is commonly used to train these models toward maximum likelihood despite that difficulty. This paper asks whether similarly practical training can support a broader range of objectives.

Pseudo-spherical contrastive divergence, or PS-CD, is derived from a family of strictly proper homogeneous scoring rules. This construction avoids computing the partition function and includes ordinary contrastive divergence as a special case. It allows different learning objectives to be selected without additional computational cost or a variational minimax optimization procedure.

The authors combine theoretical analysis with experiments on synthetic data and standard image datasets. They report effective modeling, flexibility across learning objectives, and robustness to data contamination, with advantages over maximum likelihood and f-EBMs in their evaluation. The significance is that the training criterion becomes adjustable while retaining a practical route around normalization. The reported robustness also shows that this flexibility can matter when the training data contain contamination.
summary.tldr: PS-CD generalizes contrastive divergence to flexible energy-model objectives that avoid partition-function computation and show robustness to contaminated data.

title: Pseudo-Spherical Contrastive Divergence

abstract: Holographic Reduced Representations (HRR) are a method for performing symbolic AI on top of real-valued vectors by associating each vector with an abstract concept, and providing mathematical operations to manipulate vectors as if they were classic symbolic objects. This method has seen little use outside of older symbolic AI work and cognitive science. Our goal is to revisit this approach to understand if it is viable for enabling a hybrid neural-symbolic approach to learning as a differential component of a deep learning architecture. HRRs today are not effective in a differential solution due to numerical instability, a problem we solve by introducing a projection step that forces the vectors to exist in a well behaved point in space. In doing so we improve the concept retrieval efficacy of HRRs by over $100\times$. Using multi-label classification we demonstrate how to leverage the symbolic HRR properties to develop a output layer and loss function that is able to learn effectively, and allows us to investigate some of the pros and cons of an HRR neuro-symbolic learning approach.

paragraphs: Holographic Reduced Representations associate abstract concepts with real-valued vectors and provide operations that manipulate those vectors like symbolic objects. This paper revisits the approach as a possible differentiable component inside deep learning. The aim is to combine symbolic structure with neural learning through operations that can participate directly in training.

The authors identify numerical instability as an obstacle to using these representations in a differentiable system. They introduce a projection step that moves the vectors into a better-behaved region of their representation space. With this change, they report more than a hundredfold improvement in concept retrieval efficacy, addressing a central practical weakness of the representation.

The paper then uses the symbolic properties of these vectors to design an output layer and loss function for multilabel classification. The resulting system learns effectively in that application and provides a way to examine advantages and disadvantages of the neural-symbolic approach. The contribution is both a stabilization technique and a concrete demonstration of how symbolic vector operations can be incorporated into a learned prediction system.
summary.tldr: A stabilizing projection makes Holographic Reduced Representations more effective for concept retrieval and usable in a neural-symbolic multilabel classifier.

title: Learning with Holographic Reduced Representations

abstract: Saliency methods have been widely used to highlight important input features in model predictions. Most existing methods use backpropagation on a modified gradient function to generate saliency maps. Thus, noisy gradients can result in unfaithful feature attributions. In this paper, we tackle this issue and introduce a {\it saliency guided training} procedure for neural networks to reduce noisy gradients used in predictions while retaining the predictive performance of the model. Our saliency guided training procedure iteratively masks features with small and potentially noisy gradients while maximizing the similarity of model outputs for both masked and unmasked inputs. We apply the saliency guided training procedure to various synthetic and real data sets from computer vision, natural language processing, and time series across diverse neural architectures, including Recurrent Neural Networks, Convolutional Networks, and Transformers. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we show that saliency guided training procedure significantly improves model interpretability across various domains while preserving its predictive performance.

Our saliency guided training procedure iteratively masks features with small and potentially noisy gradients while maximizing the similarity of model outputs for both masked and unmasked inputs. We apply the saliency guided training procedure to various synthetic and real data sets from computer vision, natural language processing, and time series across diverse neural architectures, including Recurrent Neural Networks, Convolutional Networks, and Transformers. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we show that saliency guided training procedure significantly improves model interpretability across various domains while preserving its predictive performance.

paragraphs: Saliency methods try to explain a prediction by highlighting the input features that matter to a neural network. Many derive those explanations from gradients, so noisy gradients can lead to misleading feature attributions. This paper tackles that problem during training by encouraging the network to rely less on features associated with small, potentially noisy gradients.

The training procedure repeatedly masks those features and compares the model's outputs on masked and original inputs. It trains the network to make these outputs similar. In effect, predictions are encouraged to remain stable when the selected low-gradient features disappear. The procedure aims to reduce noisy gradient information while preserving the model's ability to perform its prediction task.

The authors evaluate the method on synthetic and real datasets spanning vision, language, and time series, using recurrent networks, convolutional networks, and Transformers. Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations show significant interpretability improvements while retaining predictive performance. These results support the idea that the usefulness of saliency explanations can be improved by changing model training, alongside the methods used to produce explanations.
summary.tldr: Saliency-guided training improves interpretability by making predictions stable when features with small, potentially noisy gradients are masked.

title: Improving Deep Learning Interpretability by Saliency Guided Training

abstract: Deep equilibrium models are based on implicitly defined functional relations and have shown competitive performance compared with the traditional deep networks. Monotone operator equilibrium networks (monDEQ) retain interesting performance with additional theoretical guaranties. Existing certification tools for classical deep networks cannot directly be applied to monDEQs for which much fewer tools exist. We introduce a semialgebraic representation for ReLU based monDEQs which allow to approximate the corresponding input output relation by semidefinite programs (SDP). We present several applications to network certification and obtain SDP models for the following problems : robustness certification, Lipschitz constant estimation, ellipsoidal uncertainty propagation. We use these models to certify robustness of monDEQs with respect to a general $L_p$ norm. Experimental results show that the proposed models outperform existing approaches for monDEQ certification. Furthermore, our investigations suggest that monDEQs are much more robust to $L_2$ perturbations than $L_{\infty}$ perturbations.

This paper focuses on monotone operator equilibrium networks, or monDEQs, with ReLU activations. It develops a mathematical representation that makes several certification questions accessible through semidefinite programming.

The representation is semialgebraic, expressing the network through polynomial relationships and inequalities. From it, the authors construct semidefinite-program approximations to the input–output relation. They apply these models to robustness certification, estimation of Lipschitz constants, and propagation of ellipsoidal uncertainty. These tasks examine how output behavior can be bounded as inputs vary.

The resulting models certify robustness with respect to general Lp norms and outperform existing monDEQ certification approaches in the reported experiments. The investigations also suggest greater robustness to L2 perturbations than to L-infinity perturbations. That comparison is presented as an experimental indication. The broader contribution is a shared optimization-based framework for examining several kinds of guarantees in an implicitly defined network.
summary.tldr: A semialgebraic representation enables semidefinite-program certification of robustness and related properties for ReLU-based monotone equilibrium networks.

title: Semialgebraic Representation of Monotone Deep Equilibrium Models and Applications to Certification

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are shown to be more biologically plausible and energy efficient over their predecessors. However, there is a lack of an efficient and generalized training method for deep SNNs, especially for deployment on analog computing substrates. In this paper, we put forward a generalized learning rule, termed Local Tandem Learning (LTL). The LTL rule follows the teacher-student learning approach by mimicking the intermediate feature representations of a pre-trained ANN. By decoupling the learning of network layers and leveraging highly informative supervisor signals, we demonstrate rapid network convergence within five training epochs on the CIFAR-10 dataset while having low computational complexity. Our experimental results have also shown that the SNNs thus trained can achieve comparable accuracies to their teacher ANNs on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet datasets. Moreover, the proposed LTL rule is hardware friendly. It can be easily implemented on-chip to perform fast parameter calibration and provide robustness against the notorious device non-ideality issues. It, therefore, opens up a myriad of opportunities for training and deployment of SNN on ultra-low-power mixed-signal neuromorphic computing chips.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer opportunities for energy-efficient computing, but training deep versions efficiently remains challenging, particularly for analog hardware. This paper introduces Local Tandem Learning, a teacher-student approach that uses a pretrained artificial neural network to guide the training of a spiking network.

The student learns to mimic intermediate feature representations from its teacher. By separating the learning of different layers and supplying informative supervisory signals, the method reduces training complexity. On CIFAR-10, the authors demonstrate rapid convergence within five training epochs. They also report that the trained spiking networks achieve accuracies comparable to their teacher networks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet.

The proposed rule is designed to suit hardware implementation as well as model training. The authors describe its use for on-chip parameter calibration and robustness to non-ideal device behavior. These properties make the method relevant to mixed-signal neuromorphic chips, where a practical learning rule must cope with the behavior of physical computing components as well as deliver useful predictions.
summary.tldr: Local Tandem Learning trains spiking networks from intermediate teacher features, achieving rapid convergence and teacher-comparable accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Training Spiking Neural Networks with Local Tandem Learning

abstract: There still remains an extreme performance gap between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) when training from scratch on small datasets, which is concluded to the lack of inductive bias. In this paper, we further consider this problem and point out two weaknesses of ViTs in inductive biases, that is, the spatial relevance and diverse channel representation. First, on spatial aspect, objects are locally compact and relevant, thus fine-grained feature needs to be extracted from a token and its neighbors. While the lack of data hinders ViTs to attend the spatial relevance. Second, on channel aspect, representation exhibits diversity on different channels. But the scarce data can not enable ViTs to learn strong enough representation for accurate recognition. To this end, we propose Dynamic Hybrid Vision Transformer (DHVT) as the solution to enhance the two inductive biases. On spatial aspect, we adopt a hybrid structure, in which convolution is integrated into patch embedding and multi-layer perceptron module, forcing the model to capture the token features as well as their neighboring features. On channel aspect, we introduce a dynamic feature aggregation module in MLP and a brand new "head token" design in multi-head self-attention module to help re-calibrate channel representation and make different channel group representation interacts with each other. The fusion of weak channel representation forms a strong enough representation for classification. With this design, we successfully eliminate the performance gap between CNNs and ViTs, and our DHVT achieves a series of state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight model, 85.68% on CIFAR-100 with 22.8M parameters, 82.3% on ImageNet-1K with 24.0M parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/ArieSeirack/DHVT.

With little training data, the model may struggle to discover these useful patterns on its own.

These components make local neighborhoods part of feature extraction. Reported results include 85.68% on CIFAR-100 with 22.8 million parameters and 82.3% on ImageNet-1K with 24 million parameters. The findings support building local spatial structure and channel interaction directly into the architecture when learning them from limited data is difficult.
summary.tldr: DHVT adds local spatial processing and channel interaction to Vision Transformers, closing the reported performance gap with convolutional networks.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Vision Transformers and Convolutional Neural Networks on Small Datasets

abstract: When developing deep learning models, we usually decide what task we want to solve then search for a model that generalizes well on the task. An intriguing question would be: what if, instead of fixing the task and searching in the model space, we fix the model and search in the task space? Can we find tasks that the model generalizes on? How do they look, or do they indicate anything? These are the questions we address in this paper. We propose a task discovery framework that automatically finds examples of such tasks via optimizing a generalization-based quantity called agreement score. We demonstrate that one set of images can give rise to many tasks on which neural networks generalize well. These tasks are a reflection of the inductive biases of the learning framework and the statistical patterns present in the data, thus they can make a useful tool for analyzing the neural networks and their biases. As an example, we show that the discovered tasks can be used to automatically create ''adversarial train-test splits'' which make a model fail at test time, without changing the pixels or labels, but by only selecting how the datapoints should be split between the train and test sets. We end with a discussion on human-interpretability of the discovered tasks.

paragraphs: Most model development begins with a chosen task and searches for a network that generalizes well on it. This paper reverses the direction: it fixes the learning model and searches for tasks on which that model generalizes. The resulting tasks provide a way to investigate what the learning framework naturally tends to capture in a dataset.

These tasks reflect both the learning framework's inductive biases and statistical patterns in the data, making them useful objects of analysis.

One application uses discovered tasks to construct adversarial training-test splits. By choosing which examples belong in each split, the method can cause test-time failure without altering image pixels or labels. This demonstrates how task discovery can expose vulnerabilities in generalization that depend on dataset partitioning. The paper also discusses whether the discovered tasks are interpretable to people.
summary.tldr: Task discovery searches for tasks a fixed model generalizes on, revealing biases and enabling adversarial training-test splits.

title: Task Discovery: Finding the Tasks that Neural Networks Generalize on

abstract: Designing an incentive-compatible auction mechanism that maximizes the auctioneer's revenue while minimizes the bidders’ ex-post regret is an important yet intricate problem in economics. Remarkable progress has been achieved through learning the optimal auction mechanism by neural networks. In this paper, we consider the popular additive valuation and symmetric valuation setting; i.e., the valuation for a set of items is defined as the sum of all items’ valuations in the set, and the valuation distribution is invariant when the bidders and/or the items are permutated. We prove that permutation-equivariant neural networks have significant advantages: the permutation-equivariance decreases the expected ex-post regret, improves the model generalizability, while maintains the expected revenue invariant. This implies that the permutation-equivariance helps approach the theoretically optimal dominant strategy incentive compatible condition, and reduces the required sample complexity for desired generalization. Extensive experiments fully support our theory. To our best knowledge, this is the first work towards understanding the benefits of permutation-equivariance in auction mechanisms.

paragraphs: A learned auction mechanism must balance revenue with bidders' incentives to report their valuations honestly. The paper studies this problem under additive valuations, where a bundle's value is the sum of its items' values, and symmetric valuation distributions. Symmetry means that relabeling bidders or items leaves the valuation distribution unchanged.

The proposed architectural principle is permutation equivariance: when bidders or items are reordered, the mechanism's outputs reorder correspondingly. The authors prove that incorporating this structure decreases expected ex-post regret while preserving expected revenue. Here, regret concerns a bidder's incentive to benefit from changing their report after valuations are realized.

The analysis also establishes improved generalization and a reduction in the samples needed for a desired generalization level. These results explain why respecting the problem's symmetry can help learned auctions approach dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. The paper reports experiments supporting the theory. Its claims are tied to the stated additive and symmetric setting; reduced expected regret is progress toward incentive compatibility rather than an assertion that every learned mechanism achieves it exactly.
summary.tldr: Under additive, symmetric valuations, permutation-equivariant auction networks reduce expected bidder regret and improve generalization while preserving expected revenue.

title: Benefits of Permutation-Equivariance in Auction Mechanisms

abstract: We provide a differentially private algorithm for producing synthetic data simultaneously useful for multiple tasks: marginal queries and multitask machine learning (ML). A key innovation in our algorithm is the ability to directly handle numerical features, in contrast to a number of related prior approaches which require numerical features to be first converted into {high cardinality} categorical features via {a binning strategy}. Higher binning granularity is required for better accuracy, but this negatively impacts scalability. Eliminating the need for binning allows us to produce synthetic data preserving large numbers of statistical queries such as marginals on numerical features, and class conditional linear threshold queries. Preserving the latter means that the fraction of points of each class label above a particular half-space is roughly the same in both the real and synthetic data. This is the property that is needed to train a linear classifier in a multitask setting. Our algorithm also allows us to produce high quality synthetic data for mixed marginal queries, that combine both categorical and numerical features. Our method consistently runs 2-5x faster than the best comparable techniques, and provides significant accuracy improvements in both marginal queries and linear prediction tasks for mixed-type datasets.

paragraphs: Private synthetic data must protect the original records while retaining information useful for analysis. This paper proposes a differentially private generator designed for both statistical queries and multitask machine learning. Its central design choice is to handle numerical features directly, avoiding conversion into many categorical bins.

Binning creates a trade-off: finer bins can improve accuracy but make the problem larger and less scalable. Removing that step lets the method preserve many numerical marginal queries and class-conditional linear-threshold queries. The latter ask what fraction of examples from a given class fall on one side of a linear boundary. Keeping those fractions approximately consistent between real and synthetic data supplies the property needed for linear-classifier training in the multitask setting.
