paragraphs: Elo ratings summarize outcomes from paired contests and are increasingly used to rank language models through comparisons of their answers. This paper examines whether that approach behaves reliably when applied to models treated as having fixed skill levels. That setting differs from the changing abilities of players in the games for which Elo was originally designed.

The authors organize their investigation around reliability and transitivity, two properties they argue an evaluation method should satisfy. They examine Elo in both simulated and real-world scenarios and find substantial volatility in individual computations. They also show that the two desired properties do not always hold, meaning a comparative ranking can fall short of the consistency expected of an evaluation system.

These results matter when a single ranking is used to stand in for expensive direct comparisons between models. The paper develops concrete guidance informed by the two axioms to improve evaluation reliability. Its conclusion calls for reassessing current comparative practices, grounded in observed failures rather than a claim that every Elo-based ranking is unreliable.
summary.tldr: Simulations and real-world evaluations show that Elo rankings of language models can be volatile and fail reliability and transitivity requirements.

title: Elo Uncovered: Robustness and Best Practices in Language Model Evaluation

abstract: Transformers with linear attention (i.e., linear transformers) and state-space models have recently been suggested as a viable linear-time alternative to transformers with softmax attention. However, these models still underperform transformers especially on tasks that require in-context retrieval. While more expressive variants of linear transformers which replace the additive update in linear transformers with the delta rule (DeltaNet) have been found to be more effective at associative recall, existing algorithms for training such models do not parallelize over sequence length and are thus inefficient to train on modern hardware. This work describes a hardware-efficient algorithm for training linear transformers with the delta rule, which exploits a memory-efficient representation for computing products of Householder matrices. This algorithm allows us to scale up DeltaNet to standard language modeling settings. We train a 1.3B model for 100B tokens and find that it outperforms recent linear-time baselines such as Mamba and GLA in terms of perplexity and zero-shot performance on downstream tasks. We also experiment with two hybrid models which combine DeltaNet layers with (1) sliding-window attention layers every other layer or (2) two global attention layers, and find that these hybrids outperform strong transformer baselines.

paragraphs: Linear transformers offer linear-time sequence processing, but their performance has lagged behind softmax transformers, especially on tasks involving retrieval from context. DeltaNet replaces the usual additive update with the more expressive delta rule and has shown better associative recall. Its practical obstacle has been training algorithms that cannot parallelize across sequence length.

This paper introduces a hardware-efficient training algorithm that addresses that obstacle through a memory-efficient representation of products of Householder matrices. The contribution makes the delta-rule computation suitable for parallel training on modern hardware, enabling DeltaNet to scale to standard language-modeling settings. It connects an expressive update mechanism with a more practical way to train it.

The authors train a 1.3B-parameter model on 100B tokens and report better perplexity and zero-shot downstream performance than Mamba and GLA. They also test hybrids combining DeltaNet with alternating sliding-window attention layers or two global attention layers. Both hybrid designs outperform strong transformer baselines in the reported evaluations, supporting the value of combining these mechanisms.
summary.tldr: A parallel training algorithm makes DeltaNet practical at language-model scale, with strong reported results for both pure and attention-hybrid models.

title: Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length

abstract: In multiplayer games, self-interested behavior among the players can harm the social welfare. Tax mechanisms are a common method to alleviate this issue and induce socially optimal behavior. In this work, we take the initial step of learning the optimal tax that can maximize social welfare with limited feedback in congestion games. We propose a new type of feedback named \emph{equilibrium feedback}, where the tax designer can only observe the Nash equilibrium after deploying a tax plan. Existing algorithms are not applicable due to the exponentially large tax function space, nonexistence of the gradient, and nonconvexity of the objective. To tackle these challenges, we design a computationally efficient algorithm that leverages several novel components: (1) a piece-wise linear tax to approximate the optimal tax; (2) extra linear terms to guarantee a strongly convex potential function; (3) an efficient subroutine to find the exploratory tax that can provide critical information about the game. The algorithm can find an $\epsilon$-optimal tax with $O(\beta F^2/\epsilon)$ sample complexity, where $\beta$ is the smoothness of the cost function and $F$ is the number of facilities.

paragraphs: When many self-interested users share congested facilities, their choices can reduce overall welfare. Taxes can change those incentives, but choosing an effective tax is difficult when the designer has limited information. This paper studies equilibrium feedback: after deploying a tax plan, the designer observes only the Nash equilibrium that results.

The optimization problem combines an enormous space of possible tax functions with a nonconvex objective and unavailable gradients. The proposed algorithm approximates the optimal tax using piecewise-linear functions. It adds linear terms to ensure a strongly convex potential function and uses a dedicated subroutine to select exploratory taxes that reveal useful information about the game.

The authors prove that this computationally efficient procedure can find an ε-optimal tax with sample complexity O(βF²/ε), where β describes cost-function smoothness and F is the number of facilities. The result connects welfare optimization to the information obtainable from repeated equilibrium observations. It shows how structured tax choices and purposeful exploration can make learning feasible under the paper's restricted feedback model.
summary.tldr: A computationally efficient algorithm learns near-optimal congestion taxes using only the equilibria observed after tax deployment.

title: Learning Optimal Tax Design in Nonatomic Congestion Games

abstract: Traditional video restoration approaches were designed to recover clean videos from a specific type of degradation, making them ineffective in handling multiple unknown types of degradation. To address this issue, several studies have been conducted and have shown promising results. However, these studies overlook that the degradations in video usually change over time, dubbed time-varying unknown degradations (TUD). To tackle such a less-touched challenge, we propose an innovative method, termed as All-in-one VidEo Restoration Network (AverNet), which comprises two core modules, i.e., Prompt-Guided Alignment (PGA) module and Prompt-Conditioned Enhancement (PCE) module. Specifically, PGA addresses the issue of pixel shifts caused by time-varying degradations by learning and utilizing prompts to align video frames at the pixel level. To handle multiple unknown degradations, PCE recasts it into a conditional restoration problem by implicitly establishing a conditional map between degradations and ground truths. Thanks to the collaboration between PGA and PCE modules, AverNet empirically demonstrates its effectiveness in recovering videos from TUD. Extensive experiments are carried out on two synthesized datasets featuring seven types of degradations with random corruption levels. The code is available at https://github.com/XLearning-SCU/2024-NeurIPS-AverNet.

paragraphs: Restoring a video becomes harder when the type and strength of corruption change over time. A method designed for one degradation cannot readily handle several unknown ones, and handling multiple types alone does not address their variation between frames. AverNet targets this combined problem through a single restoration network with two cooperating modules.

The first module, Prompt-Guided Alignment, learns prompts that help align frames at the pixel level. It addresses pixel shifts associated with changing degradations, so the restoration process can relate corresponding image content across time. The second module, Prompt-Conditioned Enhancement, treats recovery as a conditional problem, implicitly learning a relationship between degraded inputs and their clean targets.

The two modules therefore address different parts of the task: aligning changing observations and conditioning their enhancement on the corruption. Experiments on two synthetic datasets, containing seven degradation types with randomly varied corruption levels, show that their combination can recover videos affected by time-varying unknown degradations. These results provide empirical support for jointly handling temporal alignment and adaptive restoration.
summary.tldr: AverNet combines prompt-guided frame alignment and conditional enhancement to restore videos whose unknown degradations change over time.

title: AverNet: All-in-one Video Restoration for Time-varying Unknown Degradations

abstract: Computer simulations have long presented the exciting possibility of scientific insight into complex real-world processes. Despite the power of modern computing, however, it remains challenging to systematically perform inference under simulation models. This has led to the rise of simulation-based inference (SBI), a class of machine learning-enabled techniques for approaching inverse problems with stochastic simulators. Many such methods, however, require large numbers of simulation samples and face difficulty scaling to high-dimensional settings, often making inference prohibitive under resource-intensive simulators. To mitigate these drawbacks, we introduce active sequential neural posterior estimation (ASNPE). ASNPE brings an active learning scheme into the inference loop to estimate the utility of simulation parameter candidates to the underlying probabilistic model. The proposed acquisition scheme is easily integrated into existing posterior estimation pipelines, allowing for improved sample efficiency with low computational overhead. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in the travel demand calibration setting, a high-dimensional inverse problem commonly requiring computationally expensive traffic simulators. Our method outperforms well-tuned benchmarks and state-of-the-art posterior estimation methods on a large-scale real-world traffic network, as well as demonstrates a performance advantage over non-active counterparts on a suite of SBI benchmark environments.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference works backward from observations to plausible parameters of a stochastic simulator. Neural posterior estimation learns a probability distribution over those parameters, but collecting enough simulations can be expensive. This becomes particularly difficult when the parameter space is large and each simulator run consumes substantial resources.

Active sequential neural posterior estimation, or ASNPE, introduces active learning into that process. It estimates how useful candidate simulation parameters would be to the probabilistic model and uses that assessment to guide further sampling. The acquisition scheme can be incorporated into existing posterior-estimation pipelines with low computational overhead. Its purpose is to make the simulation budget more informative, improving sample efficiency.

The authors demonstrate the method on travel-demand calibration for a large real-world traffic network, a high-dimensional problem involving expensive traffic simulation. ASNPE outperforms well-tuned benchmarks and state-of-the-art posterior estimators there. It also improves over non-active counterparts across simulation-based inference benchmarks, supporting active selection as a practical way to improve how posterior estimators use simulation samples.
summary.tldr: ASNPE actively selects informative simulation parameters to improve posterior estimation's sample efficiency with low additional computational overhead.

title: Active Sequential Posterior Estimation for Sample-Efficient Simulation-Based Inference

abstract: We demonstrate a compactness result holding broadly across supervised learning with a general class of loss functions: Any hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ is learnable with transductive sample complexity $m$ precisely when all of its finite projections are learnable with sample complexity $m$. We prove that this exact form of compactness holds for realizable and agnostic learning with respect to all proper metric loss functions (e.g., any norm on $\mathbb{R}^d$) and any continuous loss on a compact space (e.g., cross-entropy, squared loss). For realizable learning with improper metric losses, we show that exact compactness of sample complexity can fail, and provide matching upper and lower bounds of a factor of 2 on the extent to which such sample complexities can differ. We conjecture that larger gaps are possible for the agnostic case. Furthermore, invoking the equivalence between sample complexities in the PAC and transductive models (up to lower order factors, in the realizable case) permits us to directly port our results to the PAC model, revealing an almost-exact form of compactness holding broadly in PAC learning.

We prove that this exact form of compactness holds for realizable and agnostic learning with respect to all proper metric loss functions (e.g., any norm on $\mathbb{R}^d$) and any continuous loss on a compact space (e.g., cross-entropy, squared loss). We conjecture that larger gaps are possible for the agnostic case. paragraphs: This paper asks whether learning an entire hypothesis class can be characterized by learning all of its finite projections. Its compactness result says that, across broad settings, the answer is exact: the full class has transductive sample complexity m if and only if every finite projection has that same sample complexity.

The authors prove this equivalence for realizable and agnostic learning under proper metric losses, and for continuous losses on compact spaces. The result therefore links a potentially unrestricted learning problem to its finite restrictions without changing the required sample complexity. The permitted loss functions are central to the scope of that exact statement.

For realizable learning with improper metric losses, exact equality can fail. Matching upper and lower bounds show that sample complexities can differ by a factor of two; larger agnostic gaps are conjectured, not proved. Using an existing connection between transductive and PAC sample complexities in the realizable case, the authors also transfer the results to an almost-exact compactness statement for PAC learning.
summary.tldr: For broad classes of losses, transductive learnability has exactly the same sample complexity as learnability of every finite projection.

title: Transductive Learning is Compact

abstract: Video generative models are receiving particular attention given their ability to generate realistic and imaginative frames. Besides, these models are also observed to exhibit strong 3D consistency, significantly enhancing their potential to act as world simulators. In this work, we present Vidu4D, a novel reconstruction model that excels in accurately reconstructing 4D (i.e., sequential 3D) representations from single generated videos, addressing challenges associated with non-rigidity and frame distortion. This capability is pivotal for creating high-fidelity virtual contents that maintain both spatial and temporal coherence. At the core of Vidu4D is our proposed Dynamic Gaussian Surfels (DGS) technique. DGS optimizes time-varying warping functions to transform Gaussian surfels (surface elements) from a static state to a dynamically warped state. This transformation enables a precise depiction of motion and deformation over time. To preserve the structural integrity of surface-aligned Gaussian surfels, we design the warped-state geometric regularization based on continuous warping fields for estimating normals. Additionally, we learn refinements on rotation and scaling parameters of Gaussian surfels, which greatly alleviates texture flickering during the warping process and enhances the capture of fine-grained appearance details. Vidu4D also contains a novel initialization state that provides a proper start for the warping fields in DGS. Equipping Vidu4D with an existing video generative model, the overall framework demonstrates high-fidelity text-to-4D generation in both appearance and geometry.

summary.tldr: Vidu4D reconstructs coherent, deforming 3D content from a single generated video using dynamically warped Gaussian surface elements.

title: Vidu4D: Single Generated Video to High-Fidelity 4D Reconstruction with Dynamic Gaussian Surfels

abstract: This paper focuses on the soundscape art of the Ming Dynasty’s Temple of Heaven sacrificial rituals, innovatively employing generative AI hallucinations as a means to reshape spiritual perception and cultural memory. By integrating traditional archival reconstructions—ritual texts, spatial models, and restored music—with AI-generated blurred and dynamic audiovisual hallucinations, the work creates a dynamic tension between historical rigor and machine ambiguity. A three-screen interactive installation combining traditional soundscape data, AI hallucinations, and ritual timeline enables real-time audience participation to influence the hallucinations, enhancing the sacred atmosphere and individual experience of the ritual soundscape, and reflecting the fluid boundaries of memory, perception, and imagination. This project does not pursue historical reproduction but embraces the instability of AI generative systems to explore new possibilities for cultural heritage, synthetic memory, spiritual experience, and collective imagination.

A three-screen interactive installation brings together the traditional soundscape information, generated hallucinations, and a ritual timeline. The installation uses that tension to explore sacred atmosphere, individual experience, and collective imagination. Its contribution is an approach to cultural heritage art in which reconstructed evidence and synthetic memory remain visibly intertwined.
summary.tldr: An interactive installation combines reconstructed Ming ritual soundscapes with AI hallucinations to explore cultural memory and spiritual experience.

title: Between Reality and AI Hallucinations: Reimagining the Sacred Soundscape of Ming Rituals

abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) is an effective method for aligning generative models with human preferences and has been successfully applied to fine‑tune text‑to‑image diffusion models. Its practical adoption, however, is hindered by a labor‑intensive pipeline that first produces a large set of candidate images and then requires humans to rank them pairwise. We address this bottleneck with self‑supervised direct preference optimization, a new paradigm that removes the need for any pre‑generated images or manual ranking. During training, we create preference pairs on the fly through self‑supervised image transformations, allowing the model to learn from fresh and diverse comparisons at every iteration. This online strategy eliminates costly data collection and annotation while remaining plug‑and‑play for any text‑to‑image diffusion method. Surprisingly, the on‑the‑fly pairs produced by the proposed method not only match but exceed the effectiveness of conventional DPO, which we attribute to the greater diversity of preferences sampled during training. Extensive experiments with Stable Diffusion 1.5 and Stable Diffusion XL confirm that our method delivers substantial gains.

paragraphs: Direct preference optimization can improve text-to-image models by training them on preferred and less-preferred image pairs. Preparing those comparisons usually requires generating many candidate images and asking humans to rank them. This paper introduces a self-supervised version that removes both the pre-generated image collection and the manual pairwise ranking stage.

Instead, the method creates preference pairs during training through self-supervised image transformations. Each iteration can therefore use fresh comparisons, rather than drawing only from a fixed collection prepared beforehand. The authors present this online procedure as compatible with any text-to-image diffusion method, making the central change the source of preference supervision rather than a particular model architecture.

Experiments with Stable Diffusion 1.5 and Stable Diffusion XL show substantial gains. The authors report that the dynamically produced pairs exceed the effectiveness of conventional DPO and attribute this advantage to the greater diversity of preferences encountered during training. The findings suggest that removing costly annotation can also improve the training signal when self-supervised transformations supply useful, varied comparisons.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised DPO creates image preference pairs during training, eliminating manual ranking while improving results on two Stable Diffusion models.

title: Self-Supervised Direct Preference Optimization for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

abstract: Designing functional proteins is a critical yet challenging problem due to the intricate interplay between backbone structures, sequences, and side-chains. Current approaches often decompose protein design into separate tasks, which can lead to accumulated errors, while recent efforts increasingly focus on all-atom protein design. However, we observe that existing all-atom generation approaches suffering from an information shortcut issue, where models inadvertently infer sequences from side-chain information, compromising their ability to accurately learn sequence distributions. To address this, we introduce a novel rationalized information flow strategy to eliminate the information shortcut. Furthermore, motivated by the advantages of Bayesian flows over differential equation–based methods, we propose the first Bayesian flow formulation for protein backbone orientations by recasting orientation modeling as an equivalent hyperspherical generation problem with antipodal symmetry. To validate, our method delivers consistently exceptional performance in both peptide and antibody design tasks.

However, we observe that existing all-atom generation approaches suffering from an information shortcut issue, where models inadvertently infer sequences from side-chain information, compromising their ability to accurately learn sequence distributions. To address this, we introduce a novel rationalized information flow strategy to eliminate the information shortcut. Furthermore, motivated by the advantages of Bayesian flows over differential equation–based methods, we propose the first Bayesian flow formulation for protein backbone orientations by recasting orientation modeling as an equivalent hyperspherical generation problem with antipodal symmetry. paragraphs: Protein design involves coupled choices about the amino-acid sequence, backbone structure, and side chains. Solving these separately can accumulate errors, motivating methods that generate them together. The authors identify a problem in existing all-atom approaches: side-chain information can reveal sequence information, allowing a model to take a shortcut instead of accurately learning the sequence distribution.

Their method introduces an information-flow strategy designed to eliminate this shortcut. It also develops a Bayesian flow formulation for backbone orientations. To do this, orientation modeling is recast as an equivalent generation problem on a hypersphere with antipodal symmetry. That symmetry makes opposite points equivalent within the representation, allowing the orientation problem to be expressed in the proposed form.

The resulting approach combines controlled information exchange with a Bayesian treatment of orientation generation. The authors report consistently strong performance on peptide and antibody design tasks. The key implication is that jointly modeling protein components requires attention to which information each component can access: richer all-atom information can otherwise undermine the distribution the model is meant to learn.
summary.tldr: The method controls information flow to prevent sequence shortcuts and introduces Bayesian generation of backbone orientations for all-atom protein design.

title: Rationalized All-Atom Protein Design with Unified Multi-Modal Bayesian Flow

abstract: In standard autoregressive generation, an LLM predicts the next-token distribution, samples a discrete token, and then discards the distribution, passing only the sampled token as new input. To preserve this distribution’s rich information, we propose Mixture of Inputs (MoI), a training-free method for autoregressive generation. After generating a token following the standard paradigm, we construct a new input that blends the generated discrete token with the previously discarded token distribution. Specifically, we employ a Bayesian estimation method that treats the token distribution as the prior, the sampled token as the observation, and replaces the conventional one-hot vector with the continuous posterior expectation as the new model input. MoI allows the model to maintain a richer internal representation throughout the generation process, resulting in improved text quality and reasoning capabilities. On mathematical reasoning, code generation, and PhD-level QA tasks, MoI consistently improves performance across multiple models including QwQ-32B, Nemotron-Super-49B, Gemma-3-27B, and DAPO-Qwen-32B, with no additional training and negligible computational overhead.

After generating a token following the standard paradigm, we construct a new input that blends the generated discrete token with the previously discarded token distribution. Specifically, we employ a Bayesian estimation method that treats the token distribution as the prior, the sampled token as the observation, and replaces the conventional one-hot vector with the continuous posterior expectation as the new model input. paragraphs: During ordinary autoregressive generation, a language model predicts probabilities for possible next tokens, selects one, and feeds only that selection back into the model. The probability distribution is discarded. Mixture of Inputs asks whether keeping some of that richer information can improve subsequent generation without changing the model through additional training.

The method still generates a discrete token in the standard way. It then forms a continuous input using Bayesian estimation: the predicted distribution serves as a prior, and the selected token serves as the observation. The resulting posterior expectation replaces the usual one-hot input, blending information about the chosen token with information about the other possibilities.

This changes what the model receives at the next step while preserving discrete text generation. The authors report consistently improved performance across several models on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and PhD-level question answering, together with improved text quality and reasoning. They describe the computational overhead as negligible. The findings support retaining distributional information as a practical, training-free generation modification.
summary.tldr: Mixture of Inputs improves generation without training by feeding back a Bayesian blend of the sampled token and its predicted distribution.

title: Mixture of Inputs: Text Generation Beyond Discrete Token Sampling

abstract: Self-attention has emerged as a fundamental component driving the success of modern transformer architectures, which power large language models and various applications. However, a theoretical understanding of how such models actually work is still under active development. The recent work of (Marion et al., 2025) introduced the so-called "single-location regression" problem, which can provably be solved by a simplified self-attention layer but not by linear models, thereby demonstrating a striking functional separation. A rigorous analysis of self-attention with softmax for this problem is challenging due to the coupled nature of the model. In the present work, we use ideas from the classical random energy model in statistical physics to analyze softmax self-attention on the single-location problem. Our analysis yields exact analytic expressions for the population risk in terms of the overlaps between the learned model parameters and those of an oracle. Moreover, we derive a detailed description of the gradient descent dynamics for these overlaps and prove that, under broad conditions, the dynamics converge to the unique oracle attractor. Our work not only advances our understanding of self-attention but also provides key theoretical ideas that are likely to find use in further analyses of even more complex transformer architectures.

paragraphs: This paper studies softmax attention through a deliberately simplified task called single-location regression. Earlier work showed that a simplified attention layer can solve this task whereas linear models cannot. The new analysis asks how softmax attention behaves on that problem, including how its parameters evolve during learning, despite the mathematical coupling that makes the model difficult to analyze.

The authors borrow ideas from the random energy model in statistical physics. They obtain exact analytical expressions for population risk in terms of overlaps between the learned parameters and an oracle's parameters. These overlaps provide a compact way to describe alignment with the desired solution and connect parameter relationships directly to prediction error.

The paper then derives gradient-descent dynamics for the overlaps and proves convergence to the unique oracle attractor under broad conditions. This gives both a description of performance and a learning-dynamics result for the toy setting. The authors suggest that the theoretical ideas could help analyze more complex transformers; the established results themselves concern the single-location problem.
summary.tldr: An exact analysis of softmax attention on a toy regression task links parameter alignment to risk and proves conditional convergence to the oracle solution.

title: Understanding Softmax Attention Layers:\\ Exact Mean-Field Analysis on a Toy Problem

abstract: Mean-field variational inference (VI), despite its scalability, is limited by the independence assumption, making it unsuitable for scenarios with correlated data instances. Existing structured VI methods either focus on correlations among latent dimensions which lack scalability for modeling instance-level correlations, or are restricted to simple first-order dependencies, limiting their expressiveness. In this paper, we propose High-order Tree-structured Variational Inference (HoT-VI), that explicitly models $k$-order instance-level correlations among latent variables. By expressing the global posterior through overlapping $k$-dimensional local marginals, our method enables efficient parameterized sampling via a sequential procedure. To ensure the validity of these marginals, we introduce a conditional correlation parameterization method that guarantees positive definiteness of their correlation matrices. We further extend our method with a tree-structured backbone to capture more flexible dependency patterns. Extensive experiments on time-series and graph-structured datasets demonstrate that modeling higher-order correlations leads to significantly improved posterior approximations and better performance across various downstream tasks.

By expressing the global posterior through overlapping $k$-dimensional local marginals, our method enables efficient parameterized sampling via a sequential procedure. To ensure the validity of these marginals, we introduce a conditional correlation parameterization method that guarantees positive definiteness of their correlation matrices. We further extend our method with a tree-structured backbone to capture more flexible dependency patterns. paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution with a more manageable distribution. Mean-field methods gain scalability by assuming independence, but that assumption discards correlations between data instances. The authors identify a gap between methods that model correlations among latent dimensions and methods that capture only simple first-order relationships across instances.

HoT-VI explicitly represents higher-order correlations between instances’ latent variables. It builds the global posterior from overlapping local marginals of dimension k and uses a sequential procedure for efficient parameterized sampling. This provides a way to assemble richer dependencies from smaller distributions while retaining an organized sampling process across the resulting representation.

A conditional correlation parameterization guarantees that the local correlation matrices are positive definite, ensuring their validity. A tree-structured backbone adds flexibility to the dependency patterns the method can express. Experiments on time-series and graph data report better posterior approximations and improved downstream performance when higher-order correlations are modeled. These findings connect a richer dependency structure to benefits in both inference quality and subsequent tasks.
summary.tldr: HoT-VI models higher-order dependencies between instances using overlapping local distributions and efficient sequential sampling.

title: HoT-VI: Reparameterizable Variational Inference for Capturing Instance-Level High-Order Correlations

abstract: Robot sports, characterized by well-defined objectives, explicit rules, and dynamic interactions, present ideal scenarios for demonstrating embodied intelligence. In this paper, we present VolleyBots, a novel robot sports testbed where multiple drones cooperate and compete in the sport of volleyball under physical dynamics. VolleyBots integrates three features within a unified platform: competitive and cooperative gameplay, turn-based interaction structure, and agile 3D maneuvering.These intertwined features yield a complex problem combining motion control and strategic play, with no available expert demonstrations.We provide a comprehensive suite of tasks ranging from single-drone drills to multi-drone cooperative and competitive tasks, accompanied by baseline evaluations of representative reinforcement learning (RL), multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and game-theoretic algorithms. Simulation results show that on-policy RL methods outperform off-policy methods in single-agent tasks, but both approaches struggle in complex tasks that combine motion control and strategic play.We additionally design a hierarchical policy which achieves 69.5% win rate against the strongest baseline in the 3 vs 3 task, demonstrating its potential for tackling the complex interplay between low-level control and high-level strategy.To highlight VolleyBots’ sim-to-real potential, we further demonstrate the zero-shot deployment of a policy trained entirely in simulation on real-world drones.

paragraphs: VolleyBots uses drone volleyball to study how robots combine rapid physical control with cooperation and competitive strategy. The environment brings together agile three-dimensional movement, turn-based interaction, and team play under physical dynamics. Its tasks range from single-drone exercises to cooperative and competitive games involving multiple drones, without available expert demonstrations.

The authors evaluate representative reinforcement learning, multi-agent learning, and game-theoretic methods across this task suite. In single-agent simulations, on-policy reinforcement learning performs better than off-policy learning. Both approaches struggle on more complex tasks that require motion control and strategic decisions together, making that combination a central challenge exposed by the testbed.

A proposed hierarchical policy achieves a 69.5% win rate against the strongest baseline in three-versus-three play. This demonstrates potential for organizing decisions across low-level control and higher-level strategy. The paper also demonstrates zero-shot deployment of a simulation-trained policy on real drones, providing evidence of transfer potential alongside the platform's role as a benchmark for integrated robotic skills.
summary.tldr: VolleyBots benchmarks drone volleyball requiring both motion control and strategy, with promising hierarchical-policy and simulation-to-real demonstrations.

title: VolleyBots: A Testbed for Multi-Drone Volleyball Game Combining Motion Control and Strategic Play

abstract: Personalized Bayesian federated learning (PBFL) handles non-i.i.d. client data and quantifies uncertainty by combining personalization with Bayesian inference. However, current PBFL methods face two main limitations: posterior inference on clients often assumes restrictive parametric forms, and server-side posterior aggregation typically relies on naive parameter averaging. To overcome these issues, we propose FedWBA, a novel PBFL method that enhances both local inference and global aggregation. At the client level, we use particle-based variational inference for nonparametric posterior representation. At the server level, we introduce particle-based Wasserstein barycenter aggregation, offering a more geometrically meaningful approach. Theoretically, we provide local and global convergence guarantees for FedWBA. Locally, we prove a KL divergence decrease lower bound per iteration for variational inference convergence. Globally, we show that the Wasserstein barycenter converges to the true parameter as the client data size increases. Empirically, experiments show that FedWBA outperforms baselines in prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and convergence rate, with ablation studies confirming its robustness.

However, current PBFL methods face two main limitations: posterior inference on clients often assumes restrictive parametric forms, and server-side posterior aggregation typically relies on naive parameter averaging. To overcome these issues, we propose FedWBA, a novel PBFL method that enhances both local inference and global aggregation. At the client level, we use particle-based variational inference for nonparametric posterior representation. At the server level, we introduce particle-based Wasserstein barycenter aggregation, offering a more geometrically meaningful approach. Theoretically, we provide local and global convergence guarantees for FedWBA. Locally, we prove a KL divergence decrease lower bound per iteration for variational inference convergence. Globally, we show that the Wasserstein barycenter converges to the true parameter as the client data size increases. Empirically, experiments show that FedWBA outperforms baselines in prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and convergence rate, with ablation studies confirming its robustness.

paragraphs: FedWBA combines personalized federated learning with Bayesian uncertainty estimation for clients whose data distributions differ. The paper identifies two obstacles: local posterior estimates often use restrictive distribution families, and servers often combine them by simply averaging parameters. Its approach changes both how each client represents uncertainty and how the server aggregates those representations.

Clients use particle-based variational inference, representing their posterior through a collection of particles rather than a prescribed parametric form. The server combines these representations with a particle-based Wasserstein barycenter. This aggregation accounts for the geometry of the distributions being combined, making the global update more meaningful than naive parameter averaging in the proposed framework.

The theoretical analysis gives a per-iteration lower bound on the decrease in KL divergence for local inference. It also shows convergence of the global barycenter to the true parameter as client data size grows. Experiments report better prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and convergence rate than baselines, with ablations supporting robustness. The global convergence statement is an increasing-data result, distinct from the finite experimental comparisons.
summary.tldr: FedWBA uses particle-based client posteriors and Wasserstein aggregation to improve personalized federated prediction and uncertainty estimation.

title: Personalized Bayesian Federated Learning with Wasserstein Barycenter Aggregation

abstract: Linear Transformers and State Space Models have emerged as efficient alternatives to softmax Transformers for causal sequence modeling, enabling parallel training via matrix multiplication and efficient RNN-style inference. However, despite their success in causal tasks, no unified framework exists for applying Linear Transformers to bidirectional sequence modeling. We introduce LION, the first framework to systematically extend Linear Transformers to the bidirectional setting. LION generalizes three core representations commonly used in the causal case—full Linear Attention , bidirectional RNN, and chunkwise parallel form—to the bidirectional setting. These forms are theoretically equivalent and enable models to exploit the strengths of each during training and inference. We prove that a broad class of Linear Transformers can be extended using LION and validate our framework via three core examples based on the choice of decay type: LION-LIT, the bidirectional extension of [25]; LION-D, based on [44]; and LION-S, a variant using selective decay [34, 13]. Across standard bidirectional tasks, LION enables models to match or exceed the performance of softmax Transformers, while offering significantly faster training and more efficient inference than existing State Space Models.

LION generalizes three core representations commonly used in the causal case—full Linear Attention , bidirectional RNN, and chunkwise parallel form—to the bidirectional setting. These forms are theoretically equivalent and enable models to exploit the strengths of each during training and inference. paragraphs: Linear Transformers offer efficient ways to process sequences, but much of their development concerns causal tasks, where each position uses only preceding information. Bidirectional tasks allow information from both directions. LION supplies a unified framework for extending Linear Transformers to that setting while retaining multiple ways to carry out the computation.

The framework develops three theoretically equivalent representations: full linear attention, a bidirectional recurrent form, and a chunkwise parallel form. Their equivalence lets models use the computational strengths of different representations during training and inference. The authors prove that LION applies to a broad class of Linear Transformers and demonstrate it through three variants with different decay mechanisms.

Across standard bidirectional tasks, the resulting models match or exceed softmax Transformer performance. The reported comparisons also show substantially faster training and more efficient inference than existing State Space Models. The contribution combines an organizing mathematical framework with empirical evidence that linear attention can be useful beyond causal processing. The different execution forms are alternative realizations of the same modeled computation.
summary.tldr: LION extends Linear Transformers to bidirectional tasks through three equivalent computational forms, with strong reported performance and efficiency.

title: Linear Attention for Efficient Bidirectional Sequence Modeling

abstract: Existing benchmarks for evaluating mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) rely primarily on competition problems, formal proofs, or artificially challenging questions---failing to capture the nature of mathematics encountered in actual research environments. We introduce \textsc{RealMath}, a novel benchmark derived directly from research papers and mathematical forums that assesses LLMs' abilities on authentic mathematical tasks. Our approach addresses three critical challenges: sourcing diverse research-level content, enabling reliable automated evaluation through verifiable statements, and designing a continually refreshable dataset to mitigate contamination risks. Experimental results across multiple LLMs reveal surprising capabilities in handling research mathematics compared to competition problems, suggesting current models may already serve as valuable assistants for working mathematicians despite limitations on highly challenging problems. The code and dataset for \textsc{RealMath} are publicly available.
originalAbstract: Existing benchmarks for evaluating mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) rely primarily on competition problems, formal proofs, or artificially challenging questions---failing to capture the nature of mathematics encountered in actual research environments. We introduce \textsc{RealMath}, a novel benchmark derived directly from research papers and mathematical forums that assesses LLMs' abilities on authentic mathematical tasks. Our approach addresses three critical challenges: sourcing diverse research-level content, enabling reliable automated evaluation through verifiable statements, and designing a continually refreshable dataset to mitigate contamination risks. Experimental results across multiple LLMs reveal surprising capabilities in handling research mathematics compared to competition problems, suggesting current models may already serve as valuable assistants for working mathematicians despite limitations on highly challenging problems. The code and dataset for \textsc{RealMath} are publicly available.

paragraphs: RealMath evaluates language models on mathematical tasks drawn from research papers and mathematical forums. The authors argue that competition questions, formal proofs, and deliberately difficult problems do not fully represent the mathematics encountered in research work. Their benchmark changes the source of evaluation tasks to better reflect that setting.

The design addresses three practical requirements. It draws on diverse research-level material, uses verifiable statements to support reliable automated assessment, and allows the dataset to be refreshed continually. Refreshability is intended to mitigate contamination risks, helping the evaluation remain useful as models and their training material change. These requirements connect the authenticity of the tasks with the practicality of maintaining and scoring the benchmark.

Experiments across multiple language models reveal unexpectedly strong abilities on research mathematics relative to competition problems. The authors interpret this as evidence that current models may already assist working mathematicians, while acknowledging limitations on highly challenging problems. The result supports evaluating research usefulness directly rather than inferring it entirely from performance on other mathematical benchmarks.
summary.tldr: RealMath uses refreshable, verifiable tasks from research papers and forums to assess language models’ potential usefulness in mathematical research.

title: RealMath: A Continuous Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Research-Level Mathematics

abstract: Auction-based Federated Learning (AFL) fosters collaboration among self-interested data consumers (DCs) and data owners (DOs). A major challenge in AFL pertains to how DCs select and bid for DOs. Existing methods are generally static, making them ill-suited for dynamic AFL markets. To address this issue, we propose the R}einforcement Learning-based Bidding Strategy for DCs in Auction-based Federated Learning (RLB-AFL). We incorporate historical states into a Deep Q-Network to capture sequential information critical for bidding decisions. To mitigate state space sparsity, where specific states rarely reoccur for each DC during auctions, we incorporate the Gaussian Mixture Model into RLB-AFL. This facilitates soft clustering on sequential states, reducing the state space dimensionality and easing exploration and action-value function approximation. In addition, we enhance the $\epsilon$-greedy policy to help the RLB-AFL agent balance exploitation and exploration, enabling it to be more adaptable in the AFL decision-making process. Extensive experiments under 6 widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that RLB-AFL achieves superior performance compared to 8 state-of-the-art approaches. It outperforms the best baseline by 10.56% and 3.15% in terms of average total utility

paragraphs: In auction-based federated learning, data consumers choose which data owners to work with and how much to bid for their participation. These decisions occur in changing markets, where a fixed bidding rule may respond poorly to new circumstances. RLB-AFL treats bidding as a sequential decision problem that an agent can learn to navigate.

The method adds historical states to a Deep Q-Network so that decisions can reflect the progression of earlier auctions. A second component addresses the fact that any particular auction state may rarely recur. A Gaussian Mixture Model softly groups sequential states, reducing the effective dimensionality of the state space and making exploration and estimation of action values easier.

The authors also modify the exploration policy to balance trying unfamiliar actions with using actions that already appear beneficial. Experiments across six benchmark datasets compare the method with eight existing approaches and report superior performance in average total utility. Together, the components support adaptive bidding by combining market history, more manageable state representations, and a revised approach to exploration.
summary.tldr: RLB-AFL learns adaptive bids for federated learning auctions using auction history, soft state clustering, and an enhanced exploration policy.

title: A Reinforcement Learning-based Bidding Strategy for Data Consumers in Auction-based Federated Learning

abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models is a critical challenge. Existing debiasing methods often compromise performance, rely on static correction strategies, and struggle with data sparsity, particularly within minority groups. Furthermore, their utilization of sensitive attributes is often suboptimal, either depending excessively on complete attribute labeling or disregarding these attributes entirely. To overcome these limitations, we propose FairNet, a novel framework for dynamic, instance-level fairness correction. FairNet integrates a bias detector with conditional low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which enables selective activation of the fairness correction mechanism exclusively for instances identified as biased, and thereby preserve performance on unbiased instances. A key contribution is a new contrastive loss function for training the LoRA module, specifically designed to minimize intra-class representation disparities across different sensitive groups and effectively address underfitting in minority groups. The FairNet framework can flexibly handle scenarios with complete, partial, or entirely absent sensitive attribute labels. Theoretical analysis confirms that, under moderate TPR/FPR for the bias detector, FairNet can enhance the performance of the worst group without diminishing overall model performance, and potentially yield slight performance improvements. Comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse vision and language benchmarks validate the effectiveness of FairNet. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/SongqiZhou/FairNet}.

paragraphs: Fairness corrections can reduce overall model performance, particularly when the same correction is applied indiscriminately. FairNet instead makes correction conditional on the individual input. A bias detector identifies instances that need intervention, and a low-rank adaptation module activates selectively. This design aims to improve biased predictions while preserving performance on inputs that do not need correction.

The correction module is trained with a contrastive loss that reduces representation differences between sensitive groups within the same class. This targets minority-group underfitting while retaining the distinction between classes. The framework also accommodates complete, partial, or absent sensitive-attribute labels, addressing settings where those annotations are unavailable for some or all examples.

The theoretical result is conditional: with moderate true-positive and false-positive rates for the bias detector, FairNet can improve the worst-performing group without reducing overall performance, and may slightly improve it. Evaluations across vision and language benchmarks support the framework’s effectiveness. The detector’s behavior is therefore central to the stated guarantee, alongside the quality of the learned correction.
summary.tldr: FairNet selectively corrects detected bias, with conditional theoretical support for improving the worst group without sacrificing overall performance.

title: FairNet: Dynamic Fairness Correction without Performance Loss via Contrastive Conditional LoRA

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to perform complex reasoning and decision-making through free-form language interactions. However, in open-ended language action environments (e.g., negotiation or question-asking games), the action space can be formulated as a joint distribution over tokens, resulting in an extremely large and combinatorial action space. Sampling actions in such a space can lead to extreme reward sparsity, which brings large reward variance, hindering effective reinforcement learning (RL). To address this, we propose **ARIA**, a method that **A**ggregates **R**ewards in **I**ntention space to enable efficient and effective language **A**gents training. ARIA aims to project natural language actions from the high-dimensional joint token distribution space into a low-dimensional intention space, where semantically similar actions are clustered and assigned shared rewards. This intention-aware reward aggregation reduces reward variance by densifying reward signals, fostering efficient and effective policy optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ARIA not only significantly reduces gradient variance, but also delivers substantial performance gains of average 9.95% across four downstream tasks (e.g., negotiation and text-based games), consistently outperforming strong offline and online RL baselines.

paragraphs: ARIA addresses a learning problem for agents that act through unrestricted language. In negotiation or question-asking games, many different token sequences can express useful actions. Searching this enormous space can produce sparse rewards and highly variable training signals, making reinforcement learning less effective even when several utterances have similar meanings.

The method groups language actions by intention. It projects actions into a lower-dimensional space, clusters semantically similar actions, and assigns shared rewards within those groups. This changes the level at which feedback is aggregated: related expressions can contribute to a common signal instead of being treated entirely separately. The aim is to make reward information denser and reduce the variance that disrupts policy optimization.

Across four downstream tasks, including negotiation and text-based games, the authors report significantly lower gradient variance and an average performance improvement of 9.95%. ARIA also outperforms the strong offline and online reinforcement learning baselines evaluated. These findings support intention-based reward sharing as a practical way to improve learning in the tested open-ended language environments.
summary.tldr: ARIA shares rewards among language actions with similar intentions, reducing training variance and improving performance across four tasks.

title: ARIA: Training Language Agents with Intention-driven Reward Aggregation

abstract: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a cornerstone technique for determining the structures of small molecules and is especially critical in the discovery of novel natural products and clinical therapeutics. Yet, interpreting NMR spectra remains a time-consuming, manual process requiring extensive domain expertise. We introduce ChefNMR (CHemical Elucidation From NMR), an end-to-end framework that directly predicts an unknown molecule's structure solely from its 1D NMR spectra and chemical formula. We frame structure elucidation as conditional generation from an atomic diffusion model built on a non-equivariant transformer architecture. To model the complex chemical groups found in natural products, we generated a dataset of simulated 1D NMR spectra for over 111,000 natural products. ChefNMR predicts the structures of challenging natural product compounds with an unsurpassed accuracy of over 65%. This work takes a significant step toward solving the grand challenge of automating small-molecule structure elucidation and highlights the potential of deep learning in accelerating molecular discovery.

paragraphs: Determining a molecule's structure from nuclear magnetic resonance spectra often requires substantial manual interpretation and chemical expertise. ChefNMR addresses this task with an end-to-end model that takes one-dimensional NMR spectra and a chemical formula as its inputs. The intended output is the unknown molecule's structure, directly connecting spectral evidence to a structural prediction.

The paper reports accuracy above 65% on challenging natural product compounds and describes that accuracy as unsurpassed. This result supports the promise of learning a direct mapping from these inputs to molecular structures. The work's significance is its integrated approach to automating a demanding interpretation task, with potential relevance to molecular discovery and the study of natural products.
summary.tldr: ChefNMR predicts molecular structures from one-dimensional NMR spectra and chemical formulas, reporting over 65% accuracy on challenging natural products.

title: Atomic Diffusion Models for Small Molecule Structure Elucidation from NMR Spectra

abstract: Understanding long video content is a complex endeavor that often relies on densely sampled frame captions or end-to-end feature selectors, yet these techniques commonly overlook the logical relationships between textual queries and visual elements. In practice, computational constraints necessitate coarse frame subsampling, a challenge analogous to “finding a needle in a haystack.” To address this issue, we introduce a semantics-driven search framework that reformulates keyframe selection under the paradigm of Visual Semantic-Logical Search (VSLS). Specifically, we systematically define four fundamental logical dependencies: 1) spatial co-occurrence, 2) temporal proximity, 3) attribute dependency, and 4) causal order. These relations dynamically update frame sampling distributions through an iterative refinement process, enabling context-aware identification of semantically critical frames tailored to specific query requirements. Our method establishes new state-of-the-art performance on the manually annotated benchmark in keyframe selection metrics. Furthermore, when applied to downstream video question-answering tasks, the proposed approach demonstrates the best performance gains over existing methods on LongVideoBench and Video-MME, validating its effectiveness in bridging the logical gap between textual queries and visual-temporal reasoning. The code will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Long-video question answering depends on finding the few frames that contain relevant evidence. Computational limits often force systems to inspect only a sparse sample, potentially missing important events. This paper argues that frame selection should consider logical relationships between the question and visual content, beyond the relevance of isolated images or captions.

Its Visual Semantic-Logical Search framework uses four kinds of dependency: spatial co-occurrence, temporal proximity, attribute dependency, and causal order. These describe relationships such as elements appearing together or events occurring in a meaningful sequence. The framework repeatedly updates its frame-sampling distribution using these relations, refining the search toward frames that satisfy the particular query's requirements.

The authors report state-of-the-art keyframe selection metrics on a manually annotated benchmark. Applying the selected frames to downstream question answering also produces the strongest reported gains over existing methods on LongVideoBench and Video-MME. The results support treating frame selection as an iterative reasoning problem: understanding relationships among visual clues can help determine where in a long video to look next.
summary.tldr: Logic-in-Frames iteratively searches long videos using logical relationships to select more useful frames for answering questions.

title: Logic-in-Frames: Dynamic Keyframe Search via Visual Semantic-Logical Verification for Long Video Understanding

abstract: This work presents a systematic investigation into the latent knowledge encoded within Network Foundation Models (NFMs). Different from existing efforts, we focus on hidden representations analysis rather than pure downstream task performance and analyze NFMs through a three-part evaluation: Embedding Geometry Analysis to assess representation space utilization, Metric Alignment Assessment to measure correspondence with domain-expert features, and Causal Sensitivity Testing to evaluate robustness to protocol perturbations. Using five diverse network datasets spanning controlled and real-world environments, we evaluate four state-of-the-art NFMs, revealing that they all exhibit significant anisotropy, inconsistent feature sensitivity patterns, an inability to separate the high-level context, payload dependency, and other properties. Our work identifies numerous limitations across all models and demonstrates that addressing them can significantly improve model performance (up to 0.35 increase in $F_1$ scores without architectural changes).

paragraphs: This paper examines what network foundation models encode internally, going beyond their performance on downstream tasks. The aim is to understand whether their hidden representations capture meaningful network properties and respond appropriately to changes in network protocols. This makes the representation itself the object of evaluation, rather than treating a successful prediction as sufficient evidence of understanding.

The investigation uses three complementary tests. Embedding geometry analysis examines how models use their representation space. Metric alignment assessment checks correspondence with features identified by domain experts. Causal sensitivity testing measures responses to protocol perturbations. Together, these tests connect the structure of learned representations with domain knowledge and behavior under controlled changes.

Across four models and five datasets covering controlled and real-world environments, the authors find strongly uneven representation geometry, inconsistent feature sensitivity, difficulty separating high-level context, and payload dependency. Addressing identified problems improves F1 scores by up to 0.35 without changing model architectures. The findings show that representation analysis can reveal actionable weaknesses that task scores alone may leave unclear.
summary.tldr: Analyzing network models’ hidden representations reveals shared weaknesses whose correction improves F1 scores by up to 0.35 without architectural changes.

title: Demystifying Network Foundation Models

abstract: Concept erasure aims to remove unwanted attributes, such as social or demographic factors, from learned representations, while preserving their task-relevant utility. While the goal of concept erasure is protection against all adversaries, existing methods remain vulnerable to nonlinear ones. This vulnerability arises from their failure to fully capture the complex, nonlinear statistical dependencies between learned representations and unwanted attributes. Moreover, although the existence of a trade-off between utility and erasure is expected, its progression during the erasure process, i.e., the cost of erasure, remains unstudied. In this work, we introduce Obliviator, a post-hoc erasure method designed to fully capture nonlinear statistical dependencies. We formulate erasure from a functional perspective, leading to an optimization problem involving a composition of kernels that lacks a closed-form solution. Instead of solving this problem in a single shot, we adopt an iterative approach that gradually morphs the feature space to achieve a more utility-preserving erasure. Unlike prior methods, Obliviator guards unwanted attribute against nonlinear adversaries. Our gradual approach quantifies the cost of nonlinear guardedness and reveals the dynamics between attribute protection and utility-preservation over the course of erasure. The utility-erasure trade-off curves obtained by Obliviator outperform the baselines and demonstrate its strong generalizability: its erasure becomes more utility-preserving when applied to the better-disentangled representations learned by more capable models.

paragraphs: Concept erasure tries to remove unwanted attributes from learned representations while retaining information useful for the intended task. The paper argues that existing methods leave nonlinear dependencies that an adversary can exploit to recover those attributes. It also asks how much useful information is lost as erasure progresses, making the changing protection-utility trade-off a central object of study.

Obliviator formulates erasure through functions and a composition of kernels. Because the resulting optimization problem lacks a closed-form solution, it gradually transforms the feature space through iterative updates. This provides a route to protection against nonlinear adversaries while tracking how the transformation affects task utility.

The reported trade-off curves outperform the baselines, indicating a better balance between attribute protection and retained usefulness. Erasure is also more utility-preserving for better-disentangled representations produced by more capable models. That finding links the cost of removing an attribute to how information is organized in the starting representation, while the iterative approach exposes how this cost develops during erasure.
summary.tldr: Obliviator iteratively erases nonlinear attribute information while measuring and improving the trade-off between protection and task utility.

title: Obliviator Reveals the Cost of Nonlinear Guardedness in Concept Erasure

abstract: Equivariant network architectures are a well-established tool for predicting invariant or equivariant quantities. However, almost all learning problems considered in this context feature a global symmetry, i.e. each point of the underlying space is transformed with the same group element, as opposed to a local *gauge* symmetry, where each point is transformed with a different group element, exponentially enlarging the size of the symmetry group. We use gauge equivariant networks to predict topological invariants (Chern numbers) of multiband topological insulators for the first time. The gauge symmetry of the network guarantees that the predicted quantity is a topological invariant. A major technical challenge is that the relevant gauge equivariant networks are plagued by instabilities in their training, severely limiting their usefulness. In particular, for larger gauge groups the instabilities make training impossible. We resolve this problem by introducing a novel gauge equivariant normalization layer which stabilizes the training. Furthermore, we prove a universal approximation theorem for our model. We train on samples with trivial Chern number only but show that our model generalizes to samples with non-trivial Chern number and provide various ablations of our setup.

paragraphs: This paper applies gauge-equivariant neural networks to predicting Chern numbers, topological invariants of multiband topological insulators. Gauge symmetry allows a different transformation at each point, making it substantially richer than a global symmetry shared across all points. The architecture incorporates this local symmetry into the prediction process.

The abstract states that the network's gauge symmetry guarantees a topologically invariant prediction. A practical obstacle is that the relevant architectures suffer from training instabilities, severe enough to prevent training for larger gauge groups. The authors introduce a normalization layer that preserves gauge equivariance while stabilizing learning, allowing the symmetry-based model to be trained successfully.

The paper also proves a universal approximation theorem for its model. In experiments, training uses only samples with trivial Chern number, yet the model generalizes to samples with nontrivial Chern number. This result supports the value of the architecture's structural constraints in the tested setting. The theoretical approximation result, normalization method, and generalization experiments together address expressiveness, trainability, and prediction beyond the training examples' topological class.
summary.tldr: A stabilizing gauge-equivariant normalization layer enables Chern-number prediction that generalizes from trivial to nontrivial training-unseen topology.

title: Learning Chern Numbers of Multiband Topological Insulators with Gauge Equivariant Neural Networks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance across diverse reasoning and generation tasks, and are increasingly deployed as agents in dynamic environments such as code generation and recommendation systems. However, many real-world applications, such as high-frequency trading and real-time competitive gaming, require decisions under strict latency constraints, where faster responses directly translate into higher rewards. Despite the importance of this latency–quality trade-off, it remains underexplored in the context of LLM-based agents. In this work, we present the first systematic study of this trade-off in real-time decision-making tasks. To support our investigation, we introduce two new benchmarks: HFTBench, a high-frequency trading simulation, and StreetFighter, a competitive gaming platform. Our analysis reveals that optimal latency–quality balance varies by task, and that sacrificing quality for lower latency can significantly enhance downstream performance. To address this, we propose FPX, an adaptive framework that dynamically selects model size and quantization level based on real-time demands. Our method achieves the best performance on both benchmarks, improving win rate by up to 80% in Street Fighter and boosting daily yield by up to 26.52% in trading, underscoring the need for latency-aware evaluation and deployment strategies for LLM-based agents. These results demonstrate the critical importance of latency-aware evaluation and deployment strategies for real-world LLM-based agents.

paragraphs: An agent’s decision can be valuable only if it arrives in time to affect its environment. This paper studies the trade-off between response quality and latency for language-model agents in real-time tasks. It introduces HFTBench, a high-frequency-trading simulation, and StreetFighter, a competitive gaming platform, to evaluate that trade-off through task outcomes.

The analysis finds that the best balance depends on the task. In some settings, accepting lower response quality in exchange for faster action substantially improves overall performance. The proposed FPX framework responds by dynamically selecting model size and quantization level according to real-time demands, making computational configuration part of the agent’s decision process.

FPX achieves the best reported performance on both benchmarks, with win-rate improvements of up to 80% in Street Fighter and daily-yield improvements of up to 26.52% in the trading simulation. These results support evaluating agents through the combined effects of answer quality and delivery time. They also show why a fixed preference for the most capable model can miss the configuration that performs best under a particular timing constraint.
summary.tldr: FPX adapts model size and quantization to timing demands, improving outcomes in simulated trading and competitive gaming.

title: Win Fast or Lose Slow: Balancing Speed and Accuracy in Latency-Sensitive Decisions of LLMs

abstract: We have recently witnessed that ''Intelligence" and `''Compression" are the two sides of the same coin, where the language large model (LLM) with unprecedented intelligence is a general-purpose lossless compressor for various data modalities. This attribute is particularly appealing to the lossless image compression community, given the increasing need to compress high-resolution images in the current streaming media era. Consequently, a spontaneous envision emerges: Can the compression performance of the LLM elevate lossless image compression to new heights? However, our findings indicate that the naive application of LLM-based lossless image compressors suffers from a considerable performance gap compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) codecs on common benchmark datasets. In light of this, we are dedicated to fulfilling the unprecedented intelligence (compression) capacity of the LLM for lossless image compression tasks, thereby bridging the gap between theoretical and practical compression performance. Specifically, we propose P -LLM, a next-pixel prediction-based LLM, which integrates various elaborated insights and methodologies, \textit{e.g.,} pixel-level priors, the in-context ability of LLM, and a pixel-level semantic preservation strategy, to enhance the understanding capacity of pixel sequences for better next-pixel predictions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that P-LLM can beat SOTA classical and learned codecs.
originalAbstract: We have recently witnessed that ''Intelligence" and `''Compression" are the two sides of the same coin, where the language large model (LLM) with unprecedented intelligence is a general-purpose lossless compressor for various data modalities. This attribute is particularly appealing to the lossless image compression community, given the increasing need to compress high-resolution images in the current streaming media era. Consequently, a spontaneous envision emerges: Can the compression performance of the LLM elevate lossless image compression to new heights? However, our findings indicate that the naive application of LLM-based lossless image compressors suffers from a considerable performance gap compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) codecs on common benchmark datasets. In light of this, we are dedicated to fulfilling the unprecedented intelligence (compression) capacity of the LLM for lossless image compression tasks, thereby bridging the gap between theoretical and practical compression performance. Specifically, we propose P -LLM, a next-pixel prediction-based LLM, which integrates various elaborated insights and methodologies, \textit{e.g.,} pixel-level priors, the in-context ability of LLM, and a pixel-level semantic preservation strategy, to enhance the understanding capacity of pixel sequences for better next-pixel predictions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that P-LLM can beat SOTA classical and learned codecs.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether large language models can provide competitive lossless image compression, where the original image must be recoverable without losing information. The authors first find that simply applying an LLM as an image compressor leaves a substantial performance gap against established codecs on common benchmarks. Strong language modeling alone does not deliver the desired image-compression results in that setup.

Their proposed model, P-LLM, focuses on predicting the next pixel in a sequence. It combines pixel-level prior information, the model's ability to use context, and a strategy intended to preserve pixel-level semantics. These components are designed to improve how the language model interprets pixel sequences and therefore improve its predictions.

Benchmark experiments show that P-LLM can outperform both classical and learned state-of-the-art codecs. The result supports adapting LLM-based prediction specifically to image structure, rather than expecting the naive application to suffice. The paper's practical contribution is the combination of image-aware methods that turns next-pixel prediction into stronger measured lossless compression.
summary.tldr: P-LLM adapts language-model next-pixel prediction to image structure and can outperform leading lossless codecs on benchmark datasets.

title: Large Language Models for Lossless Image Compression: Next-Pixel Prediction in Language Space is All You Need

abstract: Domain generalization aims to train models that perform robustly on unseen target domains without access to target data. The realm of vision-language foundation model has opened a new venue owing to its inherent out-of-distribution generalization capability. However, the static alignment to class-level textual anchors remains insufficient to handle the dramatic distribution discrepancy from diverse domain-specific visual features. In this work, we propose a novel cross-domain Schrödinger Bridge (SB) method, namely SBGen, to handle this challenge, which explicitly formulates the stochastic semantic evolution, to gain better generalization to unseen domains. Technically, the proposed \texttt{SBGen} consists of three key components: (1) \emph{text-guided domain-aware feature selection} to isolate semantically aligned image tokens; (2) \emph{stochastic cross-domain evolution} to simulate the SB dynamics via a learnable time-conditioned drift; and (3) \emph{stochastic domain-agnostic interpolation} to construct semantically grounded feature trajectories. Empirically, \texttt{SBGen} achieves state-of-the-art performance on domain generalization in both classification and segmentation. This work highlights the importance of modeling domain shifts as structured stochastic processes grounded in semantic alignment.
