paragraphs: Visual domain generalization aims to handle unseen target domains without accessing their data during training. Vision-language foundation models offer useful generalization capabilities, but the paper argues that fixed alignment between images and class-level text descriptions cannot adequately handle large differences in visual appearance. SBGen instead models domain shifts as structured, stochastic changes in semantic features.

The method first uses text to select image tokens that align with the relevant meaning. It then learns a time-conditioned drift to simulate cross-domain evolution through a Schrödinger Bridge. A stochastic, domain-agnostic interpolation component constructs feature trajectories that remain semantically grounded. Together, these components model how visual features may change while preserving information relevant to their interpretation.

The authors report state-of-the-art results for domain generalization in both classification and segmentation. These empirical findings support their proposal to represent domain variation through a learned stochastic process. The approach matters because it moves beyond a fixed textual anchor toward modeling changes between feature distributions, while retaining semantic alignment as an organizing constraint.
summary.tldr: SBGen improves visual domain generalization by modeling semantically grounded, stochastic changes in image features across domains.

title: Learning a Cross-Modal Schrödinger Bridge for Visual Domain Generalization

abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) pretraining is more scalable than dense Transformer pretraining, because MoEs learn to route inputs to a sparse set of their feedforward parameters. However, this means that MoEs only receive a sparse backward update, leading to training instability and suboptimal performance. We present a lightweight approximation method that gives the MoE router a dense gradient update while continuing to sparsely activate its parameters. Our method, which we refer to as Default MoE, substitutes missing expert activations with default outputs consisting of an exponential moving average of expert outputs previously seen over the course of training. This allows the router to receive signals from every expert for each token, leading to significant improvements in training performance. Our Default MoE outperforms standard TopK routing in a variety of settings without requiring significant computational overhead.

paragraphs: A mixture-of-experts model saves computation by routing each input to only a small subset of its feedforward parameters. The paper focuses on a training consequence of that sparsity: backward updates are sparse too. Limited feedback can make training unstable and prevent the router from learning as effectively as it could with information from more experts.

Default MoE supplies an approximate output for experts that were not activated. Each default is an exponential moving average of outputs that the expert produced earlier in training. These stored summaries stand in for missing activations, allowing the router to receive a gradient signal involving every expert for each token while actual expert activation remains sparse.

The reported experiments show improvements over standard TopK routing across several settings without significant computational overhead. The contribution is specifically a denser learning signal for the router, achieved through lightweight approximations. Its results suggest that retaining sparse execution need not require equally sparse information for learning how inputs should be routed.
summary.tldr: Default MoE improves sparse expert routing by using historical expert outputs to give the router denser gradient feedback.

title: Dense Backpropagation Improves Training for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated great potential in interpreting remote sensing (RS) images through language-guided semantic. However, the effectiveness of these VLMs critically depends on high-quality image-text training data that captures rich semantic relationships between visual content and language descriptions. Unlike natural images, RS lacks large-scale interleaved image-text pairs from web data, making data collection challenging. While current approaches rely primarily on rule-based methods or flagship VLMs for data synthesis, a systematic framework for automated quality assessment of such synthetically generated RS vision-language data is notably absent. To fill this gap, we propose a novel score model trained on large-scale RS vision-language preference data for automated quality assessment. Our empirical results demonstrate that fine-tuning CLIP or advanced VLMs (e.g., Qwen2-VL) with the top 30% of data ranked by our score model achieves superior accuracy compared to both full-data fine-tuning and CLIP-score-based ranking approaches. Furthermore, we demonstrate applications of our scoring model for reinforcement learning (RL) training and best-of-N (BoN) test-time scaling, enabling significant improvements in VLM performance for RS tasks. Our code, model, and dataset are publicly available.

paragraphs: Remote-sensing vision-language models depend on image-text data that capture meaningful relationships between visual content and descriptions. Such paired data are harder to obtain at scale than for natural images. This paper addresses quality assessment for synthetically generated remote-sensing data, an area the authors identify as lacking a systematic automated framework.

The proposed scoring model learns from large-scale remote-sensing vision-language preference data. It ranks generated training examples by quality. In the reported experiments, fine-tuning CLIP or more advanced models such as Qwen2-VL on the highest-ranked 30% yields better accuracy than using the full dataset or selecting examples through CLIP scores.

The scoring model also supports reinforcement-learning training and best-of-N selection at test time, with significant improvements reported for remote-sensing tasks. Its role therefore extends beyond filtering a fixed training collection to guiding learning and choosing outputs. The results show that learned quality assessment can make a smaller selected dataset more effective in the evaluated settings while providing a reusable signal for other stages of model improvement.
summary.tldr: A learned quality scorer improves remote-sensing vision-language models through data selection, reinforcement learning, and test-time candidate selection.

title: Quality-Driven Curation of Remote Sensing Vision-Language Data via Learned Scoring Models

abstract: We consider the problem of structurally constrained high-dimensional linear regression. This has attracted considerable attention over the last decade, with state of the art statistical estimators based on solving regularized convex programs. While these typically non-smooth convex programs can be solved in polynomial time, scaling the state of the art optimization methods to very large-scale problems is an ongoing and rich area of research. In this paper, we attempt to address this scaling issue at the source, by asking whether one can build \emphsimpler possibly closed-form estimators, that yet come with statistical guarantees that are nonetheless comparable to regularized likelihood estimators! We answer this question in the affirmative, with variants of the classical ridge and OLS (ordinary least squares estimators) for linear regression. We analyze our estimators in the high-dimensional setting, and moreover provide empirical corroboration of its performance on simulated as well as real world microarray data.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether high-dimensional linear regression really needs computationally elaborate estimators to achieve strong statistical guarantees. The setting includes structural constraints on the regression parameters. Established approaches solve regularized convex optimization problems, which are tractable in a formal sense but can still become expensive at very large scales.

The authors tackle this cost by changing the estimator itself. They construct variants of ridge regression and ordinary least squares, seeking simpler estimators that may admit closed-form computation. Their central result is that these alternatives can retain statistical guarantees comparable to those of regularized likelihood estimators in the high-dimensional setting.

This shifts attention from accelerating an existing optimization procedure to choosing a statistically justified procedure that is simpler to compute. The paper analyzes the proposed estimators and provides empirical support using simulated data and real microarray data. The stated findings support the possibility of combining simpler estimation with comparable guarantees, rather than assuming that a more involved convex program is always required for structurally constrained regression.
summary.tldr: Variants of ridge regression and ordinary least squares offer simpler high-dimensional estimators with guarantees comparable to regularized likelihood methods.

title: Elementary Estimators for High-Dimensional Linear Regression

abstract: We develop a theoretical and computational framework to perform guaranteed tensor decomposition, which also has the potential to accomplish other tensor tasks such as tensor completion and denoising. We formulate tensor decomposition as a problem of measure estimation from moments. By constructing a dual polynomial, we demonstrate that measure optimization returns the correct CP decomposition under an incoherence condition on the rank-one factors. To address the computational challenge, we present a hierarchy of semidefinite programs based on sums-of-squares relaxations of the measure optimization problem. By showing that the constructed dual polynomial is a sum-of-squares modulo the sphere, we prove that the smallest SDP in the relaxation hierarchy is exact and the decomposition can be extracted from the solution under the same incoherence condition. One implication is that the tensor nuclear norm can be computed exactly using the smallest SDP as long as the rank-one factors of the tensor are incoherent. Numerical experiments are conducted to test the performance of the moment approach.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for decomposing a tensor into rank-one components, known as a CP decomposition. It recasts the task as estimating a measure from its moments. This reformulation creates a route to proving when an optimization problem recovers the desired decomposition.

The authors construct a dual polynomial that certifies correct recovery under an incoherence condition on the rank-one factors. To make the measure-optimization problem computationally approachable, they introduce a hierarchy of semidefinite programs using sums-of-squares relaxations. They then show that the smallest program in this hierarchy is already exact under the same incoherence condition and permits extraction of the decomposition.

One consequence is that this smallest semidefinite program also computes the tensor nuclear norm exactly when the required incoherence holds. These are conditional guarantees, with the geometry of the factors playing a central role. Numerical experiments test the moment-based approach. The authors additionally suggest potential applications to tensor completion and denoising, presenting those tasks as possibilities beyond the established decomposition results.
summary.tldr: A moment-based formulation yields exact tensor decomposition and nuclear-norm computation through a small semidefinite relaxation when factor incoherence holds.

title: Guaranteed Tensor Decomposition: A Moment Approach

abstract: This paper develops an approach for efficiently solving general convex optimization problems specified as disciplined convex programs (DCP), a common general-purpose modeling framework. Specifically we develop an algorithm based upon fast epigraph projections, projections onto the epigraph of a convex function, an approach closely linked to proximal operator methods. We show that by using these operators, we can solve any disciplined convex program without transforming the problem to a standard cone form, as is done by current DCP libraries. We then develop a large library of efficient epigraph projection operators, mirroring and extending work on fast proximal algorithms, for many common convex functions. Finally, we evaluate the performance of the algorithm, and show it often achieves order of magnitude speedups over existing general-purpose optimization solvers.

paragraphs: Disciplined convex programming provides a general framework for expressing convex optimization problems. Existing libraries commonly translate these descriptions into a standard cone form before solving them. This paper develops an alternative route that operates through projections associated with the convex functions used in the problem.

The key operation is an epigraph projection: projecting onto the set of points on or above a convex function's graph. Such operations are closely related to proximal methods. The authors show how these projections can be used to solve any disciplined convex program without the usual conversion to cone form, connecting a general modeling framework to a different collection of computational building blocks.

To make the approach practical, the paper develops a large library of efficient projection operators for common convex functions. Its evaluations show that the resulting algorithm often runs about an order of magnitude faster than existing general-purpose solvers. The finding supports this projection-based route as an effective option across evaluated problems, while retaining the abstract's qualification that the speedups occur often rather than universally.
summary.tldr: Fast epigraph projections solve disciplined convex programs without cone conversion and often substantially accelerate optimization.

title: Epigraph projections for fast general convex programming

abstract: Due to the rapid growth of data and computational resources, distributed optimization has become an active research area in recent years. While first-order methods seem to dominate the field, second-order methods are nevertheless attractive as they potentially require fewer communication rounds to converge. However, there are significant drawbacks that impede their wide adoption, such as the computation and the communication of a large Hessian matrix. In this paper we present a new algorithm for distributed training of generalized linear models that only requires the computation of diagonal blocks of the Hessian matrix on the individual workers. To deal with this approximate information we propose an adaptive approach that - akin to trust-region methods - dynamically adapts the auxiliary model to compensate for modeling errors. We provide theoretical rates of convergence for a wide class of problems including $L_1$-regularized objectives. We also demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple large benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Distributed training spreads optimization across workers, making communication part of the cost of learning. Second-order methods use curvature information and can potentially converge with fewer communication rounds. Their difficulty is that computing and communicating a large Hessian matrix can be expensive enough to undermine that advantage.

This paper proposes a distributed algorithm for generalized linear models that requires each worker to compute only diagonal blocks of the Hessian. These blocks provide an approximation to the full curvature information. The algorithm handles the resulting modeling errors through an adaptive auxiliary model, adjusting it dynamically in a way related to trust-region methods.

The authors establish convergence rates for a broad class of problems, including objectives with L1 regularization, and report state-of-the-art results on several large benchmark datasets. The contribution connects a more manageable curvature representation with an explicit mechanism for compensating for its inaccuracies. Its practical promise is to make second-order distributed training useful without requiring workers to construct the full Hessian.
summary.tldr: A distributed training algorithm uses local Hessian blocks and adaptive modeling to make second-order optimization more practical.

title: A Distributed Second-Order Algorithm You Can Trust

abstract: Proper regularization is critical for speeding up training, improving generalization performance, and learning compact models that are cost efficient. We propose and analyze regularized gradient descent algorithms for learning shallow neural networks. Our framework is general and covers weight-sharing (convolutional networks), sparsity (network pruning), and low-rank constraints among others. We first introduce covering dimension to quantify the complexity of the constraint set and provide insights on the generalization properties. Then, we show that proposed algorithms become well-behaved and local linear convergence occurs once the amount of data exceeds the covering dimension. Overall, our results demonstrate that near-optimal sample complexity is sufficient for efficient learning and illustrate how regularization can be beneficial to learn over-parameterized networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies regularized gradient descent for learning shallow neural networks. Its framework includes several ways to constrain a model, such as sharing weights, encouraging sparsity for pruning, and imposing low-rank structure. These restrictions offer different routes toward compact networks while fitting within a common analysis of learning and optimization.

The authors introduce covering dimension as a measure of the complexity of the permitted parameter set. This provides a way to relate a constraint’s structure to generalization and the amount of data needed for learning. The analysis therefore looks beyond the network’s raw parameter count to the complexity that remains after regularization.

The paper shows that the proposed algorithms have well-behaved local dynamics, including linear convergence, once the amount of data exceeds the covering dimension. Its results establish that near-optimal sample complexity is sufficient for efficient learning in the studied setting. The local nature of the convergence result matters: the conclusion concerns behavior near a solution, and the overall framework focuses on shallow networks.
summary.tldr: For shallow networks, structured regularization links effective model complexity to sufficient data and efficient local convergence.

title: Learning Compact Neural Networks with Regularization

abstract: Adversarial domain adaptation has made remarkable advances in learning transferable representations for knowledge transfer across domains. While adversarial learning strengthens the feature transferability which the community focuses on, its impact on the feature discriminability has not been fully explored. In this paper, a series of experiments based on spectral analysis of the feature representations have been conducted, revealing an unexpected deterioration of the discriminability while learning transferable features adversarially. Our key finding is that the eigenvectors with the largest singular values will dominate the feature transferability. As a consequence, the transferability is enhanced at the expense of over penalization of other eigenvectors that embody rich structures crucial for discriminability. Towards this problem, we present Batch Spectral Penalization (BSP), a general approach to penalizing the largest singular values so that other eigenvectors can be relatively strengthened to boost the feature discriminability. Experiments show that the approach significantly improves upon representative adversarial domain adaptation methods to yield state of the art results.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation seeks representations that transfer knowledge between domains. This paper examines a tension within adversarial adaptation: features can become more transferable while losing their ability to distinguish among categories. Through spectral analysis experiments, the authors investigate how changes in the strength of different feature directions contribute to that deterioration.

Their key finding is that directions associated with the largest singular values dominate transferability. Strengthening transfer through adversarial learning can consequently over-penalize other directions that contain structure important for discrimination. The analysis therefore separates the usefulness of a representation for crossing domains from its usefulness for preserving distinctions needed by the prediction task.

The proposed Batch Spectral Penalization method penalizes the largest singular values, allowing other directions to become relatively stronger. Its aim is to improve discriminability within adversarial domain adaptation. Experiments report significant improvements over representative methods and state-of-the-art results. The contribution pairs an empirical explanation of the transferability–discriminability tension with a general intervention directed at the spectral imbalance identified by that explanation.
summary.tldr: Penalizing dominant singular values improves discriminability and reported performance in adversarial domain adaptation.

title: Transferability vs. Discriminability: Batch Spectral Penalization for Adversarial Domain Adaptation

abstract: The key idea behind the unsupervised learning of disentangled representations is that real-world data is generated by a few explanatory factors of variation which can be recovered by unsupervised learning algorithms. In this paper, we provide a sober look at recent progress in the field and challenge some common assumptions. We first theoretically show that the unsupervised learning of disentangled representations is fundamentally impossible without inductive biases on both the models and the data. Then, we train more than $12000$ models covering most prominent methods and evaluation metrics in a reproducible large-scale experimental study on seven different data sets. We observe that while the different methods successfully enforce properties “encouraged” by the corresponding losses, well-disentangled models seemingly cannot be identified without supervision. Furthermore, increased disentanglement does not seem to lead to a decreased sample complexity of learning for downstream tasks. Our results suggest that future work on disentanglement learning should be explicit about the role of inductive biases and (implicit) supervision, investigate concrete benefits of enforcing disentanglement of the learned representations, and consider a reproducible experimental setup covering several data sets.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate the explanatory factors underlying observed data. The paper challenges the expectation that unsupervised learning can recover these factors without additional assumptions. Its theoretical result shows that unsupervised disentanglement is impossible without inductive biases concerning both the model and the data.

The authors also train more than 12,000 models across seven datasets, covering prominent methods and evaluation measures. The methods successfully encourage the properties targeted by their training losses. However, the experiments suggest that identifying which trained models are well disentangled still requires supervision. Encouraging a measurable property during training therefore does not, by itself, settle the model-selection problem.

The study also finds that stronger disentanglement does not seem to reduce the number of examples needed for downstream learning. This is an empirical challenge to an expected benefit, rather than a universal impossibility result about downstream usefulness. The authors call for explicit assumptions and supervision, concrete demonstrations of benefits, and reproducible evaluations across multiple datasets.
summary.tldr: Disentanglement requires inductive biases, and a large empirical study challenges assumptions about unsupervised model selection and downstream sample efficiency.

title: Challenging Common Assumptions in the Unsupervised Learning of Disentangled Representations

abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model ( Student ) from a high capacity source model ( Teacher ) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student . However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher . Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method “Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers learning from a large teacher model to a smaller student. Conventional approaches use the teacher’s training data or metadata extracted from it, but access to those resources may be impractical because of dataset size or privacy and safety concerns. This paper proposes distillation without either the original data or its metadata.

The method synthesizes Data Impressions from the trained teacher and uses them as substitutes for training examples. These synthetic inputs provide the material through which the student learns from the teacher. The key shift is to derive the transfer data from the model itself, allowing the distillation process to proceed when the original dataset is unavailable.

Across multiple benchmark datasets, the authors report generalization performance competitive with distillation that uses actual training samples. This supports the feasibility of transferring useful behavior through teacher-generated surrogate data in the evaluated settings. The zero-shot designation refers to dispensing with the original training data and metadata; the trained teacher remains the source from which the impressions and transferred learning are obtained.
summary.tldr: Teacher-generated synthetic Data Impressions enable competitive knowledge distillation without original training data or metadata.

title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks

abstract: Fueled by massive data, important decision making is being automated with the help of algorithms, therefore, fairness in algorithms has become an especially important research topic. In this work, we design new streaming and distributed algorithms for the fair k-center problem that models fair data summarization. The streaming and distributed models of computation have an attractive feature of being able to handle massive data sets that do not fit into main memory. Our main contributions are: (a) the first distributed algorithm; which has provably constant approximation ratio and is extremely parallelizable, and (b) a two-pass streaming algorithm with a provable approximation guarantee matching the best known algorithm (which is not a streaming algorithm). Our algorithms have the advantages of being easy to implement in practice, being fast with linear running times, having very small working memory and communication, and outperforming existing algorithms on several real and synthetic data sets. To complement our distributed algorithm, we also give a hardness result for natural distributed algorithms, which holds for even the special case of k-center.

Its algorithms target streaming and distributed computation, where datasets can be processed without requiring the full collection to fit into a single machine's main memory.

The authors give the first distributed algorithm for the problem with a provable constant approximation ratio and substantial parallelism. They also develop a streaming algorithm that makes two passes over the data. Its approximation guarantee matches the best previously known algorithm, even though that comparison algorithm does not operate in the streaming setting.

A complementary hardness result identifies limits for natural distributed algorithms, even for ordinary k-center. The contributions therefore pair scalable approximation methods with evidence about constraints on distributed approaches.
summary.tldr: New distributed and two-pass streaming algorithms provide provable fair k-center approximations with small resource requirements and strong reported empirical performance.

title: How to Solve Fair k-Center in Massive Data Models

abstract: This article derives lower bounds on the convergence rate of continuous-time gradient-based optimization algorithms. The algorithms are subjected to a time-normalization constraint that avoids a reparametrization of time in order to make the discussion of continuous-time convergence rates meaningful. We reduce the multi-dimensional problem to a single dimension, recover well-known lower bounds from the discrete-time setting, and provide insight into why these lower bounds occur. We present algorithms that achieve the proposed lower bounds, even when the function class under consideration includes certain nonconvex functions.

paragraphs: This paper asks how quickly gradient-based optimization can converge when an algorithm is described in continuous time. Its focus is on lower bounds: limits on the convergence speeds achievable within the setting under study. Such limits help distinguish improvements that are possible from speeds that an algorithm cannot attain under the stated constraints.

A key requirement is a normalization of time. Without it, changing the clock used to describe an algorithm could make its convergence appear arbitrarily faster without changing its underlying progress. The authors impose a constraint that prevents this reparametrization, giving continuous-time rate comparisons a meaningful common basis.

They reduce the multidimensional analysis to a one-dimensional problem, recover familiar lower bounds from discrete-time optimization, and explain why those bounds arise. They also present algorithms that attain the proposed bounds. This includes function classes containing certain nonconvex functions, showing that the bounds can be achievable beyond exclusively convex settings without claiming that result for every nonconvex problem.
summary.tldr: With time normalized appropriately, the paper derives continuous-time optimization lower bounds and algorithms that attain them.

title: Continuous-time Lower Bounds for Gradient-based Algorithms

abstract: One of the central problems in machine learning is domain adaptation. Different from past theoretical works, we consider a new model of subpopulation shift in the input or representation space. In this work, we propose a provably effective framework based on label propagation by using an input consistency loss. In our analysis we used a simple but realistic “expansion” assumption, which has been proposed in \citet{wei2021theoretical}. It turns out that based on a teacher classifier on the source domain, the learned classifier can not only propagate to the target domain but also improve upon the teacher. By leveraging existing generalization bounds, we also obtain end-to-end finite-sample guarantees on deep neural networks. In addition, we extend our theoretical framework to a more general setting of source-to-target transfer based on an additional unlabeled dataset, which can be easily applied to various learning scenarios. Inspired by our theory, we adapt consistency-based semi-supervised learning methods to domain adaptation settings and gain significant improvements.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation asks how a classifier trained in one domain can remain useful in another. This paper studies a model of subpopulation shift in the input space or in a learned representation. Its framework uses a source-domain teacher classifier as a starting point for transferring labels to the target domain.

The mechanism is label propagation through an input consistency loss, which encourages compatible predictions across related inputs. The theoretical analysis relies on an expansion assumption. Under the analyzed conditions, the resulting classifier can transfer predictions to the target domain and improve on the teacher, so propagation need not simply preserve the teacher’s existing errors.

The contribution therefore connects a conditional explanation of successful transfer with practical adaptations of existing learning methods.
summary.tldr: Under an expansion assumption, consistency-based label propagation can transfer a teacher’s predictions across domains and improve on the teacher.

title: A Theory of Label Propagation for Subpopulation Shift

abstract: Off-policy multi-step reinforcement learning algorithms consist of conservative and non-conservative algorithms: the former actively cut traces, whereas the latter do not. Recently, Munos et al. (2016) proved the convergence of conservative algorithms to an optimal Q-function. In contrast, non-conservative algorithms are thought to be unsafe and have a limited or no theoretical guarantee. Nonetheless, recent studies have shown that non-conservative algorithms empirically outperform conservative ones. Motivated by the empirical results and the lack of theory, we carry out theoretical analyses of Peng’s Q($\lambda$), a representative example of non-conservative algorithms. We prove that \emph{it also converges to an optimal policy} provided that the behavior policy slowly tracks a greedy policy in a way similar to conservative policy iteration. Such a result has been conjectured to be true but has not been proven. We also experiment with Peng’s Q($\lambda$) in complex continuous control tasks, confirming that Peng’s Q($\lambda$) often outperforms conservative algorithms despite its simplicity. These results indicate that Peng’s Q($\lambda$), which was thought to be unsafe, is a theoretically-sound and practically effective algorithm.

paragraphs: Off-policy multi-step reinforcement learning uses sequences of experience gathered under a behavior policy. Conservative methods actively cut traces, whereas non-conservative methods retain them. Despite empirical successes, the latter have often been regarded as unsafe because their theoretical guarantees were limited. This paper revisits Peng's Q(λ), a representative non-conservative algorithm.

The authors prove convergence to an optimal policy when the behavior policy slowly tracks a greedy policy in a manner similar to conservative policy iteration. This establishes a previously conjectured result and gives the method a concrete theoretical foundation. The tracking condition is essential to the stated guarantee; the result does not assert convergence for arbitrary behavior-policy changes.

Experiments on complex continuous control tasks show that Peng's Q(λ) often outperforms conservative algorithms despite its simplicity. Together, the theory and experiments strengthen the case for using non-conservative multi-step learning. They show that retaining traces can be compatible with a convergence guarantee under the stated policy evolution condition and can also be effective in demanding control tasks.
summary.tldr: Peng's Q(λ) converges to an optimal policy under a slow behavior-policy tracking condition and often beats conservative methods in continuous control experiments.

title: Revisiting Peng’s Q($λ$) for Modern Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Realistic environments often provide agents with very limited feedback. When the environment is initially unknown, the feedback, in the beginning, can be completely absent, and the agents may first choose to devote all their effort on \emph{exploring efficiently.} The exploration remains a challenge while it has been addressed with many hand-tuned heuristics with different levels of generality on one side, and a few theoretically-backed exploration strategies on the other. Many of them are incarnated by \emph{intrinsic motivation} and in particular \emph{explorations bonuses}. A common choice is to use $1/\sqrt{n}$ bonus, where $n$ is a number of times this particular state-action pair was visited. We show that, surprisingly, for a pure-exploration objective of \emph{reward-free exploration}, bonuses that scale with $1/n$ bring faster learning rates, improving the known upper bounds with respect to the dependence on the horizon $H$. Furthermore, we show that with an improved analysis of the stopping time, we can improve by a factor $H$ the sample complexity in the \emph{best-policy identification} setting, which is another pure-exploration objective, where the environment provides rewards but the agent is not penalized for its behavior during the exploration phase.

paragraphs: An agent may initially need to explore an unknown environment without receiving rewards. This paper studies pure exploration, where the immediate goal is gathering useful knowledge. It examines exploration bonuses that encourage visits to unfamiliar state–action pairs and asks how their mathematical form affects learning speed.

A common bonus decreases as the inverse square root of a pair’s visit count. For reward-free exploration, the authors show that bonuses decreasing as the inverse of the count yield faster learning rates. Specifically, they improve known upper bounds in their dependence on the horizon, the length of the decision sequence. The result identifies a benefit of this faster-decaying bonus for the stated exploration objective.

The paper also studies best-policy identification, where rewards are observed but poor choices during exploration are not penalized. An improved analysis of when learning stops reduces the sample-complexity bound by a factor equal to the horizon. Both contributions sharpen guarantees for gathering enough information before committing to a policy.
summary.tldr: Inverse-count bonuses improve reward-free exploration bounds, while sharper stopping-time analysis improves best-policy identification sample complexity.

title: Fast active learning for pure exploration in reinforcement learning

abstract: Developing machine learning methods that are privacy preserving is today a central topic of research, with huge practical impacts. Among the numerous ways to address privacy-preserving learning, we here take the perspective of computing the divergences between distributions under the Differential Privacy (DP) framework — being able to compute divergences between distributions is pivotal for many machine learning problems, such as learning generative models or domain adaptation problems. Instead of resorting to the popular gradient-based sanitization method for DP, we tackle the problem at its roots by focusing on the Sliced Wasserstein Distance and seamlessly making it differentially private. Our main contribution is as follows: we analyze the property of adding a Gaussian perturbation to the intrinsic randomized mechanism of the Sliced Wasserstein Distance, and we establish the sensitivity of the resulting differentially private mechanism. One of our important findings is that this DP mechanism transforms the Sliced Wasserstein distance into another distance, that we call the Smoothed Sliced Wasserstein Distance. This new differentially private distribution distance can be plugged into generative models and domain adaptation algorithms in a transparent way, and we empirically show that it yields highly competitive performance compared with gradient-based DP approaches from the literature, with almost no loss in accuracy for the domain adaptation problems that we consider.

It focuses on making the Sliced Wasserstein Distance differentially private, providing a distribution-comparison mechanism that can become a component of larger learning algorithms.

The authors analyze adding Gaussian perturbations to the distance's existing randomized mechanism and establish the sensitivity of the resulting private mechanism. Sensitivity is central to determining how changes in the input affect what is released. A key finding is that this procedure produces another distance, which they name the Smoothed Sliced Wasserstein Distance.

That result gives the privacy mechanism a useful interpretation as a modified distribution distance that can be incorporated into generative models and domain adaptation algorithms. Experiments show highly competitive performance against gradient-based differential privacy approaches. For the domain adaptation problems considered, the authors report almost no accuracy loss. The evidence supports protecting this foundational comparison operation as a practical route to private learning in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Adding Gaussian perturbations to Sliced Wasserstein comparisons yields a private smoothed distance with competitive empirical performance.

title: Differentially Private Sliced Wasserstein Distance

abstract: We develop theory and algorithms for average-reward on-policy Reinforcement Learning (RL). We first consider bounding the difference of the long-term average reward for two policies. We show that previous work based on the discounted return (Schulman et al. 2015, Achiam et al. 2017) results in a non-meaningful lower bound in the average reward setting. By addressing the average-reward criterion directly, we then derive a novel bound which depends on the average divergence between the policies and on Kemeny’s constant. Based on this bound, we develop an iterative procedure which produces a sequence of monotonically improved policies for the average reward criterion. This iterative procedure can then be combined with classic Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) methods, resulting in practical DRL algorithms that target the long-run average reward criterion. In particular, we demonstrate that Average-Reward TRPO (ATRPO), which adapts the on-policy TRPO algorithm to the average-reward criterion, significantly outperforms TRPO in the most challenging MuJuCo environments.

paragraphs: This paper develops on-policy reinforcement learning for the long-run average reward objective. It begins by asking how much the average reward can change when one policy replaces another. Existing bounds derived for discounted returns become uninformative in this setting, motivating an analysis that addresses average reward directly.

The new bound depends on the average divergence between the policies and on Kemeny’s constant. Using that bound, the authors construct an iterative procedure whose policies improve monotonically under the average-reward criterion. This provides a theoretical basis for policy updates designed around sustained reward rather than an adaptation of an unsuitable discounted-return bound.

The procedure can be combined with established deep reinforcement-learning methods to obtain practical algorithms. Experiments show that ATRPO significantly outperforms TRPO in the most challenging MuJoCo environments considered. The monotonic-improvement result belongs to the theoretical iterative procedure, while the practical algorithm’s advantages are demonstrated empirically.
summary.tldr: A direct average-reward policy bound supports monotonic policy improvement and motivates ATRPO, which outperforms TRPO in challenging MuJoCo evaluations.

title: On-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning for the Average-Reward Criterion

abstract: Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is a popular likelihood-free inference method for models with intractable likelihood functions. As ABC methods usually rely on comparing summary statistics of observed and simulated data, the choice of the statistics is crucial. This choice involves a trade-off between loss of information and dimensionality reduction, and is often determined based on domain knowledge. However, handcrafting and selecting suitable statistics is a laborious task involving multiple trial-and-error steps. In this work, we introduce an active learning method for ABC statistics selection which reduces the domain expert’s work considerably. By involving the experts, we are able to handle misspecified models, unlike the existing dimension reduction methods. Moreover, empirical results show better posterior estimates than with existing methods, when the simulation budget is limited.

This choice involves a trade-off between loss of information and dimensionality reduction, and is often determined based on domain knowledge. In this work, we introduce an active learning method for ABC statistics selection which reduces the domain expert’s work considerably. paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian computation estimates uncertainty about model parameters when the likelihood is too difficult to evaluate. It commonly compares summaries of simulated data with summaries of observed data. Choosing those summaries is consequential: reducing their dimensionality can make comparison more manageable, but it can also discard information needed for useful inference.

This paper introduces an active learning approach that involves a domain expert in selecting the summary statistics. The aim is to reduce the repeated manual experimentation otherwise needed to identify suitable summaries. Expert knowledge remains part of the process, while the selection method reduces the work required to put that knowledge to use.

The authors report that expert involvement enables the method to handle misspecified models, unlike the existing dimension reduction methods they discuss. Their empirical results also show better posterior estimates than existing methods when simulations are limited. The contribution therefore concerns both the human effort involved in selecting summaries and the quality of inference achievable with a restricted simulation budget.
summary.tldr: Expert-guided active learning reduces summary-statistic selection work and improves approximate Bayesian inference in experiments with limited simulations.

title: Approximate Bayesian Computation with Domain Expert in the Loop

abstract: Pre-training serves as a broadly adopted starting point for transfer learning on various downstream tasks. Recent investigations of lottery tickets hypothesis (LTH) demonstrate such enormous pre-trained models can be replaced by extremely sparse subnetworks (a.k.a. matching subnetworks) without sacrificing transferability. However, practical security-crucial applications usually pose more challenging requirements beyond standard transfer, which also demand these subnetworks to overcome adversarial vulnerability. In this paper, we formulate a more rigorous concept, Double-Win Lottery Tickets, in which a located subnetwork from a pre-trained model can be independently transferred on diverse downstream tasks, to reach BOTH the same standard and robust generalization, under BOTH standard and adversarial training regimes, as the full pre-trained model can do. We comprehensively examine various pre-training mechanisms and find that robust pre-training tends to craft sparser double-win lottery tickets with superior performance over the standard counterparts. For example, on downstream CIFAR-10/100 datasets, we identify double-win matching subnetworks with the standard, fast adversarial, and adversarial pre-training from ImageNet, at 89.26%/73.79%, 89.26%/79.03%, and 91.41%/83.22% sparsity, respectively. Furthermore, we observe the obtained double-win lottery tickets can be more data-efficient to transfer, under practical data-limited (e.g., 1% and 10%) downstream schemes. Our results show that the benefits from robust pre-training are amplified by the lottery ticket scheme, as well as the data-limited transfer setting. Codes are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/Double-Win-LTH.

paragraphs: A sparse subnetwork extracted from a pretrained model can sometimes retain the full model’s ability to transfer to new tasks. This paper asks for a stronger result: preserving both ordinary predictive performance and adversarial robustness. It calls subnetworks meeting these requirements double-win lottery tickets.

The definition covers transfer under both standard and adversarial training. A qualifying subnetwork must independently reach the full pretrained model’s standard and robust generalization across diverse downstream tasks. The authors compare different pretraining mechanisms and find that robust pretraining tends to yield sparser qualifying subnetworks with better performance than standard pretraining.

For transfer from ImageNet to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, adversarial pretraining yields reported matching subnetworks at 91.41% and 83.22% sparsity, respectively. The study also observes that these subnetworks can transfer more efficiently when downstream data are scarce, including settings using 1% or 10% of the data. These findings suggest that robust pretraining’s benefits can become more pronounced when combined with subnetwork selection and limited transfer data.
summary.tldr: Robust pretraining can yield sparse subnetworks that preserve both standard and adversarial transfer performance while using limited downstream data efficiently.

title: Data-Efficient Double-Win Lottery Tickets from Robust Pre-training

abstract: We propose Adversarially Trained Actor Critic (ATAC), a new model-free algorithm for offline reinforcement learning (RL) under insufficient data coverage, based on the concept of relative pessimism. ATAC is designed as a two-player Stackelberg game framing of offline RL: A policy actor competes against an adversarially trained value critic, who finds data-consistent scenarios where the actor is inferior to the data-collection behavior policy. We prove that, when the actor attains no regret in the two-player game, running ATAC produces a policy that provably 1) outperforms the behavior policy over a wide range of hyperparameters that control the degree of pessimism, and 2) competes with the best policy covered by data with appropriately chosen hyperparameters. Compared with existing works, notably our framework offers both theoretical guarantees for general function approximation and a deep RL implementation scalable to complex environments and large datasets. In the D4RL benchmark, ATAC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms on a range of continuous control tasks.

We prove that, when the actor attains no regret in the two-player game, running ATAC produces a policy that provably 1) outperforms the behavior policy over a wide range of hyperparameters that control the degree of pessimism, and 2) competes with the best policy covered by data with appropriately chosen hyperparameters. paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve decisions using an existing dataset, even when that dataset covers only part of the possible behavior. ATAC addresses this setting through relative pessimism: it evaluates a proposed policy against the policy that collected the data, looking for plausible reasons the proposal could perform worse.

The method casts learning as a two-player Stackelberg game between an actor and a value critic. The actor proposes a policy, while the adversarially trained critic searches for scenarios consistent with the data in which that policy loses to the behavior policy. This makes the comparison with existing behavior central to the learning objective.

The guarantees require the actor to attain no regret in this game. Under that condition, ATAC outperforms the behavior policy across a broad range of pessimism settings; with appropriately chosen settings, it also competes with the best policy covered by the data. The paper supports general function approximation theoretically and supplies a scalable deep-learning implementation. On the reported D4RL continuous-control tasks, ATAC consistently exceeds the compared state-of-the-art offline methods.
summary.tldr: ATAC trains an actor against a pessimistic critic to improve offline policies relative to the behavior represented in their data.

title: Adversarially Trained Actor Critic for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: People usually believe that network pruning not only reduces the computational cost of deep networks, but also prevents overfitting by decreasing model capacity. However, our work surprisingly discovers that network pruning sometimes even aggravates overfitting. We report an unexpected sparse double descent phenomenon that, as we increase model sparsity via network pruning, test performance first gets worse (due to overfitting), then gets better (due to relieved overfitting), and gets worse at last (due to forgetting useful information). While recent studies focused on the deep double descent with respect to model overparameterization, they failed to recognize that sparsity may also cause double descent. In this paper, we have three main contributions. First, we report the novel sparse double descent phenomenon through extensive experiments. Second, for this phenomenon, we propose a novel learning distance interpretation that the curve of l2 learning distance of sparse models (from initialized parameters to final parameters) may correlate with the sparse double descent curve well and reflect generalization better than minima flatness. Third, in the context of sparse double descent, a winning ticket in the lottery ticket hypothesis surprisingly may not always win.

paragraphs: Network pruning removes parameters and is often expected to reduce both computation and overfitting. This paper reports that pruning can sometimes make overfitting worse. Across extensive experiments, increasing sparsity produces a non-monotonic pattern: test performance first deteriorates, then improves, and finally deteriorates again. The authors call this phenomenon sparse double descent.

Their interpretation attributes the initial decline to greater overfitting, the recovery to reduced overfitting, and the final decline to loss of useful information. To help explain the pattern, they examine the l2 distance between a sparse model’s initialized and final parameters. They propose that this learning distance may track the sparse double-descent curve well and reflect generalization better than minima flatness.

The findings also qualify expectations around the lottery ticket hypothesis: a subnetwork regarded as a winning ticket may not always win in this setting. The practical implication is that removing more parameters does not necessarily improve generalization smoothly. Sparsity itself can create a changing balance between overfitting and retained information.
summary.tldr: Pruning can worsen, relieve, and then worsen test performance as sparsity increases, a phenomenon termed sparse double descent.

title: Sparse Double Descent: Where Network Pruning Aggravates Overfitting

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely applied for graph anomaly detection. As one of the key components for GNN design is to select a tailored spectral filter, we take the first step towards analyzing anomalies via the lens of the graph spectrum. Our crucial observation is the existence of anomalies will lead to the ‘right-shift’ phenomenon, that is, the spectral energy distribution concentrates less on low frequencies and more on high frequencies. This fact motivates us to propose the Beta Wavelet Graph Neural Network (BWGNN). Indeed, BWGNN has spectral and spatial localized band-pass filters to better handle the ‘right-shift’ phenomenon in anomalies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BWGNN on four large-scale anomaly detection datasets. Our code and data are released at https://github.com/squareRoot3/Rethinking-Anomaly-Detection.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are widely used to detect anomalies, and their spectral filters determine which kinds of graph variation they emphasize. This paper studies anomalies through the graph spectrum to inform that design choice. Its central observation is a shift in spectral energy associated with the presence of anomalies.

The authors describe this as a right-shift: less energy is concentrated at low frequencies and more at high frequencies. They use this observation to develop the Beta Wavelet Graph Neural Network, or BWGNN. Its band-pass filters are localized both spectrally and spatially, allowing the architecture to target frequency ranges while retaining locality on the graph.

BWGNN is evaluated on four large-scale anomaly-detection datasets, where the authors demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution connects an observed property of anomalies to a specific neural-network design. It suggests that selecting filters around the spectral behavior of anomalies is a useful way to tailor graph learning to the detection task.
summary.tldr: BWGNN uses localized band-pass filters motivated by the observed shift of graph spectral energy toward higher frequencies in the presence of anomalies.

title: Rethinking Graph Neural Networks for Anomaly Detection

abstract: Despite remarkable progress on visual recognition tasks, deep neural-nets still struggle to generalize well when training data is scarce or highly imbalanced, rendering them extremely vulnerable to real-world examples. In this paper, we present a surprisingly simple yet highly effective method to mitigate this limitation: using pure noise images as additional training data. Unlike the common use of additive noise or adversarial noise for data augmentation, we propose an entirely different perspective by directly training on pure random noise images. We present a new Distribution-Aware Routing Batch Normalization layer (DAR-BN), which enables training on pure noise images in addition to natural images within the same network. This encourages generalization and suppresses overfitting. Our proposed method significantly improves imbalanced classification performance, obtaining state-of-the-art results on a large variety of long-tailed image classification datasets (CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and CelebA-5). Furthermore, our method is extremely simple and easy to use as a general new augmentation tool (on top of existing augmentations), and can be incorporated in any training scheme. It does not require any specialized data generation or training procedures, thus keeping training fast and efficient.

paragraphs: Image classifiers can overfit when training examples are scarce or unevenly distributed across classes. This paper proposes adding pure random-noise images to training alongside natural images. The noise images are complete training inputs, rather than small perturbations added to existing images, making the proposal a different use of noise from familiar augmentation techniques.

The enabling component is Distribution-Aware Routing Batch Normalization, or DAR-BN. This layer allows one network to train on both natural images and pure noise. The authors report that the resulting training encourages generalization and suppresses overfitting. The method can also be layered on top of existing augmentations without requiring specialized image-generation or training procedures.

Experiments report significant improvements and state-of-the-art results across CIFAR-10-LT, CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and CelebA-5. These results support the usefulness of pure-noise training for the evaluated imbalanced classification problems. The approach matters because the additional training data are simple to generate, and the abstract reports that training remains fast and efficient.
summary.tldr: Training with pure random-noise images through DAR-BN improves generalization and reported performance on multiple imbalanced image-classification datasets.

title: Pure Noise to the Rescue of Insufficient Data: Improving Imbalanced Classification by Training on Random Noise Images

abstract: This paper proposes a unified diffusion framework (dubbed UniDiffuser) to fit all distributions relevant to a set of multi-modal data in one model. Our key insight is – learning diffusion models for marginal, conditional, and joint distributions can be unified as predicting the noise in the perturbed data, where the perturbation levels (i.e. timesteps) can be different for different modalities. Inspired by the unified view, UniDiffuser learns all distributions simultaneously with a minimal modification to the original diffusion model – perturbs data in all modalities instead of a single modality, inputs individual timesteps in different modalities, and predicts the noise of all modalities instead of a single modality. UniDiffuser is parameterized by a transformer for diffusion models to handle input types of different modalities. Implemented on large-scale paired image-text data, UniDiffuser is able to perform image, text, text-to-image, image-to-text, and image-text pair generation by setting proper timesteps without additional overhead. In particular, UniDiffuser is able to produce perceptually realistic samples in all tasks and its quantitative results (e.g., the FID and CLIP score) are not only superior to existing general-purpose models but also comparable to the bespoken models (e.g., Stable Diffusion and DALL-E 2) in representative tasks (e.g., text-to-image generation).

paragraphs: Multimodal generation involves several related tasks: generating one modality alone, generating it from another, or generating both together. UniDiffuser brings the corresponding marginal, conditional, and joint distributions into one diffusion framework. Its key observation is that these tasks can share noise prediction when each modality is allowed its own perturbation level.

The model perturbs every modality, receives separate diffusion timesteps for them, and predicts their respective noise. A transformer handles the different input types. On paired image-text data, choosing suitable timesteps enables image generation, text generation, text-to-image generation, image-to-text generation, and paired generation. The abstract reports switching among these tasks without additional overhead.

The authors report perceptually realistic samples across all these tasks. Quantitative results exceed those of existing general-purpose models and are comparable to specialized models on representative tasks, including text-to-image generation. This supports the value of sharing one model across several generation distributions, while the comparison with specialized systems is specifically qualified by the tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: UniDiffuser uses separate noise levels for each modality to support unconditional, conditional, and joint image-text generation in one transformer.

title: One Transformer Fits All Distributions in Multi-Modal Diffusion at Scale

abstract: This paper is concerned with online filtering of discretely observed nonlinear diffusion processes. Our approach is based on the fully adapted auxiliary particle filter, which involves Doob’s $h$-transforms that are typically intractable. We propose a computational framework to approximate these $h$-transforms by solving the underlying backward Kolmogorov equations using nonlinear Feynman-Kac formulas and neural networks. The methodology allows one to train a locally optimal particle filter prior to the data-assimilation procedure. Numerical experiments illustrate that the proposed approach can be orders of magnitude more efficient than state-of-the-art particle filters in the regime of highly informative observations, when the observations are extreme under the model, and if the state dimension is large.

paragraphs: Online filtering estimates the evolving state of a system as observations arrive. This paper considers nonlinear diffusion processes observed at discrete times. It starts from a fully adapted auxiliary particle filter, an approach whose use involves Doob h-transforms. These mathematical transformations are typically intractable, creating a computational obstacle to applying the filter.

The proposed framework approximates the transformations by solving their underlying backward Kolmogorov equations. It combines nonlinear Feynman–Kac formulas with neural networks to perform this computation. The resulting methodology allows a locally optimal particle filter to be trained before the stage in which observations are assimilated, moving this learning work ahead of online filtering.

Numerical experiments illustrate efficiency gains that can reach orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art particle filters. The reported advantages concern highly informative observations, observations that are extreme under the model, and large state dimensions. These findings support the approach in those demanding regimes; the abstract presents them as experimental evidence of possible gains, rather than a uniform speed advantage across all filtering problems.
summary.tldr: Neural approximations of Doob h-transforms enable pretrained particle filters that can be orders of magnitude more efficient in challenging observation and dimensionality regimes.

title: Computational Doob h-transforms for Online Filtering of Discretely Observed Diffusions

abstract: We propose $\epsilon$-Exploring Thompson Sampling ($\epsilon$-TS), a modified version of the Thompson Sampling (TS) algorithm for multi-armed bandits. In $\epsilon$-TS, arms are selected greedily based on empirical mean rewards with probability $1-\epsilon$, and based on posterior samples obtained from TS with probability $\epsilon$. Here, $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ is a user-defined constant. By reducing exploration, $\epsilon$-TS improves computational efficiency compared to TS while achieving better regret bounds. We establish that $\epsilon$-TS is both minimax optimal and asymptotically optimal for various popular reward distributions, including Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, and Gamma. A key technical advancement in our analysis is the relaxation of the requirement for a stringent anti-concentration bound of the posterior distribution, which was necessary in recent analyses that achieved similar bounds. As a result, $\epsilon$-TS maintains the posterior update structure of TS while minimizing alterations, such as clipping the sampling distribution or solving the inverse of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between reward distributions, as done in previous work. Furthermore, our algorithm is as easy to implement as TS, but operates significantly faster due to reduced exploration. Empirical evaluations confirm the efficiency and optimality of $\epsilon$-TS.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling chooses among uncertain options using samples from posterior reward distributions. This paper proposes epsilon-Exploring Thompson Sampling, which uses that decision rule only with a user-selected probability epsilon. Otherwise, it chooses greedily according to observed mean rewards. Epsilon is a fixed value strictly between zero and one.

Reducing posterior-based exploration improves computational efficiency while retaining the original posterior update structure. The authors prove both minimax and asymptotic optimality for several common reward distributions, including Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, and Gamma. These guarantees describe strong regret behavior in both worst-case and long-run senses for the covered settings.

A key analytical change relaxes a demanding anti-concentration requirement on the posterior that appeared in recent analyses. This enables the guarantees with fewer algorithmic alterations, avoiding machinery such as clipping sampling distributions or inverting a divergence between reward distributions used in previous work. Empirical evaluations support the method’s efficiency and optimality. The result shows that this particular reduction in exploration can preserve strong theoretical performance while making the algorithm faster and simple to implement.
summary.tldr: Mixing greedy decisions with occasional Thompson sampling improves speed while achieving minimax and asymptotic optimality for several common reward distributions.

title: Thompson Sampling with Less Exploration is Fast and Optimal

abstract: Large language models show impressive results at predicting structured text such as code, but also commonly introduce errors and hallucinations in their output. When used to assist software developers, these models may make mistakes that users must go back and fix, or worse, introduce subtle bugs that users may miss entirely. We propose Randomized Utility-driven Synthesis of Uncertain REgions (R-U-SURE) , an approach for building uncertainty-aware suggestions based on a decision-theoretic model of goal-conditioned utility, using random samples from a generative model as a proxy for the unobserved possible intents of the end user. Our technique combines minimum-Bayes-risk decoding, dual decomposition, and decision diagrams in order to efficiently produce structured uncertainty summaries, given only sample access to an arbitrary generative model of code and an optional AST parser. We demonstrate R-U-SURE on three developer-assistance tasks, and show that it can be applied different user interaction patterns without retraining the model and leads to more accurate uncertainty estimates than token-probability baselines. We also release our implementation as an open-source library at https://github.com/google-research/r_u_sure.

paragraphs: Code-generating language models can produce errors that developers must repair or subtle bugs they may overlook. R-U-SURE addresses how to communicate uncertainty in suggestions when the developer’s intended result is unknown. It treats samples from a generative model as proxies for different possible user intents and evaluates suggestions according to their usefulness across those possibilities.

The method combines minimum-Bayes-risk decoding, dual decomposition, and decision diagrams to construct structured uncertainty summaries efficiently. Its requirements are sample access to a code generator and, optionally, a parser for abstract syntax trees. This makes the uncertainty mechanism usable with an arbitrary generative code model without requiring retraining.

The authors demonstrate the approach on three developer-assistance tasks and apply it to different interaction patterns. It produces more accurate uncertainty estimates than the token-probability baselines evaluated. The contribution is to make uncertainty depend on the utility of a structured suggestion under plausible user goals, connecting what the assistant presents to the range of outcomes the user may actually want.
summary.tldr: R-U-SURE builds structured uncertainty summaries for code suggestions by evaluating their utility across sampled proxies for possible user intents.

title: R-U-SURE? Uncertainty-Aware Code Suggestions By Maximizing Utility Across Random User Intents

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) achieve remarkable performance in graph machine learning tasks but can be hard to train on large-graph data, where their learning dynamics are not well understood. We investigate the training dynamics of large-graph GNNs using graph neural tangent kernels (GNTKs) and graphons. In the limit of large width, optimization of an overparametrized NN is equivalent to kernel regression on the NTK. Here, we investigate how the GNTK evolves as another independent dimension is varied: the graph size. We use graphons to define limit objects—graphon NNs for GNNs, and graphon NTKs for GNTKs—, and prove that, on a sequence of graphs, the GNTKs converge to the graphon NTK. We further prove that the spectrum of the GNTK, which is related to the problem’s learning directions, converges to the spectrum of the GNTK. This implies that in the large-graph limit, the GNTK fitted on a graph of moderate size can be used to solve the same task on the large graph, and to infer the learning dynamics of the large-graph GNN. These results are verified empirically on node regression and classification tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how graph neural-network training behaves as graphs become large. It uses graph neural tangent kernels, which connect the optimization of sufficiently wide networks to kernel regression. The authors separate two different kinds of scale: network width, which underlies that connection, and graph size, which is the main variable studied here.

Graphons provide mathematical limit objects for describing increasingly large graphs. Using them, the authors define limiting versions of both graph neural networks and their tangent kernels. They prove convergence of the graph kernels along a graph sequence and establish a spectral convergence result. The spectral analysis matters because kernel spectra are related to the directions in which learning proceeds.

The resulting large-graph picture supports using a kernel fitted on a moderately sized graph to solve the same task on a larger graph and infer the larger network’s learning dynamics. Experiments on node regression and classification verify the reported results. The contribution gives a theoretical basis for this transfer in the analyzed graph-limit setting, rather than an unrestricted claim about transferring between unrelated graphs.
summary.tldr: Graph-limit analysis shows how neural tangent kernels can connect learning on moderate-sized graphs to the dynamics of much larger graphs.

title: Graph Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence on Large Graphs

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) for clinical time series data has received significant attention in recent literature, since these data are highly rich and provide important information about a patient’s physiological state. However, most existing SSL methods for clinical time series are limited in that they are designed for unimodal time series, such as a sequence of structured features (e.g., lab values and vitals signs) or an individual high-dimensional physiological signal (e.g., an electrocardiogram). These existing methods cannot be readily extended to model time series that exhibit multimodality, with structured features and high-dimensional data being recorded at each timestep in the sequence. In this work, we address this gap and propose a new SSL method — Sequential Multi-Dimensional SSL — where a SSL loss is applied both at the level of the entire sequence and at the level of the individual high-dimensional data points in the sequence in order to better capture information at both scales. Our strategy is agnostic to the specific form of loss function used at each level – it can be contrastive, as in SimCLR, or non-contrastive, as in VICReg. We evaluate our method on two real-world clinical datasets, where the time series contains sequences of (1) high-frequency electrocardiograms and (2) structured data from lab values and vitals signs. Our experimental results indicate that pre-training with our method and then fine-tuning on downstream tasks improves performance over baselines on both datasets, and in several settings, can lead to improvements across different self-supervised loss functions.

paragraphs: Clinical records can combine ordinary structured measurements with complex physiological signals over time. A single timestep may contain both laboratory values or vital signs and a high-dimensional recording. Existing self-supervised methods often target just one of these forms, making them difficult to extend directly to sequences that contain both.

Sequential Multi-Dimensional Self-Supervised Learning applies learning objectives at two scales: the complete sequence and the individual high-dimensional observations within it. This aims to capture information in both the longitudinal record and its detailed components. The framework does not depend on one particular objective; each level can use contrastive losses such as SimCLR or non-contrastive losses such as VICReg.

The authors evaluate pretraining followed by downstream fine-tuning on two real-world clinical datasets containing electrocardiogram sequences and structured laboratory and vital-sign data. Performance improves over baselines on both datasets. In several settings, improvements also hold across different self-supervised losses, supporting the usefulness of the two-scale organization beyond a single choice of training objective.
summary.tldr: Self-supervision at both sequence and individual-signal levels improves downstream learning on two multimodal clinical time-series datasets.

title: Sequential Multi-Dimensional Self-Supervised Learning for Clinical Time Series

abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) aims to estimate the return of a target policy using some pre-collected observational data generated by a potentially different behavior policy. In many cases, there exist unmeasured variables that confound the action-reward or action-next-state relationships, rendering many existing OPE approaches ineffective. This paper develops an instrumental variable (IV)-based method for consistent OPE in confounded sequential decision making. Similar to single-stage decision making, we show that IV enables us to correctly identify the target policy’s value in infinite horizon settings as well. Furthermore, we propose a number of policy value estimators and illustrate their effectiveness through extensive simulations and real data analysis from a world-leading short-video platform.

In many cases, there exist unmeasured variables that confound the action-reward or action-next-state relationships, rendering many existing OPE approaches ineffective. This paper develops an instrumental variable (IV)-based method for consistent OPE in confounded sequential decision making.
