paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how well a target decision policy would perform using observations collected under another policy. A major obstacle arises when unmeasured variables affect both the actions taken and their rewards or subsequent states. In that situation, observed associations can misrepresent the consequences of following the target policy.

This paper develops an instrumental-variable approach to that problem in sequential decision making. The authors show that instrumental variables can identify the target policy's value even in an infinite-horizon setting, where decisions and their consequences continue over time. This extends the role of instrumental variables beyond evaluating a single decision.

The work also proposes several estimators for policy value and illustrates their effectiveness through simulations and analysis of data from a short-video platform. Its theoretical contribution concerns consistent evaluation despite unmeasured confounding within the instrumental-variable framework. Its practical contribution is to turn that identification result into estimators that can be applied to observational decision data.
summary.tldr: An instrumental-variable framework enables consistent evaluation of policies from confounded sequential observational data.

title: An Instrumental Variable Approach to Confounded Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: Detection of periodic patterns of interest within noisy time series data plays a critical role in various tasks, spanning from health monitoring to behavior analysis. Existing learning techniques often rely on labels or clean versions of signals for detecting the periodicity, and those employing self-supervised methods are required to apply proper augmentations, which is already challenging for time series and can result in collapse—all representations collapse to a single point due to strong augmentation. In this work, we propose a novel method to detect the periodicity in time series without the need for any labels or requiring tailored positive or negative data generation mechanisms. We mitigate the collapse issue by ensuring the learned representations retain information from the original samples without imposing any variance constraints on the batch. Our experiments in three time-series tasks against state-of-the-art learning methods show that the proposed approach consistently outperforms prior works, achieving performance improvements of more than 45–50%, showing its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Finding repeating patterns in noisy time series matters for applications such as health monitoring and behavior analysis. Many learning methods depend on labels or clean reference signals. Self-supervised alternatives can require carefully designed signal transformations, and overly strong transformations can make the learned representations collapse to the same point.

The proposed method detects periodicity without labels and without tailored mechanisms for generating positive or negative examples. Its central idea is to retain information from the original samples in the learned representations. This addresses collapse without imposing constraints on the variance of representations across a batch, changing how the method preserves useful differences between signals.

The authors evaluate the approach on three time-series tasks against leading learning methods. They report consistent improvements over prior work, with performance improvements described as exceeding 45–50%. These findings support the usefulness of the approach in the tested settings. The broader contribution is a way to learn periodic structure while reducing dependence on supervision and task-specific example construction.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised method detects periodic signals by preserving sample information, avoiding labels and tailored positive or negative example generation.

title: An Unsupervised Approach for Periodic Source Detection in Time Series

abstract: Compressing high-capability Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a favored strategy for resource-efficient inferences. While state-of-the-art (SoTA) compression methods boast impressive advancements in preserving benign task performance, the potential risks of compression in terms of safety and trustworthiness have been largely neglected. This study conducts the first, thorough evaluation of three (3) leading LLMs using five (5) SoTA compression techniques across eight (8) trustworthiness dimensions. Our experiments highlight the intricate interplay between compression and trustworthiness, revealing some interesting patterns. We find that quantization is currently a more effective approach than pruning in achieving efficiency and trustworthiness simultaneously. For instance, a 4-bit quantized model retains the trustworthiness of its original counterpart, but model pruning significantly degrades trustworthiness, even at 50% sparsity. Moreover, employing quantization within a moderate bit range could unexpectedly improve certain trustworthiness dimensions such as ethics and fairness. Conversely, extreme quantization to very low bit levels (3 bits) tends to reduce trustworthiness significantly. This increased risk cannot be uncovered by looking at benign performance alone, in turn, mandating comprehensive trustworthiness evaluation in practice. These findings culminate in practical recommendations for simultaneously achieving high utility, efficiency, and trustworthiness in LLMs. Code and models are available at https://decoding-comp-trust.github.io.
originalAbstract: Compressing high-capability Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a favored strategy for resource-efficient inferences. While state-of-the-art (SoTA) compression methods boast impressive advancements in preserving benign task performance, the potential risks of compression in terms of safety and trustworthiness have been largely neglected. This study conducts the first, thorough evaluation of three (3) leading LLMs using five (5) SoTA compression techniques across eight (8) trustworthiness dimensions. Our experiments highlight the intricate interplay between compression and trustworthiness, revealing some interesting patterns. We find that quantization is currently a more effective approach than pruning in achieving efficiency and trustworthiness simultaneously. For instance, a 4-bit quantized model retains the trustworthiness of its original counterpart, but model pruning significantly degrades trustworthiness, even at 50% sparsity. Moreover, employing quantization within a moderate bit range could unexpectedly improve certain trustworthiness dimensions such as ethics and fairness. Conversely, extreme quantization to very low bit levels (3 bits) tends to reduce trustworthiness significantly. This increased risk cannot be uncovered by looking at benign performance alone, in turn, mandating comprehensive trustworthiness evaluation in practice. These findings culminate in practical recommendations for simultaneously achieving high utility, efficiency, and trustworthiness in LLMs. Code and models are available at https://decoding-comp-trust.github.io.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model can make inference cheaper, but retaining ordinary task performance does not establish that its trustworthiness has been preserved. This study evaluates three leading language models using five compression techniques across eight trustworthiness dimensions. It examines how efficiency changes interact with properties that benign task evaluations can miss.

Within these experiments, quantization offers a better balance of efficiency and trustworthiness than pruning. A reported 4-bit quantized model preserves its original counterpart’s trustworthiness, whereas pruning significantly harms trustworthiness even at 50% sparsity. The findings also show that moderate quantization can improve particular dimensions, including ethics and fairness, so the relationship is not simply that more compression always causes worse outcomes.

At very low precision, however, the picture changes: 3-bit quantization tends to substantially reduce trustworthiness. These results make the compression choice and its severity relevant to evaluation, beyond whether standard task scores remain strong. The paper’s practical implication is that compressed models need comprehensive trustworthiness assessment because benign performance alone does not reveal the observed risks.
summary.tldr: Compression affects LLM trustworthiness in ways ordinary task scores miss, with moderate quantization outperforming pruning in the reported evaluation.

title: Decoding Compressed Trust: Scrutinizing the Trustworthiness of Efficient LLMs Under Compression

abstract: Identifying how much a model $\hat{p}_{Y|X}^{\theta}$ knows about the stochastic real-world process $p_{Y|X}$ it was trained on is important to ensure it avoids producing incorrect or "hallucinated" answers or taking unsafe actions. But this is difficult for generative models because probabilistic predictions do not distinguish between per-response noise (aleatoric uncertainty) and lack of knowledge about the process (epistemic uncertainty), and existing epistemic uncertainty quantification techniques tend to be overconfident when the model underfits. We propose a general strategy for teaching a model to both approximate $p_{Y|X}$ and also estimate the remaining gaps between $\hat{p}_{Y|X}^{\theta}$ and $p_{Y|X}$: train it to predict pairs of independent responses drawn from the true conditional distribution, allow it to "cheat" by observing one response while predicting the other, then measure how much it cheats. Remarkably, we prove that being good at cheating (i.e. cheating whenever it improves your prediction) is equivalent to being second-order calibrated, a principled extension of ordinary calibration that allows us to construct provably-correct frequentist confidence intervals for $p_{Y|X}$ and detect incorrect responses with high probability. We demonstrate empirically that our approach accurately estimates how much models don’t know across ambiguous image classification, (synthetic) language modeling, and partially-observable navigation tasks, outperforming existing techniques.

paragraphs: Uncertain predictions can reflect randomness in the world or gaps in a model's understanding. Those two causes require different interpretations, but ordinary probabilistic predictions do not separate them. This paper develops a way to estimate the knowledge gaps, including situations where existing uncertainty methods become overconfident because a model underfits.

The training strategy uses pairs of independent responses drawn from the true distribution for the same input. The model predicts the pair and is also allowed to see one response while predicting the other. Measuring how much this extra information improves prediction provides a signal about what the model has not learned about the underlying process.

The authors prove that using this opportunity whenever it helps is equivalent to second-order calibration. This property supports provably correct frequentist confidence intervals for the true conditional distribution and high-probability detection of incorrect responses. Experiments on ambiguous image classification, synthetic language modeling, and partially observable navigation show more accurate estimates of missing knowledge than existing techniques. The theoretical guarantee concerns the stated calibration property, rather than every model trained with paired examples.
summary.tldr: Predicting paired responses and measuring the benefit of seeing one helps models quantify gaps in their knowledge.

title: Experts Don’t Cheat: Learning What You Don’t Know By Predicting Pairs

abstract: In machine learning and neural network optimization, algorithms like incremental gradient, single shuffle SGD, and random reshuffle SGD are popular due to their cache-mismatch efficiency and good practical convergence behavior. However, their optimization properties in theory, especially for non-convex smooth functions, remain incompletely explored. This paper delves into the convergence properties of SGD algorithms with arbitrary data ordering, within a broad framework for non-convex smooth functions. Our findings show enhanced convergence guarantees for incremental gradient and single shuffle SGD. Particularly if $n$ is the training set size, we improve $n$ times the optimization term of convergence guarantee to reach accuracy $\epsilon$ from $O \left( \frac{n}{\epsilon} \right)$ to $O \left( \frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$.

paragraphs: Incremental gradient and shuffled variants of stochastic gradient descent are widely used because they combine practical convergence behavior with efficient data access. Their theoretical behavior is less fully understood for smooth, nonconvex objectives. This paper examines convergence when the training data can be processed in arbitrary orders, providing a broad framework for analyzing these optimization methods.

The main improvements concern incremental gradient and single-shuffle stochastic gradient descent. By allowing arbitrary data ordering in the analysis, the framework addresses how convergence can be justified beyond a narrow choice of ordering. The work strengthens guarantees for these existing methods, focusing on the mathematical account of their progress toward a specified accuracy.

If n denotes the training-set size, the authors improve the optimization term in the convergence guarantee from O(n / epsilon) to O(1 / epsilon). This is an n-fold improvement in that term. Its meaning is a sharper dependence within the bound, not a reported n-fold wall-clock speedup or a claim that every part of the algorithm’s cost becomes independent of dataset size.
summary.tldr: A convergence analysis improves the optimization term for incremental gradient and single-shuffle SGD by a factor equal to the training-set size.

title: On Convergence of Incremental Gradient for Non-convex Smooth Functions

abstract: Many processes in biology and drug discovery involve various 3D interactions between molecules, such as protein and protein, protein and small molecule, etc. Given that different molecules are usually represented in different granularity, existing methods usually encode each type of molecules independently with different models, leaving it defective to learn the various underlying interaction physics. In this paper, we first propose to universally represent an arbitrary 3D complex as a geometric graph of sets, shedding light on encoding all types of molecules with one model. We then propose a Generalist Equivariant Transformer (GET) to effectively capture both domain-specific hierarchies and domain-agnostic interaction physics. To be specific, GET consists of a bilevel attention module, a feed-forward module and a layer normalization module, where each module is E(3) equivariant and specialized for handling sets of variable sizes. Notably, in contrast to conventional pooling-based hierarchical models, our GET is able to retain fine-grained information of all levels. Extensive experiments on the interactions between proteins, small molecules and RNA/DNAs verify the effectiveness and generalization capability of our proposed method across different domains.

paragraphs: Molecular interactions involve objects represented at different levels of detail, such as proteins and small molecules. Using separate encoders for each molecular type can make it difficult to learn the interaction physics they share. This paper proposes a common representation: describe a three-dimensional molecular complex as a geometric graph whose elements are sets.

The Generalist Equivariant Transformer processes this representation with bilevel attention, feed-forward transformations, and layer normalization. Each module handles sets of varying sizes and is E(3) equivariant, meaning its behavior respects the corresponding transformations of three-dimensional geometry. The architecture aims to capture both molecule-specific hierarchies and physical relationships that apply across molecular types.

A key design claim is that GET retains fine-grained information at every level, unlike conventional hierarchical models based on pooling. Experiments involving proteins, small molecules, RNA, and DNA support its effectiveness and generalization across the evaluated domains. The contribution is a shared geometric modeling framework that accommodates different molecular granularities while maintaining the detailed information needed to describe their interactions.
summary.tldr: GET uses a shared geometric representation and equivariant transformer to learn interactions across molecular types while retaining fine-grained hierarchical information.

title: Generalist Equivariant Transformer Towards 3D Molecular Interaction Learning

abstract: Music generation schemes using language modeling rely on a vocabulary of audio tokens, generally provided as codes in a discrete latent space learnt by an auto-encoder. Multi-stage quantizers are often employed to produce these tokens, therefore the decoding strategy used for token prediction must be adapted to account for multiple codebooks: either it should model the joint distribution over all codebooks, or fit the product of the codebook marginal distributions. Modelling the joint distribution requires a costly increase in the number of auto-regressive steps, while fitting the product of the marginals yields an inexact model unless the codebooks are mutually independent. In this work, we introduce an independence-promoting loss to regularize the auto-encoder used as the tokenizer in language models for music generation. The proposed loss is a proxy for mutual information based on the maximum mean discrepancy principle, applied in reproducible kernel Hilbert spaces. Our criterion is simple to implement and train, and it is generalizable to other multi-stream codecs. We show that it reduces the statistical dependence between codebooks during auto-encoding. This leads to an increase in the generated music quality when modelling the product of the marginal distributions, while generating audio much faster than the joint distribution model.

paragraphs: Music language models often work with audio tokens produced by an autoencoder using several codebooks. Predicting these token streams creates a tradeoff. Modeling their full joint distribution requires more sequential prediction steps, while modeling each codebook's marginal distribution separately is an imperfect approximation unless the codebooks are mutually independent.

This paper addresses that tradeoff by changing how the audio tokenizer is trained. It introduces an additional loss that encourages independence between codebooks. The loss uses maximum mean discrepancy in a kernel-based function space as a proxy for mutual information. Its purpose is to make separate predictions across codebooks better match the statistical structure of the tokens themselves.

The authors show that the loss reduces dependence between codebooks during autoencoding. When the music model uses a product of marginal distributions, this change improves generated music quality while retaining much faster audio generation than the joint-distribution model. The contribution therefore links tokenizer design to generation efficiency, and the proposed criterion can also extend to other codecs with multiple streams.
summary.tldr: Encouraging independence between audio codebooks improves music generation with separate token-stream predictions while retaining their speed advantage over joint modeling.

title: An Independence-promoting Loss for Music Generation with Language Models

abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive Bayesian framework for FANOVA models. We provide guidelines for tuning and practical implementation to improve scalability of learning and prediction. Our model is very flexible and can handle different levels of sparsity across and within decomposition orders, as well as among covariates. This flexibility enables the modeling of complex real-world data while enhancing interpretability. Additionally, it allows our model to unify diverse deterministic and Bayesian non-parametric approaches into a single equation, making comparisons and understanding easier. Notably, our model serves as the Bayesian counterpart of several deterministic methods allowing uncertainty quantification. This general framework unlocks potential for novel model developments that have been previously overlooked, such as the proposed Dirichlet mixing model that addresses limitations of existing models.

paragraphs: FANOVA models describe a function through components associated with individual variables and their interactions. This paper develops a Bayesian framework for deciding which components matter and estimating them. The aim is to represent complex relationships while retaining an interpretable account of how different variables contribute.

The framework allows different amounts of sparsity across interaction orders, within an order, and among covariates. In plain language, it can accommodate situations where only some variables or interactions are useful, without requiring every part of the decomposition to follow the same pattern. The authors also provide tuning and implementation guidance intended to improve the scalability of learning and prediction.

A central contribution is expressing several deterministic and Bayesian nonparametric approaches within one formulation. This makes their relationships easier to compare and supplies Bayesian counterparts that support uncertainty quantification. The framework also suggests additional model designs: the paper introduces a Dirichlet mixing model intended to address limitations of existing approaches. Its contribution is therefore both a modeling framework and a way to organize and extend earlier methods.
summary.tldr: A unified Bayesian FANOVA framework supports flexible component selection, uncertainty quantification, and connections among existing modeling approaches.

title: A Unified View of FANOVA: A Comprehensive Bayesian Framework for Component Selection and Estimation

abstract: The abundance of data has led to the emergence of a variety of optimization techniques that attempt to leverage available side information to provide more anticipative decisions. The wide range of methods and contexts of application have motivated the design of a universal unitless measure of performance known as the coefficient of prescriptiveness. This coefficient was designed to quantify both the quality of contextual decisions compared to a reference one and the prescriptive power of side information. To identify policies that maximize the former in a data-driven context, this paper introduces a distributionally robust contextual optimization model where the coefficient of prescriptiveness substitutes for the classical empirical risk minimization objective. We present a bisection algorithm to solve this model, which relies on solving a series of linear programs when the distributional ambiguity set has an appropriate nested form and polyhedral structure. Studying a contextual shortest path problem, we evaluate the robustness of the resulting policies against alternative methods when the out-of-sample dataset is subject to varying amounts of distribution shift.

paragraphs: Contextual optimization uses side information to make decisions that anticipate their circumstances. The coefficient of prescriptiveness is a unitless measure designed to assess contextual decisions against a reference decision and quantify the usefulness of that information. This paper uses the coefficient directly as the objective for learning a decision policy.

The authors place this objective inside a distributionally robust optimization model, replacing the usual empirical-risk objective. The formulation accounts for uncertainty about the data distribution through an ambiguity set. They present a bisection algorithm that solves a sequence of linear programs when that set has the required nested form and polyhedral structure.

The evaluation studies a contextual shortest-path problem and compares the resulting policies with alternatives under different amounts of out-of-sample distribution shift. This tests robustness in the setting motivating the formulation. The abstract does not specify a comparative winner; its stated contribution is the robust prescriptiveness objective, a solver under explicit structural conditions, and an evaluation of policy behavior under shift.
summary.tldr: A distributionally robust model optimizes contextual prescriptiveness directly and admits a linear-program-based solver under structural conditions.

title: Robust Data-driven Prescriptiveness Optimization

abstract: Learning to sample from intractable distributions over discrete sets without relying on corresponding training data is a central problem in a wide range of fields, including Combinatorial Optimization. Currently, popular deep learning-based approaches rely primarily on generative models that yield exact sample likelihoods. This work introduces a method that lifts this restriction and opens the possibility to employ highly expressive latent variable models like diffusion models. Our approach is conceptually based on a loss that upper bounds the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence and evades the requirement of exact sample likelihoods. We experimentally validate our approach in data-free Combinatorial Optimization and demonstrate that our method achieves a new state-of-the-art on a wide range of benchmark problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to generate useful discrete solutions when examples from the desired distribution are unavailable. That problem appears in combinatorial optimization, where learning a sampler can help search among many possible configurations. Existing neural approaches commonly require models that can calculate the exact probability of each generated sample, restricting the kinds of generators they can use.

The authors introduce a training objective that removes this requirement. Their loss upper-bounds reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of disagreement between distributions. This gives training a way to control distributional mismatch without directly evaluating exact sample probabilities. The construction opens the approach to expressive models with hidden variables, including diffusion models.

Experiments evaluate the framework on combinatorial optimization problems without corresponding training examples. The authors report new state-of-the-art results across a wide range of benchmarks. The contribution therefore combines a more flexible training formulation with empirical evidence that the additional modeling freedom can help solve discrete optimization problems.
summary.tldr: A new training objective enables diffusion models to tackle combinatorial optimization without example solutions or exact sample likelihoods.

title: A Diffusion Model Framework for Unsupervised Neural Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Many scientific models are composed of multiple discrete components, and scientists often make heuristic decisions about which components to include. Bayesian inference provides a mathematical framework for systematically selecting model components, but defining prior distributions over model components and developing associated inference schemes has been challenging. We approach this problem in a simulation-based inference framework: We define model priors over candidate components and, from model simulations, train neural networks to infer joint probability distributions over both model components and associated parameters. Our method, simulation-based model inference (SBMI), represents distributions over model components as a conditional mixture of multivariate binary distributions in the Grassmann formalism. SBMI can be applied to any compositional stochastic simulator without requiring likelihood evaluations. We evaluate SBMI on a simple time series model and on two scientific models from neuroscience, and show that it can discover multiple data-consistent model configurations, and that it reveals non-identifiable model components and parameters. SBMI provides a powerful tool for data-driven scientific inquiry which will allow scientists to identify essential model components and make uncertainty-informed modelling decisions.

paragraphs: Scientific simulators often combine several optional components, leaving researchers to decide both which components belong and what their parameters should be. Simulation-based model inference, or SBMI, tackles these choices jointly. It defines priors over candidate components and trains neural networks on simulations to infer distributions over model structure together with its associated parameters.

For component configurations, SBMI uses a conditional mixture of multivariate binary distributions expressed in the Grassmann formalism. This provides a representation for uncertainty about which components are included. The method applies to compositional stochastic simulators without evaluating likelihoods, making simulated outputs the basis for learning the joint inference procedure.

Evaluations use a simple time-series model and two neuroscience models. SBMI discovers multiple configurations consistent with the data and reveals components and parameters that are not identifiable. This matters because scientific evidence may support several explanations rather than one uniquely determined simulator. Representing those alternatives can help researchers judge which components are essential and make modeling decisions informed by uncertainty.
summary.tldr: SBMI jointly infers simulator components and parameters from simulations, exposing alternative explanations and non-identifiability.

title: Simultaneous identification of models and parameters of scientific simulators

abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), different reward functions can define the same optimal policy but result in drastically different learning performance. For some, the agent gets stuck with a suboptimal behavior, and for others, it solves the task efficiently. Choosing a good reward function is hence an extremely important yet challenging problem. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach for using rewards for learning. We introduce max-reward RL, where an agent optimizes the maximum rather than the cumulative reward. Unlike earlier works, our approach works for deterministic and stochastic environments and can be easily combined with state-of-the-art RL algorithms. In the experiments, we study the performance of max-reward RL algorithms in two goal-reaching environments from Gymnasium-Robotics and demonstrate its benefits over standard RL. The code is available at https://github.com/veviurko/To-the-Max.

paragraphs: Reward design can strongly affect how quickly a reinforcement learning agent learns, even when different rewards define the same optimal policy. Some choices lead to efficient learning while others leave the agent with inferior behavior. This paper explores changing the way rewards are used as an alternative approach to that design problem.

The proposed max-reward formulation optimizes the maximum reward rather than cumulative reward. This changes the learning objective from adding rewards across experience to focusing on the highest reward. The authors develop an approach that handles both deterministic and stochastic environments and can be combined with state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms.

Experiments examine two goal-reaching environments from Gymnasium-Robotics and demonstrate benefits over standard reinforcement learning in those settings. The findings show that changing reward aggregation can be useful for the evaluated tasks. They do not establish a universal advantage for every reward structure, but provide evidence that the choice between cumulative and maximum reward is a meaningful part of designing a learning system.
summary.tldr: Max-reward reinforcement learning optimizes the highest reward instead of cumulative reward and shows benefits in two evaluated goal-reaching environments.

title: To the Max: Reinventing Reward in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper contributes a new approach for distributional reinforcement learning which elucidates a clean separation of transition structure and reward in the learning process. Analogous to how the successor representation (SR) describes the expected consequences of behaving according to a given policy, our distributional successor measure (SM) describes the distributional consequences of this behaviour. We formulate the distributional SM as a distribution over distributions and provide theory connecting it with distributional and model-based reinforcement learning. Moreover, we propose an algorithm that learns the distributional SM from data by minimizing a two-level maximum mean discrepancy. Key to our method are a number of algorithmic techniques that are independently valuable for learning generative models of state. As an illustration of the usefulness of the distributional SM, we show that it enables zero-shot risk-sensitive policy evaluation in a way that was not previously possible.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to represent the consequences of an agent’s behavior while keeping the environment’s transition structure separate from rewards. The successor representation summarizes expected consequences under a given policy. The proposed distributional successor measure extends that idea to describe a distribution of consequences, retaining information that an expectation alone does not convey.

The authors formulate this measure as a distribution over distributions and establish theoretical connections to distributional and model-based reinforcement learning. They also introduce a procedure for learning it from data. Its objective uses a two-level maximum mean discrepancy, matching the nested structure of the representation. The learning procedure includes techniques that the authors identify as independently useful for generative models of states.

The practical demonstration is zero-shot, risk-sensitive policy evaluation. This connects the richer representation to evaluating behavior with attention to risk, rather than only average outcomes. The contribution is therefore both a representation that separates dynamics from rewards and a learning method that makes that representation usable for a previously unavailable form of policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: A distributional successor measure separates transition structure from rewards and enables zero-shot, risk-sensitive policy evaluation.

title: A Distributional Analogue to the Successor Representation

abstract: We consider the prediction of general tensor properties of crystalline materials, including dielectric, piezoelectric, and elastic tensors. A key challenge here is how to make the predictions satisfy the unique tensor equivariance to both O(3) and crystal space groups. To this end, we propose a General Materials Tensor Network (GMTNet), which is carefully designed to satisfy the required symmetries. To evaluate our method, we curate a dataset and establish evaluation metrics that are tailored to the intricacies of crystal tensor predictions. Experimental results show that our GMTNet not only achieves promising performance on crystal tensors of various orders but also generates predictions fully consistent with the intrinsic crystal symmetries. Our code is publicly available as part of the AIRS library (https://github.com/divelab/AIRS).

paragraphs: Predicting a crystal’s material properties involves more than estimating a single number. Properties such as dielectric, piezoelectric, and elastic responses are represented by tensors, whose components must behave consistently with the material’s symmetries. This paper addresses the challenge of predicting these properties while respecting both O(3) transformations and crystal space-group symmetries.

The authors introduce the General Materials Tensor Network, or GMTNet, with an architecture designed to satisfy these symmetry requirements. The central idea is to make the relevant transformation rules part of the prediction method itself. This matters because a tensor prediction must represent the same underlying material response consistently when the crystal is transformed in ways governed by those symmetries.

The work also provides a curated dataset and evaluation measures tailored to crystal tensors. Experiments report promising prediction performance across tensors of different orders, together with full consistency with intrinsic crystal symmetries. These findings support the combination of predictive modeling and explicit symmetry requirements for this family of material properties.
summary.tldr: GMTNet predicts crystal tensor properties using an architecture designed to preserve the required spatial and crystal symmetries.

title: A Space Group Symmetry Informed Network for O(3) Equivariant Crystal Tensor Prediction

abstract: A long-standing goal in deep learning has been to characterize the learning behavior of black-box models in a more interpretable manner. For graph neural networks (GNNs), considerable advances have been made in formalizing what functions they can represent, but whether GNNs will learn desired functions during the optimization process remains less clear. To fill this gap, we study their training dynamics in function space. In particular, we find that the optimization of GNNs through gradient descent implicitly leverages the graph structure to update the learned function. This phenomenon is dubbed as kernel-graph alignment, which has been empirically and theoretically corroborated. This new analytical framework from the optimization perspective enables interpretable explanations of when and why the learned GNN functions generalize, which are relevant to their limitations on heterophilic graphs. From a practical standpoint, it also provides high-level principles for designing new algorithms. We exemplify this by showing that a simple and efficient non-parametric algorithm, obtained by explicitly using graph structure to update the learned function, can consistently compete with nonlinear GNNs.

paragraphs: Knowing which functions a graph neural network can represent does not establish which ones training will actually learn. This paper investigates that gap by studying training dynamics in function space. The focus is how the learned function changes during optimization, bringing the learning process itself into the explanation of model behavior.

The authors find that gradient descent implicitly uses graph structure when updating the learned function. They call this phenomenon kernel-graph alignment and support it with theoretical and empirical evidence. Their framework explains when and why learned graph functions generalize, including connections to the difficulties graph neural networks encounter on heterophilic graphs.

The analysis also supplies practical design principles. To demonstrate this, the authors construct a simple, efficient non-parametric algorithm that explicitly uses graph structure to update its learned function. It consistently competes with nonlinear graph neural networks in their evaluation. The result shows how an explanation of optimization behavior can motivate an effective algorithm, connecting a theoretical account of learning with a concrete modeling approach.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how gradient descent implicitly uses graph structure in GNN function updates and turns that insight into a competitive non-parametric algorithm.

title: How Graph Neural Networks Learn: Lessons from Training Dynamics

abstract: Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) is fragile in scenarios with insufficient labeled samples. A vanilla extension of ERM to unlabeled samples is Entropy Minimization (EntMin), which employs the soft-labels of unlabeled samples to guide their learning. However, EntMin emphasizes prediction discriminability while neglecting prediction diversity. To alleviate this issue, in this paper, we rethink the guidance information to utilize unlabeled samples. By analyzing the learning objective of ERM, we find that the guidance information for labeled samples in a specific category is the corresponding label encoding. Inspired by this finding, we propose a Label-Encoding Risk Minimization (LERM). It first estimates the label encodings through prediction means of unlabeled samples and then aligns them with their corresponding ground-truth label encodings. As a result, the LERM ensures both prediction discriminability and diversity, and it can be integrated into existing methods as a plugin. Theoretically, we analyze the relationships between LERM and ERM as well as EntMin. Empirically, we verify the superiority of the LERM under several label insufficient scenarios. The codes are available at https://github.com/zhangyl660/LERM.

paragraphs: When labeled examples are scarce, learning only by minimizing supervised training error can be fragile. Entropy minimization extends training to unlabeled data by encouraging confident predictions. The authors identify a gap in that guidance: it emphasizes distinguishable predictions while overlooking diversity across the predictions made on unlabeled samples.

Label-Encoding Risk Minimization approaches the problem by examining what guides learning in the supervised objective. The analysis identifies each category's label encoding as that guidance. LERM estimates label encodings from mean predictions on unlabeled examples, then aligns those estimates with the corresponding ground-truth encodings. This supplies a training objective designed to support both prediction discriminability and diversity.

The method can be added to existing approaches as a plugin. The paper analyzes its theoretical relationships with empirical risk minimization and entropy minimization, and reports superior performance in several scenarios with insufficient labels. Its contribution is therefore a different source of guidance for unlabeled data, linking the structure of supervised label encodings to an objective that addresses both confidence and diversity.
summary.tldr: LERM guides unlabeled-data learning by aligning estimated label encodings with target encodings to encourage discriminable and diverse predictions.

title: Rethinking Guidance Information to Utilize Unlabeled Samples: A Label Encoding Perspective

abstract: We present Premier-TACO, a multitask feature representation learning approach designed to improve few-shot policy learning efficiency in sequential decision-making tasks. Premier-TACO leverages a subset of multitask offline datasets for pretraining a general feature representation, which captures critical environmental dynamics and is fine-tuned using minimal expert demonstrations. It advances the temporal action contrastive learning (TACO) objective, known for state-of-the-art results in visual control tasks, by incorporating a novel negative example sampling strategy. This strategy is crucial in significantly boosting TACO’s computational efficiency, making large-scale multitask offline pretraining feasible. Our extensive empirical evaluation in a diverse set of continuous control benchmarks including Deepmind Control Suite, MetaWorld, and LIBERO demonstrate Premier-TACO’s effective- ness in pretraining visual representations, significantly enhancing few-shot imitation learning of novel tasks.

paragraphs: Premier-TACO aims to make learning a new control policy possible with only a small amount of expert demonstration data. It first learns a general visual representation from a subset of offline datasets spanning multiple tasks. That representation is intended to capture important environmental dynamics, giving later task learning a useful starting point.

The method extends temporal action contrastive learning, or TACO, by changing how negative examples are sampled during pretraining. Negative examples provide comparisons within the contrastive objective, so selecting them is part of how the representation is learned. The new sampling strategy substantially improves computational efficiency, making large-scale offline pretraining across multiple tasks feasible.

The pretrained representation is then fine-tuned using minimal expert demonstrations. Evaluations span DeepMind Control Suite, MetaWorld, and LIBERO, where the authors report significant improvements in few-shot imitation learning on novel tasks. The findings connect more efficient representation pretraining with reduced demonstration requirements during downstream learning, showing the value of reusing knowledge of dynamics across the evaluated control problems.
summary.tldr: Premier-TACO makes multitask visual pretraining more efficient through negative-example sampling and improves imitation learning from few demonstrations on novel tasks.

title: Premier-TACO is a Few-Shot Policy Learner: Pretraining Multitask Representation via Temporal Action-Driven Contrastive Loss

abstract: A simple and effective method for the inference-time alignment of generative models is the best-of-$n$ policy, where $n$ samples are drawn from a reference policy, ranked based on a reward function, and the highest ranking one is selected. A commonly used analytical expression in the literature claims that the KL divergence between the best-of-$n$ policy and the reference policy is equal to $\log (n) - (n-1)/n.$ We disprove the validity of this claim, and show that it is an upper bound on the actual KL divergence. We also explore the tightness of this upper bound in different regimes, and propose a new estimator for the KL divergence and empirically show that it provides a tight approximation. We also show that the win rate of the best-of-$n$ policy against the reference policy is upper bounded by $n/(n+1)$ and derive bounds on the tightness of this characterization. We conclude with analyzing the tradeoffs between win rate and KL divergence of the best-of-$n$ alignment policy, which demonstrate that very good tradeoffs are achievable with $n < 1000$.

paragraphs: Best-of-n alignment generates n candidates from a reference model, scores them with a reward function, and returns the highest-ranked candidate. This paper examines how that selection changes the output distribution and how often the selected output wins against the reference policy. These quantities describe two sides of the method’s alignment tradeoff.

The authors correct a commonly used claim about KL divergence, a measure of distributional change. The expression log(n) − (n−1)/n is an upper bound on the actual divergence, rather than an exact formula. They study when this bound is tight and propose a new divergence estimator that gives a close approximation in their empirical evaluation.

They also prove that the win rate against the reference policy is at most n/(n+1), with bounds describing the tightness of that characterization. Combining the results, they analyze the balance between improved win rate and departure from the reference distribution. Their analysis indicates that very good tradeoffs are achievable with fewer than one thousand candidates, while preserving the distinction between upper bounds and quantities actually attained.
summary.tldr: The paper corrects an exact-divergence claim for best-of-n alignment and derives bounds describing its win-rate and distribution-shift tradeoff.

title: Theoretical guarantees on the best-of-n alignment policy

abstract: Self-play has powered breakthroughs in two-player and multi-player games. Here we show that self-play is a surprisingly effective strategy in another domain. We show that robust and naturalistic driving emerges entirely from self-play in simulation at unprecedented scale – 1.6 billion km of driving. This is enabled by Gigaflow, a batched simulator that can synthesize and train on 42 years of subjective driving experience per hour on a single 8-GPU node. The resulting policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on three independent autonomous driving benchmarks. The policy outperforms the prior state of the art when tested on recorded real-world scenarios, amidst human drivers, without ever seeing human data during training. The policy is realistic when assessed against human references and achieves unprecedented robustness, averaging 17.5 years of continuous driving between incidents in simulation.

paragraphs: This paper applies self-play to autonomous driving, training a policy entirely through interactions in simulation rather than human driving data. The authors report that robust and naturalistic behavior emerges after 1.6 billion kilometers of simulated driving. The work examines whether self-play can succeed beyond the game settings where it has been especially influential.

The training scale is enabled by Gigaflow, a batched simulator that can generate and train on 42 years of subjective driving experience per hour using a single node with eight GPUs. The resulting policy achieves state-of-the-art performance on three independent driving benchmarks. It also exceeds the prior state of the art in evaluations using recorded real-world scenarios amid human drivers.

The authors find that the policy behaves realistically when compared with human references, despite never seeing human data during training. In simulation, it averages 17.5 years of continuous driving between incidents. That robustness figure describes simulated performance. Together, the findings support large-scale simulated self-play as a source of driving behavior that performs well in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Large-scale simulated self-play produces a driving policy with strong benchmark performance and realistic behavior without human training data.

title: Robust Autonomy Emerges from Self-Play

abstract: Graph clustering is an important algorithmic technique for analysing massive graphs, and has been widely applied in many research fields of data science. While the objective of most graph clustering algorithms is to find a vertex set of low conductance, there has been a sequence of recent studies that highlight the importance of the inter-connection between clusters when analysing real-world datasets. Following this line of research, in this work we study bipartite-like clusters and present efficient and online algorithms that find such clusters in both undirected graphs and directed ones. We conduct experimental studies on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and show that our algorithms significantly speedup the running time of existing clustering algorithms while preserving their effectiveness.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often looks for groups with relatively few connections leading outside them, an objective associated with low conductance. This paper follows a different emphasis: connections between groups can themselves be important for understanding a graph. It studies bipartite-like clusters, bringing that interconnection structure into the clustering problem.

The authors present efficient online algorithms for finding these clusters in both undirected and directed graphs. Covering both settings matters because the methods address graphs where connections are symmetric as well as graphs where their direction carries information. The work links the search for bipartite-like structure to the computational challenge of analyzing massive graphs.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the proposed algorithms substantially accelerate existing clustering algorithms while preserving their effectiveness. The stated benefit therefore combines faster execution with maintained clustering performance in the evaluated settings. More broadly, the paper contributes methods for studying relationships between clusters, expanding the kinds of graph organization that efficient clustering procedures can usefully expose.
summary.tldr: Online algorithms find bipartite-like clusters in directed and undirected graphs, accelerating tested clustering methods while preserving their effectiveness.

title: Online Sparsification of Bipartite-Like Clusters in Graphs

abstract: Existing control techniques often assume access to complete dynamics or perfect simulators with fully observable states, which are necessary to verify whether the system remains within a safe set (forward invariance) or safe actions are persistently feasible at all times. However, many systems contain latent variables that make their dynamics partially unidentifiable or cause distribution shifts in the observed statistics between offline and online data, even when the underlying mechanistic dynamics are unchanged. Such “spurious” distribution shifts can break many techniques that use data to learn system models or safety certificates. To address this limitation, we propose a technique for designing probabilistic safety certificates for systems with latent variables. A key technical enabler is the formulation of invariance conditions in probability space, which can be constructed using observed statistics in the presence of distribution shifts due to latent variables. We use this invariance condition to construct a safety certificate that can be implemented efficiently in real-time control. The proposed safety certificate can persistently find feasible actions that control long-term risk to stay within tolerance. Stochastic safe control and (causal) reinforcement learning have been studied in isolation until now. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed work is the first to use causal reinforcement learning to quantify long-term risk for the design of safety certificates. This integration enables safety certificates to efficiently ensure long-term safety in the presence of latent variables. The effectiveness of the proposed safety certificate is demonstrated in numerical simulations.

paragraphs: Hidden variables complicate safe control because observed data may not fully identify a system’s dynamics. They can also change observed statistics between offline training and online operation even when the underlying mechanisms remain unchanged. This paper addresses such shifts, which can undermine safety methods that depend on learned models or certificates derived from observational data.

The proposed approach expresses invariance conditions in probability space and constructs them from observed statistics despite shifts caused by latent variables. These conditions underpin a probabilistic safety certificate designed for efficient real-time control. The certificate can persistently identify feasible actions that keep long-term risk within a specified tolerance, making the safety objective explicitly probabilistic.

A central element is the use of causal reinforcement learning to quantify long-term risk for certificate design. This connects risk estimation with the continuing task of selecting safe actions under partially unidentifiable dynamics. Numerical simulations demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. Its stated guarantee concerns controlling risk within tolerance in the presence of latent variables, rather than asserting that every possible trajectory is risk-free.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic safety certificate uses causal reinforcement learning to control long-term risk despite hidden variables and their induced distribution shifts.

title: Safety Certificate against Latent Variables with Partially Unidentifiable Dynamics

abstract: This work highlights a semantics misalignment in 3D human pose estimation. For the task of test-time adaptation, the misalignment manifests as overly smoothed and unguided predictions. The smoothing settles predictions towards some average pose. Furthermore, when there are occlusions or truncations, the adaptation becomes fully unguided. To this end, we pioneer the integration of a semantics-aware motion prior for the test-time adaptation of 3D pose estimation. We leverage video understanding and a well-structured motion-text space to adapt the model motion prediction to adhere to video semantics during test time. Additionally, we incorporate a missing 2D pose completion based on the motion-text similarity. The pose completion strengthens the motion prior’s guidance for occlusions and truncations. Our method significantly improves state-of-the-art 3D human pose estimation TTA techniques, with more than 12% decrease in PA-MPJPE on 3DPW and 3DHP.

paragraphs: The paper identifies a semantic problem in adapting three-dimensional human pose estimators at test time. Predictions can become overly smooth and drift toward an average pose, losing the meaning of the observed motion. When body parts are occluded or outside the frame, the adaptation can also lack useful guidance.

The proposed approach introduces a motion prior informed by semantics. It combines video understanding with a structured motion-text space so that predicted motion better follows what the video depicts. It also completes missing two-dimensional poses using motion-text similarity, strengthening the prior’s guidance when the visible pose information is incomplete.

Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art test-time adaptation methods, including more than a 12% reduction in PA-MPJPE on 3DPW and 3DHP. The results support using motion meaning as an adaptation signal alongside pose information. The two components work toward the same goal: keeping predictions tied to the observed activity even when smoothing or missing body observations would otherwise weaken that connection.
summary.tldr: A semantics-aware motion prior and missing-pose completion improve test-time adaptation for three-dimensional human pose estimation.

title: Semantics-aware Test-time Adaptation for 3D Human Pose Estimation

abstract: Analyzing inherent temporal dynamics is a critical pathway for time series classification, where Reservoir Computing (RC) exhibits effectiveness and high efficiency. However, typical RC considers recursive updates from adjacent states, struggling with long-term dependencies. In response, this paper proposes a Spectral-Aware Reservoir Computing framework (SARC), incorporating spectral insights to enhance long-term dependency modeling. Prominent frequencies are initially extracted to reveal explicit or implicit cyclical patterns. For each prominent frequency, SARC further integrates a Frequency-informed Reservoir Network (FreqRes) to adequately capture both sequential and cyclical dynamics, thereby deriving effective dynamic features. Synthesizing these features across various frequencies, SARC offers a multi-scale analysis of temporal dynamics and improves the modeling of long-term dependencies. Experiments on public datasets demonstrate that SARC achieves state-of-the-art results, while maintaining high efficiency compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Time-series classification depends on recognizing how a signal evolves. Reservoir computing can extract temporal dynamics efficiently, but typical systems update through neighboring states and struggle to capture relationships over longer intervals. SARC addresses this weakness by using frequency information to expose repeating patterns that may be explicit or hidden in the signal.

The framework first identifies prominent frequencies. For each frequency, a Frequency-informed Reservoir Network captures both the sequential progression of the data and its cyclical behavior. SARC then combines the resulting dynamic features across frequencies. This provides several temporal scales for describing the same input, helping connect local evolution with patterns that recur over longer periods.

Experiments on public datasets report state-of-the-art classification performance while retaining high efficiency relative to existing methods. The findings support supplementing reservoir dynamics with spectral structure, rather than expecting adjacent-state recursion alone to capture every useful dependency. The method’s central contribution is a coordinated representation of sequential and cyclical behavior across the extracted frequencies.
summary.tldr: SARC combines frequency-informed reservoir networks to capture sequential and cyclical patterns, improving long-range time-series classification while retaining efficiency.

title: Spectral-Aware Reservoir Computing for Fast and Accurate Time Series Classification

abstract: Solving time-dependent parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) is challenging for data-driven methods, as these models must adapt to variations in parameters such as coefficients, forcing terms, and initial conditions. State-of-the-art neural surrogates perform adaptation through gradient-based optimization and meta-learning to implicitly encode the variety of dynamics from observations. This often comes with increased inference complexity. Inspired by the in-context learning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), we introduce Zebra, a novel generative auto-regressive transformer designed to solve parametric PDEs without requiring gradient adaptation at inference. By leveraging in-context information during both pre-training and inference, Zebra dynamically adapts to new tasks by conditioning on input sequences that incorporate context example trajectories. As a generative model, Zebra can be used to generate new trajectories and allows quantifying the uncertainty of the predictions. We evaluate Zebra across a variety of challenging PDE scenarios, demonstrating its adaptability, robustness, and superior performance compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: Data-driven solvers for time-dependent partial differential equations must adapt when coefficients, forcing terms, or initial conditions change. Existing neural surrogates often use gradient-based adaptation or meta-learning to handle this variation, which can increase inference complexity. Zebra instead learns to adapt through examples supplied in its input context.

The model is a generative autoregressive transformer trained to use context trajectories during both pretraining and inference. At inference, it conditions on sequences containing those example trajectories to respond to a new task without gradient adaptation. The change in behavior therefore comes through the supplied context rather than an inference-time optimization of model parameters.

Because Zebra is generative, it can produce new trajectories and support quantification of prediction uncertainty. Across several challenging PDE scenarios, the authors report adaptability, robustness, and better performance than existing approaches. The contribution brings in-context adaptation to equation solving, combining task adjustment through examples with generative prediction in a setting where changing dynamical conditions are central to the problem.
summary.tldr: Zebra solves parametric PDE tasks by conditioning on example trajectories, adapting without inference-time gradient updates.

title: Zebra: In-Context Generative Pretraining for Solving Parametric PDEs

abstract: Understanding the decision-making process of machine learning models provides valuable insights into the task, the data, and the reasons behind a model’s failures. In this work, we propose a method that performs inherently interpretable predictions through the instance-wise sparsification of input images. To align the sparsification with human perception, we learn the masking in the space of semantically meaningful pixel regions rather than on pixel-level. Additionally, we introduce an explicit way to dynamically determine the required level of sparsity for each instance. We show empirically on semi-synthetic and natural image datasets that our inherently interpretable classifier produces more meaningful, human-understandable predictions than state-of-the-art benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper builds interpretability into image classification by controlling which parts of each input remain available for prediction. The method sparsifies images separately for each instance, making the selected visual information part of the classifier’s decision process. The aim is to make predictions understandable through the evidence the model actually uses.

The selection operates over semantically meaningful pixel regions. Learning masks at this level aligns the selected information with human perception more directly than selecting individual pixels. The method also explicitly determines how much sparsity each image requires, allowing the amount of retained information to vary across instances rather than imposing one level on all inputs.

Experiments on semi-synthetic and natural image datasets show more meaningful, human-understandable predictions than the state-of-the-art benchmarks used in the study. The contribution combines two choices: selecting coherent visual regions and adapting the amount selected to the image. Together, they support an inherently interpretable classifier whose prediction process exposes a more understandable subset of its input.
summary.tldr: The method makes image predictions more interpretable by selecting meaningful pixel regions and adapting how much information each image retains.

title: From Pixels to Perception: Interpretable Predictions via Instance-wise Grouped Feature Selection

abstract: We present an Adversarially Pre-trained Transformer (APT) that is able to perform zero-shot meta-learning on tabular prediction tasks without using any real-world dataset to pre-train the model, extending on the recent development of Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) and TabPFN. Specifically, APT is pre-trained with adversarial synthetic data agents, who continue to shift their underlying data generating distribution and deliberately challenge the model with different synthetic datasets. In addition, we propose a mixture block model architecture that is able to handle classification tasks with arbitrary number of classes, addressing the class size limitation – a crucial weakness of prior tabular zero-shot learning algorithms. In experiments, we show that our framework matches state-of-the-art performance on small tabular classification tasks without filtering on dataset characteristics such as number of classes and number of missing values, while maintaining an average runtime under one second. On common benchmark dataset suites in both classification and regression, we show that adversarial pre-training was able to enhance TabPFN’s performance. In our analysis, we demonstrate that the adversarial synthetic data agents were able to generate a more diverse collection of data compared to the ordinary random generator in TabPFN. In addition, we demonstrate that our mixture block neural design has improved generalizability and greatly accelerated pre-training.

paragraphs: APT is a Transformer for zero-shot meta-learning on tabular prediction tasks that uses no real-world datasets during pretraining. Building on Prior-Data Fitted Networks and TabPFN, it learns from synthetic data. Its distinctive feature is that adversarial data agents continually change their generating distributions to present challenging datasets.

The framework also introduces a mixture block architecture that can handle classification with arbitrary numbers of classes. This addresses the class-count restriction of earlier tabular zero-shot methods. The paper's analysis finds that adversarial agents generate more diverse data than TabPFN's ordinary random generator, while the mixture block design improves generalizability and substantially accelerates pretraining.

On small tabular classification tasks, APT matches state-of-the-art performance with an average runtime below one second, without filtering datasets by characteristics such as class count or missing values. Adversarial pretraining also improves TabPFN on classification and regression benchmark suites. These results support both richer synthetic training challenges and a more flexible architecture as useful ways to improve tabular prediction without real-world pretraining data.
summary.tldr: APT learns from adversarial synthetic datasets and supports arbitrary class counts, matching leading small-table classification performance with subsecond average runtime.

title: Zero-shot Meta-learning for Tabular Prediction Tasks with Adversarially Pre-trained Transformer

abstract: Open World Object Detection (OWOD) requires the detector to continuously identify and learn new categories. Existing methods rely on the large language model (LLM) to describe the visual attributes of known categories and use these attributes to mark potential objects. The performance of such methods is influenced by the accuracy of LLM descriptions, and selecting appropriate attributes during incremental learning remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel OWOD framework, termed OW-VAP, which operates independently of LLM and requires only minimal object descriptions to detect unknown objects. Specifically, we propose a Visual Attribute Parser (VAP) that parses the attributes of visual regions and assesses object potential based on the similarity between these attributes and the object descriptions. To enable the VAP to recognize objects in unlabeled areas, we exploit potential objects within background regions. Finally, we propose Probabilistic Soft Label Assignment (PSLA) to prevent optimization conflicts from misidentifying background as foreground. Comparative results on the OWOD benchmark demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods with a +13 improvement in U-Recall and a +8 increase in U-AP for unknown detection capabilities. Furthermore, OW-VAP approaches the unknown recall upper limit of the detector.

paragraphs: Open-world object detection requires recognizing potential objects beyond the categories a detector already knows, then learning new categories over time. Existing attribute-based approaches depend on language-model descriptions whose accuracy affects detection. OW-VAP instead operates independently of a large language model and needs only minimal object descriptions.

Its Visual Attribute Parser examines image regions and compares their parsed attributes with object descriptions to judge whether they could contain objects. Training also draws on potential objects in background regions, helping the parser recognize objects that lack labels. Because background can be mistakenly treated as foreground, a probabilistic soft-label assignment mechanism addresses the resulting conflicts during optimization.

On the open-world detection benchmark, the authors report improvements of 13 in U-Recall and 8 in U-AP over existing state-of-the-art methods. They also report approaching the detector’s upper limit for unknown-object recall. These findings support visual attribute parsing as a way to strengthen unknown detection while reducing dependence on generated category descriptions. The soft-label component addresses the ambiguity introduced by learning from potentially unlabeled objects.
summary.tldr: OW-VAP detects unknown objects through visual attribute parsing and probabilistic labels, improving open-world detection without an LLM.

title: OW-VAP: Visual Attribute Parsing for Open World Object Detection

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as mainstream framework in visual generation. Building upon this success, the integration of Mixture of Experts (MoE) methods has shown promise in enhancing model scalability and performance. In this paper, we introduce Race-DiT, a novel MoE model for diffusion transformers with a flexible routing strategy, Expert Race. By allowing tokens and experts to compete together and select the top candidates, the model learns to dynamically assign experts to critical tokens. Additionally, we propose per-layer regularization to address challenges in shallow layer learning, and router similarity loss to prevent mode collapse, ensuring better expert utilization. Extensive experiments on ImageNet validate the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing significant performance gains while promising scaling properties.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models divide processing among specialized components, making the routing decision central to how those components are used. This paper applies that idea to diffusion transformers for visual generation. Its model, Race-DiT, introduces an Expert Race routing strategy intended to make expert assignment more flexible as the model scales.

Expert Race lets tokens and experts compete together, selecting the strongest candidates for assignment. This allows the model to learn dynamic allocations of experts to critical tokens. The design focuses on matching processing resources to the tokens that need them, rather than treating expert selection as a separate fixed pattern across all inputs.

The authors also introduce per-layer regularization to address difficulties learning in shallow layers, plus a router similarity loss to counter mode collapse and improve expert utilization. Experiments on ImageNet report significant performance gains and promising scaling behavior. The findings support the combined routing and regularization design as an effective way to use expert capacity in diffusion transformers on the evaluated image-generation setting.
summary.tldr: Race-DiT dynamically matches tokens with experts and adds routing regularization, producing reported ImageNet gains with promising scaling behavior.

title: Expert Race: A Flexible Routing Strategy for Scaling Diffusion Transformer with Mixture of Experts

abstract: Generalization and approximation capabilities of message passing graph neural networks (MPNNs) are often studied by defining a compact metric on a space of input graphs under which MPNNs are equicontinuous. Such analyses are of two varieties: 1) when the metric space includes graphs of unbounded sizes, the theory is only appropriate for dense graphs, and, 2) when studying sparse graphs, the metric space only includes graphs of uniformly bounded size. In this work, we present a unified approach, defining a compact metric on the space of graphs of all sizes, both sparse and dense, under which MPNNs are equicontinuous. This leads to more powerful universal approximation theorems and generalization bounds than previous works. The theory is based on, and extends, a recent approach to graph limit theory called graphop analysis.

This leads to more powerful universal approximation theorems and generalization bounds than previous works. The theory is based on, and extends, a recent approach to graph limit theory called graphop analysis.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common mathematical setting for studying message passing graph neural networks on sparse and dense graphs of arbitrary size. Earlier approaches faced a split: theories allowing unbounded graph sizes were appropriate for dense graphs, while theories addressing sparse graphs restricted how large the graphs could become. That separation limited what a single analysis could cover.

The authors construct a compact metric space that includes both kinds of graphs across all sizes. The metric provides a way to compare graph inputs, while equicontinuity ensures that the studied networks respond in a uniformly controlled way to changes measured by that metric. Their construction builds on and extends graphop analysis, an approach to graph limits.

The resulting framework supports stronger universal approximation theorems and generalization bounds than the previous approaches described in the abstract. Its contribution is theoretical: it broadens the graph settings in which approximation and generalization can be analyzed together, bringing sparse graphs of unrestricted size into the same framework as dense ones.
summary.tldr: A graphop-based framework strengthens approximation and generalization theory for message passing networks on sparse and dense graphs of arbitrary size.

title: A Graphop Analysis of Graph Neural Networks on Sparse Graphs: Generalization and Universal Approximation

abstract: We study the robustness of stochastic mirror descent (SMD) under heavy-tailed noise, focusing on whether the method retains its convergence guarantees when run with infinite-variance stochastic gradient input. To address this question in a principled manner, we begin by introducing a continuous-time model of SMD as a stochastic differential equation (SDE) driven by a centered Lévy noise process with finite $p$-th order moments, $1 < p \leq 2$. This scheme—which we call the Lévy mirror flow (LMF)—arises naturally as the scaling limit of SMD in the presence of heavy-tailed noise. In particular, when $p < 2$—the heavy noise regime—the trajectories of LMF generically exhibit jump discontinuities of arbitrary magnitude which, if frequent enough, lead to infinite variance. Nonetheless, despite this highly singular behavior, we show that LMF attains $\epsilon$-optimality within $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-p/(p-1)})$ time in the convex case, and within $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1/(p-1)})$ time for (relatively) strongly convex objectives. These guarantees provide a transparent characterization of the impact of frequent long jumps on the convergence of the process, and percolate to a series of matching discrete-time guarantees for several variants of SMD under heavy-tailed noise.
