paragraphs: Stochastic optimization must cope with errors in gradient estimates, and heavy-tailed errors can include exceptionally large disturbances. This paper asks whether stochastic mirror descent retains convergence guarantees when those errors can have infinite variance. It develops a continuous-time model driven by centered Lévy noise with a finite p-th moment, for p greater than one and at most two.

The resulting Lévy mirror flow arises as a scaling limit of stochastic mirror descent. When p is below two, its paths can have jumps of arbitrary size; sufficiently frequent jumps can produce infinite variance. Despite this behavior, the authors prove bounds on the time required to reach a prescribed level of optimization accuracy for convex and relatively strongly convex objectives.

For error tolerance epsilon, the bounds scale as epsilon to the power minus p divided by p minus one in the convex case, and minus one divided by p minus one, up to logarithmic factors, under relative strong convexity. Matching discrete-time guarantees extend the analysis to several mirror-descent variants, quantifying how heavier noise changes convergence.
summary.tldr: Mirror descent can retain quantified convergence guarantees under heavy-tailed noise, including noise with infinite variance.

title: Bregman meets Lévy: Stochastic Mirror Descent with Heavy-Tailed Noise in Continuous and Discrete Time

abstract: We study unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) where measuring cross-domain discrepancy is critical. Most UDA approaches fix a single $f$-divergence a priori, which can be suboptimal across heterogeneous shifts. We propose a framework that (i) tightens the variational lower bound of an $f$-divergence by inserting a learnable, monotone $L$-Lipschitz transform $\tau$ (Tighter-VR), and (ii) selects the divergence family adaptively from data via a likelihood-based criterion. The resulting estimator yields more informative and statistically efficient discrepancy estimates while recovering prior fixed-divergence methods as special cases. Theoretically, we derive a target-risk bound whose three components are a transformed source risk, a Tighter-VR discrepancy between domains, and an ideal-hypothesis residual; we further provide finite-sample guarantees using standard complexity measures. Empirically, on Office-31, Office-Home, Digits, and VisDA-2017, our method consistently improves accuracy over strong baselines, showing that coupling Tighter-VR with adaptive divergence selection is useful for UDA.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation depends on measuring how a source domain differs from a target domain. This paper questions the common choice of fixing one divergence measure in advance: a measure that works well for one shift can be less suitable for another. It makes both discrepancy estimation and the choice of divergence adaptable.

The proposed Tighter-VR construction inserts a learnable monotone transform with a bounded Lipschitz constant into a variational lower bound. This tightens the representation used to estimate divergence. A likelihood-based criterion then selects the divergence family from data. The framework includes earlier fixed-divergence approaches as special cases and yields more informative, statistically efficient discrepancy estimates.

The theoretical target-risk bound combines transformed source risk, the proposed domain discrepancy, and an ideal-hypothesis residual. Finite-sample guarantees supplement that analysis. Experiments on Office-31, Office-Home, Digits, and VisDA-2017 consistently improve accuracy over strong baselines. These findings support adapting the discrepancy measure to the shift, while the residual term makes clear that discrepancy is only one component of the risk bound.
summary.tldr: Learning a tighter divergence representation and selecting its family from data improves domain adaptation in the reported benchmarks.

title: Domain Adaptation with Adaptive $f$-Divergence: Tighter Variational Representation and Generalization Bounds

abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models, while it also involves a persistent tradeoff between optimization stability and learning efficiency. Token-level importance weighting supports fine-grained credit assignment, but it often introduces high variance and unstable parameter updates, whereas sequence-level optimization provides more stable learning dynamics while failing to fully exploit informative local signals. We introduce Trust-Gated Policy Optimization (TGPO), an efficient policy optimization framework that integrates two complementary mechanisms, namely sequence anchors and information gates. TGPO aligns token-wise updates with a stable sequence-level reference, which reduces the influence of extreme local likelihood fluctuations on the gradient, and a trust-based information gate adaptively modulates the contribution of token-level signals. By retaining and reweighting gradients from imperfect trajectories rather than excluding them, TGPO improves gradient utilization and sample efficiency while maintaining stable optimization behavior. Empirical results across seven mathematical reasoning datasets and multiple model scales show that TGPO consistently enhances learning efficiency and overall performance in outcome-supervised reinforcement learning settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve language-model reasoning, but detailed learning signals can also destabilize updates. Token-level importance weighting offers fine-grained credit assignment while introducing high variance. Sequence-level optimization is more stable but can overlook useful local information. TGPO combines mechanisms intended to retain the strengths of both.

Sequence anchors align token updates with a stable reference for the entire response, reducing the effect of extreme local likelihood fluctuations on gradients. Trust-based information gates then adjust how much each token-level signal contributes. This lets the method regulate local information according to its trust mechanism while maintaining a sequence-level reference.

TGPO also retains and reweights gradients from imperfect trajectories, making use of training signals that would otherwise be excluded. Across seven mathematical reasoning datasets and multiple model sizes, experiments show consistent gains in learning efficiency and overall performance under outcome supervision. The findings support carefully weighting partial information as a way to improve sample use while preserving stable optimization.
summary.tldr: TGPO combines sequence-level anchors with trust-gated token signals to improve the stability and efficiency of reasoning-model reinforcement learning.

title: TGPO: Efficient Policy Optimization through Sequence Anchor and Information Gating

abstract: Simulating the conditioned dynamics of diffusion processes, given their initial and terminal states, is an important but challenging problem in the sciences. The difficulty is particularly pronounced for rare events, for which the unconditioned dynamics rarely reach the terminal state. In this work, we propose a novel approach for learning diffusion bridges based on a self-consistency property of the optimal control. The resulting algorithm learns the conditioned dynamics in an iterative online manner, and exhibits strong performance in a range of empirical settings without requiring differentiation through simulated trajectories. Beyond the diffusion bridge setting, we draw connections between our self-consistency framework and recent advances in the wider stochastic optimal control literature.
originalAbstract: Simulating the conditioned dynamics of diffusion processes, given their initial and terminal states, is an important but challenging problem in the sciences. The difficulty is particularly pronounced for rare events, for which the unconditioned dynamics rarely reach the terminal state. In this work, we propose a novel approach for learning diffusion bridges based on a self-consistency property of the optimal control. The resulting algorithm learns the conditioned dynamics in an iterative online manner, and exhibits strong performance in a range of empirical settings without requiring differentiation through simulated trajectories. Beyond the diffusion bridge setting, we draw connections between our self-consistency framework and recent advances in the wider stochastic optimal control literature.

paragraphs: A diffusion bridge describes a random evolving system conditioned on both its starting state and its ending state. Learning to simulate such paths is difficult when the desired endpoint is a rare event: the original, unconditioned process seldom reaches it. The paper addresses this problem by learning the conditioned dynamics directly.

Its central ingredient is a self-consistency property of the optimal control associated with the bridge. That property supplies the basis for losses used to learn the dynamics through repeated online updates. The resulting algorithm does not require differentiating through simulated trajectories, so its learning procedure avoids that particular computational requirement.

The authors report strong empirical performance across a range of settings, supporting self-consistency as a useful learning principle for diffusion bridges. They also connect the framework to recent work in stochastic optimal control. This broadens the conceptual contribution: the bridge algorithm is an instance of a control-based learning approach with links beyond endpoint-conditioned simulation.
summary.tldr: Control self-consistency provides an online method for learning diffusion bridges without differentiating through simulated trajectories.

title: Control Consistency Losses for Diffusion Bridges

abstract: Competitive programming is increasingly being used to evaluate the algorithmic reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on full-information tasks where all problem inputs are provided upfront. This overlooks a critical dimension of algorithmic reasoning: the ability of generated programs to operate when key information is not revealed upfront. Interactive problems, a distinctive component of competitive programming, embody this challenge. These problems require programs to engage in multi-round interaction with an interactor (a judge program) under strict protocol constraints and limited query budgets, with new information revealed only in response to queries. To address this gap, we introduce InteractBench, a benchmark comprising 322 high-quality interactive problems curated from Codeforces, AtCoder, IOI, and ICPC. Each problem is packaged with executable local interactors, enabling fully offline evaluation. Unlike existing benchmarks, InteractBench assesses whether model-generated code can acquire information and track state dynamically. Our evaluation reveals a significant interaction gap: even the most advanced reasoning models achieve limited success on interactive problems. Beyond success rates, we propose a fine-grained failure taxonomy to diagnose the root causes of these deficiencies. Although algorithmic logic errors remain dominant, protocol violations and query-budget overruns are frequent. Code is available at https://github.com/kmsgk0/InteractBench.

paragraphs: Most competitive-programming benchmarks give a program all its inputs upfront. InteractBench tests a different ability: writing programs that must discover missing information through interaction. Such programs query a judge, receive answers, and update their state while obeying a communication protocol and staying within a limited query budget.

The benchmark contains 322 interactive problems drawn from Codeforces, AtCoder, IOI, and ICPC. Each includes an executable local interactor, allowing evaluation to run fully offline. This setup checks whether model-generated code can acquire information dynamically and use it correctly across multiple rounds, extending evaluation beyond algorithms that operate on fully revealed inputs.

The authors find a substantial interaction gap, with even advanced reasoning models achieving limited success. Their failure taxonomy distinguishes algorithmic mistakes from other causes. Logic errors are most common, but protocol violations and excessive querying also occur frequently. These results show why a final success rate alone is insufficient to describe performance: a program can fail through its reasoning, its communication behavior, or its management of scarce information-gathering opportunities.
summary.tldr: InteractBench tests whether generated programs can discover hidden information through constrained interaction, exposing substantial weaknesses in advanced reasoning models.

title: InteractBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Competitive Programming under Unrevealed Information

abstract: Activations have become the primary memory bottleneck in large-batch LLM training. However, existing compression methods fail to exploit the spectral structure of activations, resulting in slow convergence or limited compression. To address this, we bridge the relationship between the algorithm’s fast convergence and the requirements for subspace projection, and show that an effective compression should yield an unbiased estimate of the original activation with low variance. We propose Principal-Random Subspace for LLM Activation Compression (PRAC), which novelly decomposes activations into two components: a principal subspace captured via SVD to retain dominant information, and a random subspace sampled from the orthogonal complement to approximate the tail. By introducing a precise scaling factor, we prove that PRAC yields an unbiased gradient estimator with minimum variance under certain conditions. Extensive experiments on pre-training and fine-tuning tasks demonstrate that PRAC achieves up to 36% total memory reduction with negligible performance degradation and minimal computational cost.

paragraphs: Activations stored during large-batch language model training can dominate memory use. Compressing them helps only if the resulting training signal remains useful. This paper connects fast convergence to the quality of subspace projection, arguing that effective compression should reconstruct activations without systematic bias and with low variance.

PRAC divides an activation into two parts. Singular value decomposition captures a principal subspace containing dominant information. A random subspace drawn from the orthogonal complement approximates the remaining tail. This combines deliberate preservation of strong components with a sampled representation of information outside those components.

A carefully chosen scaling factor gives PRAC an unbiased gradient estimator, with minimum variance under the conditions established in the analysis. That qualification matters: the minimum-variance claim is conditional. Experiments on pre-training and fine-tuning report up to 36% lower total memory use, negligible performance degradation, and minimal computational cost. The findings support preserving activation structure while sampling the residual as an effective memory-saving strategy.
summary.tldr: PRAC combines principal and random activation subspaces to reduce training memory while preserving an unbiased gradient estimate.

title: PRAC: Principal-Random Subspace for LLM Activation Compression and Memory-Efficient Training

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) possess broad conceptual knowledge acquired through large-scale text pretraining, yet their potential to supervise models in other modalities remains underexplored. In this work, we propose LaViD—Language-to-Visual Knowledge Distillation—a simple and effective framework for transferring high-level semantic knowledge from a language-only teacher to a vision-only student model. Instead of relying on paired multimodal data, LaViD elicits conceptual signals from an LLM by prompting it to generate multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that probe semantic distinctions between visual classes. Each class is mapped to a soft label distribution over these MCQs, forming a rich conceptual signature that guides the student through an auxiliary distillation loss. Notably, despite using a language-only teacher without access to image data, LaViD consistently outperforms recent methods like MaKD that distill from vision-language models across multiple fine-grained benchmarks. It also achieves competitive or superior performance compared to state-of-the-art visual distillation methods such as DKD and MLKD, with further gains when combined with logit standardization. On the Waterbirds dataset, LaViD substantially improves worst-group accuracy, demonstrating enhanced robustness to spurious correlations with distillation. Code is available at https://github.com/lliangthomas/lavid.

paragraphs: LaViD investigates whether a language-only model can teach useful conceptual distinctions to a vision-only model. The teacher never needs to inspect images. Instead, the framework draws on knowledge acquired through text pretraining and converts it into supervision that helps the visual student distinguish fine-grained classes, without relying on paired multimodal data.

The language model generates multiple-choice questions about semantic differences between visual classes. Each class receives a soft label distribution over these questions, forming a conceptual signature. An auxiliary distillation loss uses these signatures to guide student training. This gives the student information about relationships and distinctions among classes beyond their individual class labels.

Across multiple fine-grained benchmarks, LaViD consistently outperforms MaKD, which distills knowledge from vision-language models. It also matches or exceeds the visual distillation methods DKD and MLKD, with further improvements from logit standardization. On Waterbirds, improved worst-group accuracy supports greater robustness to spurious correlations. The findings show that conceptual supervision from a language-only teacher can transfer usefully into visual recognition.
summary.tldr: LaViD turns a language model's conceptual questions into supervision that improves fine-grained visual recognition and robustness.

title: Large Language Model Teaches Visual Students: Cross-Modality Transfer of Fine-Grained Conceptual Knowledge

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has evolved to be one of the main methods for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). However, existing RLHF methods are non-robust, and their performance deteriorates if the downstream task differs significantly from the preference dataset used in fine-tuning. In order to mitigate this problem, we introduce a distributionally robust RLHF for fine-tuning LLMs. In particular, our goal is to ensure that a fine-tuned model retains its performance even when the distribution of prompts significantly differs from the distribution encountered during fine-tuning. We formulate distributionally robust optimization (DRO) version of two popular fine-tuning methods – (1) reward-based RLHF and (2) reward-free DPO (direct preference optimization). We propose a minibatch gradient descent based algorithms for both of them, and theoretically prove convergence guarantees for the algorithms. Subsequently, we evaluate our algorithms on an out-of-distribution (OOD) task by first training the model on the Unified-Feedback dataset and evaluating its performance on two different datasets. The experimental results show that our robust training improves the accuracy of the learned reward models on average, and markedly on some tasks, such as reasoning. Furthermore, we show that the robust versions of policy optimization methods, similarly improve performance on OOD tasks.

paragraphs: Preference-based fine-tuning can lose effectiveness when deployment prompts differ substantially from the prompts represented in training feedback. This paper develops robust training methods intended to preserve performance under that distribution shift. The problem is therefore about how well learned preferences transfer to different downstream tasks.

The authors formulate distributionally robust versions of two approaches: reward-based reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization, which does not require a separate reward model. They propose minibatch gradient-descent algorithms for both formulations and prove convergence guarantees. The framework brings robustness to both learning through an explicit reward signal and optimizing a policy directly from preferences.

The evaluation trains on Unified-Feedback and tests on two other datasets. Robust training improves reward-model accuracy on average, with particularly marked gains on some tasks, including reasoning. Robust policy optimization also improves performance on the tested out-of-distribution tasks. These results provide empirical evidence that accounting for prompt-distribution changes during training can help both preference assessment and the resulting model behavior.
summary.tldr: Distributionally robust versions of RLHF and DPO improve tested performance when deployment tasks differ from the preference-training data.

title: Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a cornerstone for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models, where group-based approaches such as GRPO have emerged as efficient paradigms that optimize policies by leveraging intra-group performance differences. However, these methods typically rely on absolute numerical rewards, introducing intrinsic limitations. In verifiable tasks, identical group evaluations often result in sparse supervision, while in open-ended scenarios, the score range instability of reward models undermines advantage estimation based on group means. To address these limitations, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Relative Rewards (RLRR), a framework that shifts reward shaping from absolute scoring to relative ranking. Complementing this framework, we introduce the Ranking Reward Model, a listwise preference model tailored for group-based optimization to directly generate relative rankings. By transforming raw evaluations into robust relative signals, RLRR effectively mitigates signal sparsity and reward instability. Experimental results demonstrate that RLRR yields consistent performance improvements over standard group-based baselines across reasoning benchmarks and open-ended generation tasks.

paragraphs: Group-based reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO learn from performance differences among outputs in the same group. Absolute numerical rewards can make those differences difficult to use. Identical evaluations provide sparse supervision on verifiable tasks, while unstable reward-model score ranges can disrupt estimates based on the group’s average score.

Reinforcement Learning with Relative Rewards changes the reward formulation to emphasize rankings within a group. The paper also introduces a Ranking Reward Model that evaluates preferences over a list and directly produces relative rankings. This pairs the training framework with an evaluator designed to supply the kind of comparative signal it needs.

By converting evaluations into relative signals, RLRR mitigates both sparse supervision and reward instability. Experiments show consistent improvements over standard group-based baselines on reasoning benchmarks and open-ended generation tasks. The significance is that reward representation itself can affect learning quality: a group optimizer benefits from feedback that expresses useful comparisons among its candidate outputs, and the reported results support ranking as an effective way to provide those comparisons.
summary.tldr: RLRR replaces absolute reward scoring with relative rankings to improve supervision and stability in group-based reinforcement learning.

title: From Absolute to Relative: Rethinking Reward Shaping in Group-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning agents are increasingly used in safety-critical domains but remain vulnerable to stealthy backdoor attacks. Existing outer-loop attacks face a trade-off between perceptual stealth, poisoning efficiency, and value-function consistency, often making the attack ineffective or easily exposed. To address these challenges, we propose SpecDRL, a unified framework that (1) embeds triggers in the least sensitive subspaces of the state manifold via Subspace-Aware Injection, exploiting perceptual blind spots, (2) selects the most influential time steps for poisoning through Value-Guided Strategic Sampling based on Return-to-Go and Temporal-Difference error, and (3) preserves reward integrity via Bellman-Consistent Dynamic Reward Poisoning, which analytically enforces $\epsilon$consistency of value functions and bounds global return deviations. Experiments across 12 Atari environments demonstrate that SpecDRL achieves near-100% attack success, accelerates backdoor convergence, and maintains benign task performance.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks on reinforcement-learning agents must balance several objectives: conceal the trigger, influence learning efficiently, and avoid inconsistencies that expose or weaken the attack. This paper presents SpecDRL as a framework that coordinates those objectives across the agent’s observations, experience trajectory, and reward-based value learning.

Its first component places triggers in relatively insensitive subspaces of the state representation, targeting perceptual blind spots. A second component uses return-to-go and temporal-difference error to identify influential moments in a trajectory. A third modifies reward poisoning under analytical constraints that enforce bounded value-function inconsistency and bound deviations in overall return.

These components connect where a trigger is embedded, when poisoned experience is introduced, and how its learning effects remain compatible with value estimates. Across 12 Atari environments, the authors report near-100% attack success, faster backdoor convergence, and preserved benign task performance. The results demonstrate a vulnerability in the evaluated agents: successful ordinary behavior can coexist with highly effective triggered behavior. The stated analytical bounds concern value consistency and return deviation, while attack effectiveness is supported by the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: SpecDRL coordinates concealed triggers, influential trajectory moments, and value-consistent reward poisoning to achieve strong backdoor attacks in Atari evaluations.

title: Toward Subspace-Perturbed Trajectory-Aware Backdoor Attacks in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) relies on static datasets and often enforces conservative constraints to mitigate out-of-distribution errors, but this inevitably gives rise to learning dataset biases and limited behavioral generalization. Recent Data Augmentation (DA) methods leverage generative models to enrich offline data, yet they mainly operate within a single rollout paradigm and tend to preserve the original trajectory-level connectivity of the dataset. As a result, such methods often introduce local variations and fail to recover connections between distinct behavior patterns. In this paper, we propose Bidirectional Trajectory Diffusion (BiTrajDiff), a novel DA framework that explicitly addresses this limitation. BiTrajDiff decomposes trajectory synthesis into two independent diffusion processes that generate forward-future and backward-history segments conditioned on shared intermediate anchor states. By stitching the generated segments at these anchors, BiTrajDiff can synthesize trajectories that bridge disconnected behavior patterns and recover global trajectory-level connectivity absent from the original data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BiTrajDiff consistently outperforms advanced DA methods across a range of offline RL backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/Plankson/BiTrajDiff.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns behavior from a fixed dataset. Conservative learning rules help control errors on unfamiliar behavior, but can also preserve the dataset’s biases. Generating extra trajectories offers a way to broaden that experience. The paper argues that existing augmentation methods mostly make local variations while leaving separate behavior patterns disconnected at the level of complete trajectories.

BiTrajDiff constructs trajectories around shared intermediate states called anchors. One diffusion process generates a possible future from an anchor, while another independently generates a history leading into it. Joining these segments at the shared state can create connections between behavior patterns that the original dataset never linked. This changes the structure of the available experience, rather than only adding nearby variants of existing trajectories.

Across the evaluated offline reinforcement-learning backbones, BiTrajDiff consistently outperforms advanced data-augmentation methods. The results support its central proposition: augmentation can be more useful when it recovers connections between behaviors, giving a learner access to coherent combinations absent from its recorded experience.
summary.tldr: BiTrajDiff joins independently generated past and future trajectory segments at shared states to connect behaviors missing from offline training data.

title: BiTrajDiff: Bidirectional Trajectory Generation with Diffusion Models for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Zero-shot methods detect LLM-generated text by computing statistical signatures using a surrogate model. Existing approaches typically employ a fixed surrogate for all inputs regardless of the unknown source. We systematically examine this design and find that detection performance varies substantially depending on surrogate-source alignment. We observe that while no single surrogate achieves optimal performance universally, a well-matched surrogate typically exists within a diverse pool for any given input. This finding transforms robust detection into a routing problem: selecting the most appropriate surrogate for each input. We propose DetectRouter, a prototype-based framework that learns text-detector affinity through two-stage training. The first stage constructs discriminative prototypes from white-box models; the second generalizes to black-box sources by aligning geometric distances with observed detection scores. Experiments on EvoBench and MAGE benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple detection criteria and model families.

paragraphs: Zero-shot detectors of machine-generated text often calculate statistical signals using a surrogate language model. This paper examines the common choice of using the same surrogate for every input. It finds that detection quality depends substantially on how well that surrogate matches the unknown model that produced the text.

The authors observe that no single surrogate is best across all inputs, but a diverse pool typically contains a suitable match. DetectRouter therefore learns to select a detector for each text. Its first training stage builds discriminative prototypes using white-box models. The second aligns distances in the learned representation space with observed detection scores, extending the routing approach to black-box sources.

Experiments on EvoBench and MAGE show consistent improvements across multiple detection criteria and model families. These results support treating surrogate selection as a learned routing decision instead of a fixed design choice. The useful empirical premise is that an appropriate surrogate typically exists in the pool; the method seeks to recognize that affinity for each input.
summary.tldr: DetectRouter improves zero-shot generated-text detection by selecting a surrogate model suited to each input.

title: Minimizing Mismatch Risk: A Prototype-Based Routing Framework for Zero-shot LLM-generated Text Detection

abstract: Learning to rank can be cast as a probabilistic modeling problem over permutations, where the goal is to estimate the likelihood of an observed total ordering of items. This formulation naturally involves full-order probabilities of the form $\mathbb{P}(z_1 \leq \cdots \leq z_n)$, whose exact computation and optimization are intractable due to the factorial growth of the permutation space with respect to the list size. In this work, we introduce the Full-Order Bound (FOB), a tractable lower bound on the probability of an observed ordering, constructed from a subset of ordering constraints that factorizes across items while preserving full-order structure and order-reversal invariance. Under log-concave latent densities, the bound induces a convex inner tightening problem over latent cut points, which we solve efficiently during training using a safe-region gradient ascent (SRGA) procedure. Experiments on synthetic ranking tasks and large-scale learning-to-rank benchmarks show that FOB improves full-list ordering metrics and remains competitive on NDCG, while an optional metric-aligned variant recovers NDCG gains. Our code is available at https://github.com/tyxaaron/FOB.

paragraphs: Learning to rank can be framed as assigning probability to an entire ordering of items. Directly computing and optimizing that probability becomes intractable as the number of possible permutations grows factorially. This paper seeks a manageable training objective that still represents the structure of the complete list.

The Full-Order Bound is a lower bound on the probability of an observed ordering. It uses a subset of ordering constraints that factorizes across items while preserving full-order structure and invariance to order reversal. Under the stated assumption of log-concave latent densities, tightening the bound over latent cut points becomes a convex inner problem. A safe-region gradient ascent procedure solves that problem during training.

Experiments on synthetic tasks and large learning-to-rank benchmarks show improved full-list ordering metrics, with competitive NDCG performance. An optional variant aligned with the evaluation metric recovers NDCG gains. The results show how a tractable approximation to whole-order probability can support ranking objectives while retaining a meaningful connection to complete-list correctness.
summary.tldr: The Full-Order Bound makes whole-list ranking probabilities tractable to optimize and improves full-order metrics in experiments.

title: Learning to Rank by Directly Optimizing Full-Order Probabilities

abstract: Recent progress in multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly improved reasoning LLMs’ performances on complex interactive tasks. Despite advances in stabilization techniques such as fine-grained credit assignment and trajectory filtering, instability remains pervasive and often leads to training collapse. We argue that this instability stems from inefficient exploration in multi-turn settings, where policies continue to generate low-information actions that neither reduce uncertainty nor advance task progress. To address this issue, we propose Token- and Turn-level Policy Optimization (T$^2$PO), an uncertainty-aware framework that explicitly controls exploration at fine-grained levels. At the token level, T$^2$PO monitors uncertainty dynamics and triggers a thinking intervention once the marginal uncertainty change falls below a threshold. At the turn level, T$^2$PO identifies interactions with negligible exploration progress and dynamically resamples such turns to avoid wasted rollouts. We evaluate T$^2$PO in diverse environments, including WebShop, ALFWorld, and Search QA, demonstrating substantial gains in training stability and performance improvements with better exploration efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/WillDreamer/T2PO.

paragraphs: Multi-turn reinforcement learning can collapse when agents keep producing actions that neither resolve uncertainty nor advance a task. Better reward assignment alone may not prevent that wasted exploration. T²PO explicitly monitors exploration at both the token and interaction levels to make training more stable.

At the token level, the method intervenes in thinking when the marginal change in uncertainty falls below a threshold. At the turn level, it detects interactions with negligible exploratory progress and resamples them. These controls aim to redirect computation while a rollout is being constructed rather than merely discard poor trajectories afterward.

Evaluations on WebShop, ALFWorld, and Search QA show improved stability, exploration efficiency, and task performance. The contribution is a fine-grained mechanism for recognizing when additional generation has stopped being informative. It connects training reliability to the quality of exploratory actions, extending the stabilization problem beyond how rewards are assigned to completed trajectories.
summary.tldr: T²PO uses token- and turn-level uncertainty signals to redirect uninformative exploration and stabilize multi-turn agent training.

title: T$^2$PO: Uncertainty-Guided Exploration Control for Stable Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The Tubal Nuclear Norm (TNN), derived from the tensor Singular Value Decomposition (t-SVD), is a widely used low-rank modeling tool that promotes sparsity of frequency-domain singular values. However, as a direct extension of the matrix nuclear norm, TNN applies a uniform element-wise penalty to transformed singular values, without explicitly distinguishing sparsity across frequency components from low-rankness within each component. This can be restrictive for real-world tensor data that exhibit multi-level spectral structures, where spectral energy is concentrated in a subset of frequency components while active components remain low-rank. To overcome this limitation, we propose the tensor $\ell_p$-Schatten-$q$ quasi-norm ($p,q\in(0,1]$), which enables explicit control of dual spectral sparsity by jointly regularizing inter-frequency sparsity and intra-frequency low-rankness. This formulation includes TNN as a special case and subsumes several existing tensor regularizers by coupling global frequency sparsity with local spectral low-rankness, yielding a more flexible modeling principle. We establish minimax error bounds under the proposed dual spectral sparsity model, develop a reweighted optimization algorithm for the resulting nonconvex problem, and demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness on noisy and Poisson tensor completion as well as image clustering tasks.

paragraphs: Low-rank tensor modeling seeks compact structure in multidimensional data. The widely used Tubal Nuclear Norm penalizes transformed singular values uniformly, without separately controlling which frequency components are active and how much complexity each active component contains. This can be restrictive when only a few frequencies carry substantial energy and those frequencies also have low-rank structure.

The paper introduces a tensor lp-Schatten-q quasi-norm with parameters p and q between zero and one, inclusive. It jointly regulates sparsity across frequencies and low-rankness within each frequency, giving explicit control over both levels. The formulation includes the Tubal Nuclear Norm as a special case and encompasses several existing regularizers.

The authors establish minimax error bounds under their dual spectral sparsity model and develop a reweighted algorithm for the resulting nonconvex optimization. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness and robustness on noisy tensor completion, Poisson tensor completion, and image clustering. The contribution joins a more flexible structural model with theoretical error analysis and an algorithm for using it.
summary.tldr: A new tensor regularizer separately controls sparsity across frequencies and low-rank structure within them, with theory and practical optimization.

title: Refining Dual Spectral Sparsity in Transformed Tensor Singular Values

abstract: Neural networks are typically trained with a single learning rate across all layers. While recent empirical evidence suggests that assigning layer-specific learning rates can accelerate training, a principled understanding of the conditions and mechanisms under which non-uniform learning rates are beneficial remains limited. In this work, we investigate non-uniform learning rates through the lens of Stackelberg optimization. Specifically, we demonstrate that training neural networks with a smaller learning rate for the body layers and a larger learning rate for the final layer can be interpreted as a two-time-scale alternating gradient descent algorithm applied to a Stackelberg reformulation of the original objective. We establish finite-time convergence guarantees for the algorithm under broad conditions that accommodate constraint sets and non-smooth activation functions. Beyond convergence, we identify two mechanisms by which non-uniform learning rates can outperform uniform learning rates: (i) we show that certain problem instances induce a Stackelberg objective with stronger optimization structure than the original objective, yielding faster convergence to globally optimal solutions, (ii) our numerical analysis reveals that the Stackelberg objective can exhibit substantially sharper local curvature, especially in early training, which leads to more informative gradients and learning acceleration. Experiments in supervised learning and reinforcement learning support our findings.

paragraphs: Different neural-network layers need not learn at the same speed. This paper studies why using a smaller learning rate in the body and a larger one in the final layer can help. It interprets this arrangement through Stackelberg optimization, connecting the two update speeds to an alternating optimization procedure for a reformulated objective.

The authors establish finite-time convergence guarantees under broad conditions that allow constraints and non-smooth activations. They also identify a mechanism for faster optimization: in certain problem instances, the Stackelberg objective has stronger optimization structure than the original objective. In those instances, this can yield faster convergence to globally optimal solutions.

A second mechanism comes from numerical analysis. The reformulated objective can have substantially sharper local curvature, particularly early in training, producing more informative gradients and accelerating learning. Experiments in supervised and reinforcement learning support the analysis. The paper provides conditional explanations for when unequal learning rates help, linking the practical choice of layer-specific step sizes to properties of the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: A Stackelberg interpretation explains conditions under which a faster-learning final layer can accelerate neural-network training.

title: Rethinking Neural Network Learning Rates: A Stackelberg Perspective

abstract: Editing the content of an image with a pretrained text-to-image model remains challenging. Existing methods often distort fine details or introduce unintended artifacts. We propose using coupled stochastic differential equations (coupled SDEs) to guide the sampling process of any pre-trained generative model that can be sampled by solving an SDE, including diffusion and rectified flow models. By driving both the source image and the edited image with the same correlated noise, our approach steers new samples toward the desired semantics while preserving visual similarity to the source. The method works out-of-the-box—without retraining or auxiliary networks—and achieves high prompt fidelity along with near-pixel-level consistency. These results position coupled SDEs as a simple yet powerful tool for controlled generative AI.

We propose using coupled stochastic differential equations (coupled SDEs) to guide the sampling process of any pre-trained generative model that can be sampled by solving an SDE, including diffusion and rectified flow models. By driving both the source image and the edited image with the same correlated noise, our approach steers new samples toward the desired semantics while preserving visual similarity to the source. The method works out-of-the-box—without retraining or auxiliary networks—and achieves high prompt fidelity along with near-pixel-level consistency. These results position coupled SDEs as a simple yet powerful tool for controlled generative AI.

paragraphs: Editing an image with a text prompt requires changing its meaning while preserving details that should remain recognizable. Existing approaches can distort those details or add artifacts. This paper proposes coordinating the source and edited images during sampling through coupled stochastic differential equations, making their generative evolution depend on shared, correlated noise.

The coupling links the two sampling processes while allowing the edited image to move toward the requested semantics. This supplies a direct mechanism for balancing the requested change with visual similarity to the source. The method applies to pretrained generative models that can be sampled by solving an SDE, including diffusion and rectified flow models. It requires neither retraining nor auxiliary networks.

The authors report high fidelity to editing prompts together with near-pixel-level consistency with the source. These findings indicate that coordinated randomness can preserve detailed visual correspondence while supporting semantic changes. The contribution is a sampling-time control method whose applicability is defined by the model’s ability to support SDE-based sampling.
summary.tldr: Coupled SDE sampling uses shared correlated noise to edit image semantics while preserving fine visual detail, without retraining.

title: Semantic Editing with Coupled Stochastic Differential Equations

abstract: We dream of a future where point clouds from all domains can come together to shape a single model that benefits them all. Toward this goal, we present Utonia, a first step toward training a single self-supervised point transformer encoder across heterogeneous domains, spanning remote sensing, outdoor LiDAR, indoor RGB-D sequences, object-centric CAD models, and point clouds lifted from RGB-only videos. Despite their distinct sensing geometries, densities, and priors, Utonia learns a consistent representation space that transfers across domains. This unification improves perception capability while revealing intriguing emergent behaviors that arise only when domains are trained jointly. Beyond perception, we observe that Utonia representations can also benefit embodied and multimodal reasoning: conditioning vision-language-action policies on Utonia features improves robotic manipulation, and integrating them into vision-language models yields gains on spatial reasoning. We hope Utonia can serve as a step toward foundation models for sparse 3D data, and support downstream applications in AR/VR, robotics, and autonomous driving.
originalAbstract: We dream of a future where point clouds from all domains can come together to shape a single model that benefits them all. Toward this goal, we present Utonia, a first step toward training a single self-supervised point transformer encoder across heterogeneous domains, spanning remote sensing, outdoor LiDAR, indoor RGB-D sequences, object-centric CAD models, and point clouds lifted from RGB-only videos. Despite their distinct sensing geometries, densities, and priors, Utonia learns a consistent representation space that transfers across domains. This unification improves perception capability while revealing intriguing emergent behaviors that arise only when domains are trained jointly. Beyond perception, we observe that Utonia representations can also benefit embodied and multimodal reasoning: conditioning vision-language-action policies on Utonia features improves robotic manipulation, and integrating them into vision-language models yields gains on spatial reasoning. We hope Utonia can serve as a step toward foundation models for sparse 3D data, and support downstream applications in AR/VR, robotics, and autonomous driving.

Utonia explores whether one self-supervised point transformer encoder can learn across this diversity. Its training spans remote sensing, outdoor LiDAR, indoor RGB-D sequences, object-centered CAD data, and point clouds derived from RGB-only videos.

The model learns a shared representation space that transfers across these domains. Joint training improves perception and produces behaviors the authors observe only when the domains are trained together. This makes the combination of heterogeneous data part of the contribution: the aim is a representation that benefits from differences among sources while remaining useful across them.

The authors also test uses beyond perception. Adding Utonia features to vision-language-action policies improves robotic manipulation, while integrating them into vision-language models improves spatial reasoning. These observations support the broader usefulness of its 3D representations. The paper presents Utonia as an initial step toward foundation models for sparse 3D data, with AR/VR, robotics, and autonomous driving identified as potential application areas.
summary.tldr: Utonia jointly learns from diverse point-cloud domains, producing transferable features that also improve manipulation and spatial reasoning.

title: Utonia: Toward One Encoder for All Point Clouds

abstract: Given a generalist model, learning a task-relevant specialist representation is fundamental for downstream applications. Identifiability, the asymptotic guarantee of recovering the ground-truth representation, is critical because it sets the ultimate limit of any model, even with infinite data and computation. We study this problem in a completely nonparametric setting, without relying on interventions, parametric forms, or structural constraints. We first prove that the structure between time steps and tasks is identifiable in a fully unsupervised manner, even when sequences lack strict temporal dependence and may exhibit disconnections, and task assignments can follow arbitrarily complex and interleaving structures. We then prove that, within each time step, the task-relevant latent representation can be disentangled from the irrelevant part under a simple sparsity regularization, without any additional information or parametric constraints. Together, these results establish a hierarchical foundation: task structure is identifiable across time steps, and task-relevant latent representations are identifiable within each step. To our knowledge, each result provides a first general nonparametric identifiability guarantee, and together they mark a step toward provably moving from generalist to specialist models.

paragraphs: Turning a general-purpose model into a specialist requires isolating the representation relevant to a particular task. This paper studies whether that underlying representation can, in principle, be recovered. Its focus is identifiability: an asymptotic guarantee that concerns what recovery is possible even with unlimited data and computation, rather than a measured improvement on a downstream benchmark.

The first result concerns structure across tasks and time steps. The authors prove unsupervised identification in a nonparametric setting that accommodates disconnected sequences, a lack of strict temporal dependence, and complex interleaving task assignments. This establishes a way to recover task organization without imposing a fixed parametric form or relying on interventions.

The second result operates within a time step. Under a sparsity regularization, task-relevant latent information can be separated from irrelevant information without additional information or parametric constraints. Together, the results form a hierarchy: identify how tasks are organized across time, then identify their relevant representations within each step. The sparsity condition belongs specifically to the latter guarantee and is part of what enables that separation.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nonparametric identifiability results for task structure across time and task-relevant latent representations under sparsity regularization.

title: From Generalist to Specialist Representation

abstract: Generating realistic adversarial examples for tabular data remains challenging due to heterogeneous feature types and asymmetric inter-feature dependencies. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted constraints or undirected similarity criteria to delimit the feasible attack region, which often fail to capture the structural dependency governing tabular generation. Consequently, standard attacks typically produce perturbations that are statistically likely yet semantically inconsistent and prone to optimization stagnation via gradient masking. To address this, we propose LCSA, a white-box framework that formulates adversarial generation as optimization over structurally admissible perturbations. LCSA leverages an ensemble of heterogeneous neural Structural Causal Models to infer dependencies and introduces a structure-aware ripple mechanism. Unlike attacks that perturb features in isolation, this mechanism propagates updates downstream, acting as a structural preconditioner that conditions gradient flow to mitigate masking effects. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LCSA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in 45 of 50 evaluated configurations, yielding adversarial examples with superior structural consistency and transferability.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples for tabular data must respect relationships among different kinds of features. A change can look statistically plausible while violating the directional dependencies that make a record coherent. The paper argues that handcrafted constraints and undirected similarity measures often miss this structure, while optimization can also stall because of gradient masking.

Its ripple mechanism propagates a feature update downstream through those dependencies, so related features change together. This propagation also acts as a structural preconditioner, modifying gradient flow to mitigate masking.

Across 50 evaluated configurations, LCSA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in 45 and produces adversarial examples with better structural consistency and transferability. The result supports treating inter-feature dependencies as part of attack construction itself. Its contribution combines more coherent perturbations with an optimization mechanism designed to move through the learned structure instead of changing each feature independently.
summary.tldr: LCSA propagates adversarial feature changes through learned tabular dependencies to improve structural consistency and attack effectiveness.

title: Ripple Perturbations Through Structure: Likelihood-Constrained Adversarial Attacks on Heterogeneous Tabular Data

abstract: Inference-time scaling has recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning capability of large language models. Among various approaches, Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) has become a particularly important framework, enabling iterative generation, evaluation, rejection, and resampling of intermediate reasoning trajectories. A central component in this process is the reward model, which evaluates partial solutions and guides the allocation of computation during inference. However, in practice, true reward models are never available. All deployed systems rely on approximate reward models, raising a fundamental question: Why and when do approximate reward models suffice for effective inference-time scaling? In this work, we provide a theoretical answer. We identify the Bellman error of the approximate reward model as the key quantity governing the effectiveness of SMC-based inference-time scaling. For a reasoning process of length $T$, we show that if the Bellman error of the approximate reward model is bounded by $O(1/T)$, then combining this reward model with SMC reduces the computational complexity of reasoning from exponential in $T$ to polynomial in $T$. This yields an exponential improvement in inference efficiency despite using only approximate rewards.

paragraphs: Spending more computation during generation can improve language-model reasoning, but deciding which partial solutions deserve that computation is crucial. Sequential Monte Carlo repeatedly generates, evaluates, rejects, and resamples reasoning trajectories. A reward model guides these choices, even though practical systems only have approximations to the true rewards.

This paper provides a theoretical condition under which those approximations are sufficient. It identifies the approximate reward model's Bellman error as the key quantity governing the effectiveness of Sequential Monte Carlo. For a reasoning process with T steps, the authors show that a Bellman error bounded on the order of 1/T enables a change in computational complexity from exponential to polynomial in T.

The result establishes a conditional exponential efficiency improvement despite imperfect rewards. Its significance is that exact reward evaluation is not required for this theoretical benefit; a sufficiently controlled approximation can suffice. The error condition becomes more demanding as the reasoning process grows longer. The claim therefore connects the quality of intermediate evaluation to the potential computational benefit of inference-time search.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that sufficiently small Bellman error lets approximate reward models give Sequential Monte Carlo an exponential reasoning-efficiency improvement.

title: On the Power of (Approximate) Reward Models for Inference-Time Scaling: Sequential Monte Carlo and Beyond

abstract: This position paper argues that prompts used to deploy large language models (LLMs) in public-sector settings should be treated as governed artefacts rather than private, transient inputs. Prompts encode role instructions, decision framings, and value claims; prompt choice can materially shift outputs even when model weights and input records are held fixed. Existing governance tools, including model and dataset documentation, organisation-level policies, and post-training alignment, rarely make the local prompt collections used in deployment transparent, contestable, or auditable. We propose Prompt Commons: a versioned, community-maintained repository of prompt templates with provenance metadata, licensing, and moderation logs. Using a pilot dataset collected with community partners in a large North American city (443 human prompts; 3,317 after augmentation), we illustrate three governance states (open, curated, veto-enabled) and a negotiation-oriented ensemble method that aggregates stakeholder prompts into compromise recommendations. We close with falsifiable implications and an evaluation agenda for prompt-layer governance.

paragraphs: Prompts used in public-sector AI encode roles, ways of framing decisions, and value judgments. The authors argue that these prompts deserve formal governance because changing them can materially change outputs even when model weights and input records stay fixed. Existing documentation and organizational policies rarely make local deployment prompts transparent, contestable, or auditable.

The proposed Prompt Commons is a community-maintained repository of versioned prompt templates. It includes provenance information, licensing, and moderation records so that prompts become artifacts with an inspectable history. This makes the prompt collection itself an object of governance, bringing attention to a layer of deployment that broader model and dataset documentation may overlook.

Using a pilot dataset gathered with community partners in a large North American city, the paper illustrates open, curated, and veto-enabled governance arrangements. The dataset contains 443 human prompts and 3,317 after augmentation. It also illustrates an ensemble method that combines stakeholder prompts into compromise recommendations, then sets out testable implications and an evaluation agenda for governing this layer.
summary.tldr: Public-sector prompts should be versioned, auditable community artifacts because their framing can materially change AI outputs.

abstract: We introduce a new perceptron-based discriminative learning algorithm forlabeling structured data such as sequences, trees, and graphs. Since it is fully kernelized and uses pointwise label prediction, large features, including arbitrary number of hidden variables, can beincorporated with polynomial time complexity. This is in contrast to existing labelers that can handle only features of asmall number of hidden variables, such as Maximum Entropy Markov Models and Conditional Random Fields. We also introduce several kernel functions for labeling sequences, trees andgraphs and efficient algorithms for them.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a perceptron-based discriminative algorithm for labeling structured inputs such as sequences, trees, and graphs. The central challenge it addresses is incorporating features that involve many hidden variables. The authors contrast this goal with existing labelers, including maximum entropy Markov models and conditional random fields, that handle features involving only a small number of hidden variables.

The proposed algorithm combines a fully kernelized formulation with pointwise label prediction. According to the paper, this combination permits large features involving arbitrarily many hidden variables while retaining polynomial time complexity. These two design choices are therefore central to the stated ability to use richer features in structured labeling.

The authors also introduce kernel functions for sequences, trees, and graphs, together with efficient algorithms for computing them. The contribution includes both a learning procedure and kernels suited to its structured inputs. Its stated computational result explains why incorporating the described feature scope can remain tractable within this particular labeling framework.
summary.tldr: A kernelized perceptron labeler uses pointwise prediction to incorporate features involving arbitrarily many hidden variables in polynomial time.

title: Kernel-based discriminative learning algorithms for labeling sequences, trees, and graphs

abstract: Inference in Conditional Random Fields and Hidden Markov Models is done using the Viterbi algorithm, an efficient dynamic programming algorithm. In many cases, general (non-local and non-sequential) constraints may exist over the output sequence, but cannot be incorporated and exploited in a natural way by this inference procedure. This paper proposes a novel inference procedure based on integer linear programming (ILP) and extends CRF models to naturally and efficiently support general constraint structures. For sequential constraints, this procedure reduces to simple linear programming as the inference process. Experimental evidence is supplied in the context of an important NLP problem, semantic role labeling.

This paper proposes a novel inference procedure based on integer linear programming (ILP) and extends CRF models to naturally and efficiently support general constraint structures. paragraphs: Sequence models often need to choose an output that satisfies relationships extending beyond neighboring positions. The paper explains that Viterbi inference, used for conditional random fields and hidden Markov models, does not naturally incorporate general nonlocal or nonsequential constraints. These requirements call for an inference procedure that can express broader output structure.

The authors formulate inference using integer linear programming and extend conditional random fields to support general constraints naturally and efficiently. This makes constraints part of the output-selection problem itself. When the constraints are sequential, the formulation simplifies to ordinary linear programming, showing that the optimization requirements depend on the structure of the constraints.

Experimental evidence comes from semantic role labeling, a natural-language processing task. The contribution is an inference framework for combining a model's predictions with constraints over the output sequence. The sequential special case also clarifies that introducing a general optimization formulation does not mean every supported problem requires integer optimization.
summary.tldr: Integer linear programming enables CRF inference with general output constraints and simplifies to linear programming for sequential constraints.

title: Integer linear programming inference for conditional random fields

abstract: We present Infinite SVM (iSVM), a Dirichlet process mixture of large-margin kernel machines for multi-way classification. An iSVM enjoys the advantages of both Bayesian nonparametrics in handling the unknown number of mixing components, and large-margin kernel machines in robustly capturing local nonlinearity of complex data. We develop an efficient variational learning algorithm for posterior inference of iSVM, and we demonstrate the advantages of iSVM over Dirichlet process mixture of generalized linear models and other benchmarks on both synthetic and real Flickr image classification datasets.
originalAbstract: We present Infinite SVM (iSVM), a Dirichlet process mixture of large-margin kernel machines for multi-way classification. An iSVM enjoys the advantages of both Bayesian nonparametrics in handling the unknown number of mixing components, and large-margin kernel machines in robustly capturing local nonlinearity of complex data. We develop an efficient variational learning algorithm for posterior inference of iSVM, and we demonstrate the advantages of iSVM over Dirichlet process mixture of generalized linear models and other benchmarks on both synthetic and real Flickr image classification datasets.

paragraphs: Infinite SVM addresses classification among multiple categories when complex data may require different local decision rules. It combines a collection of large-margin kernel machines within a Dirichlet process mixture. This brings together two capabilities: handling an unknown number of mixture components and representing nonlinear patterns within the portions of data associated with those components.

The Bayesian nonparametric part handles uncertainty about how many components the mixture needs. The kernel machines provide the ability to capture local nonlinear relationships robustly. The model therefore connects flexibility in the mixture’s structure with flexibility in its classification rules, rather than treating the number of components and the form of each classifier as unrelated design choices.

The authors develop an efficient variational algorithm for posterior inference, making the combined model learnable in practice. Experiments on synthetic data and real Flickr image classification datasets demonstrate advantages over a Dirichlet process mixture of generalized linear models and other benchmarks. These findings support the proposed combination in the evaluated classification settings.
summary.tldr: Infinite SVM combines an adaptable mixture structure with large-margin kernel classifiers to model complex multiclass data.

title: Infinite SVM: a Dirichlet Process Mixture of Large-margin Kernel Machines

abstract: Differential privacy is a cryptographically-motivated privacy definition which has gained significant attention over the past few years. Differentially private solutions enforce privacy by adding random noise to the data or a function computed on the data, and the challenge in designing such algorithms is to optimize the privacy-accuracy-sample size tradeoff. This work studies differentially-private statistical estimation, and shows upper and lower bounds on the convergence rates of differentially private approximations to statistical estimators. Our results reveal a connection between differential privacy and the notion of B-robustness in robust statistics, by showing that unless an estimator is B-robust, we cannot approximate it well with differential privacy over a large class of distributions. We then provide an upper bound on the convergence rate of a differentially private approximation to a B-robust estimator with a bounded range. We show that the bounded range condition is necessary if we wish to ensure a strict form of differential privacy.

This work studies differentially-private statistical estimation, and shows upper and lower bounds on the convergence rates of differentially private approximations to statistical estimators. Our results reveal a connection between differential privacy and the notion of B-robustness in robust statistics, by showing that unless an estimator is B-robust, we cannot approximate it well with differential privacy over a large class of distributions. We then provide an upper bound on the convergence rate of a differentially private approximation to a B-robust estimator with a bounded range. paragraphs: Differentially private estimation introduces randomness to protect information about the data, creating a tradeoff among privacy, accuracy, and sample size. This paper studies how accurately private procedures can approximate statistical estimators as more data become available. It establishes both upper and lower bounds, addressing achievable performance as well as barriers to improvement.

The key finding connects private estimation with B-robustness, a property from robust statistics. Over a large class of distributions, an estimator that lacks this property cannot be approximated well under differential privacy. The scope of that statement matters: it identifies an obstacle to broad approximation guarantees, rather than asserting that every particular estimation problem must be difficult.

For a B-robust estimator whose output range is bounded, the authors provide an upper bound on the convergence rate of a private approximation. They also show that the bounded-range condition is necessary for the strict form of differential privacy they consider. Together, these results make robustness and output range central to understanding which private approximation guarantees are possible.
summary.tldr: The paper links private estimation rates to B-robustness and establishes the role of bounded estimator ranges under strict differential privacy.

title: Convergence Rates for Differentially Private Statistical Estimation

abstract: The kernel method is a potential approach to analyzing structured data such as sequences, trees, and graphs; however, unordered trees have not been investigated extensively. Kimura et al. (2011) proposed a kernel function for unordered trees on the basis of their subpaths, which are vertical substructures of trees responsible for hierarchical information in them. Their kernel exhibits practically good performance in terms of accuracy and speed; however, linear-time computation is not guaranteed theoretically, unlike the case of the other unordered tree kernel proposed by Vishwanathan and Smola (2003). In this paper, we propose a theoretically guaranteed linear-time kernel computation algorithm that is practically fast, and we present an efficient prediction algorithm whose running time depends only on the size of the input tree. Experimental results show that the proposed algorithms are quite efficient in practice.

paragraphs: Tree-structured data records hierarchical relationships, and kernels provide a way to compare such structures for learning. The paper focuses on unordered trees and a kernel based on vertical subpaths. These subpaths capture hierarchical information without relying on an ordering of sibling branches, making them useful structural components for comparing trees.

An earlier subpath kernel had shown good practical accuracy and speed, but its computation lacked a theoretical linear-time guarantee. The authors develop an algorithm that supplies that guarantee while remaining fast in practice. The contribution strengthens the computational foundation of the subpath approach by connecting its observed efficiency with a formal running-time result.

The paper also presents an efficient prediction algorithm whose running time depends only on the size of the input tree. This addresses the cost of using the learned predictor as well as computing the kernel itself. Experiments show that both proposed algorithms are efficient in practice. The resulting contribution is a more computationally dependable way to use hierarchical subpath information in kernel-based learning.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a guaranteed linear-time subpath kernel algorithm for unordered trees and an efficient input-size-dependent prediction method.

title: Fast Computation of Subpath Kernel for Trees
